I — a

## INTRODUCTION

<margin>4 30/48</margin>
When our edition of the *Thoughts* <note>original: *Pensées*, Pascal’s most famous work, a collection of fragments on Christian apologetics</note> appeared, the Hachette publishing house <note>A major French publishing firm founded by Louis Hachette in 1826</note> was kind enough to ask us to undertake the publication of the complete works of Blaise Pascal. They granted us full liberty to include not only the writings of his father and sisters, but also the documents we deemed necessary to clarify the life and labors of Blaise Pascal.

<margin>210</margin>
In this *Introduction*, we first explain the general plan upon which we have designed this edition. Regarding the portion we are publishing today—which follows a chronological order up to the *Memorial* <note>The "Mémorial" is a brief, intense record of a mystical experience Pascal had on November 23, 1654, which he kept sewn into the lining of his coat until his death</note> of November 23, 1654, representing his definitive conversion—we believed it would be useful to guide the reader through the series of documents we are presenting. We have done this by providing a brief summary of the events to which they relate and by publishing a chronological table of facts concerning Pascal, from the birth of Étienne Pascal (1588) to the closing date of November 23, 1654.

<margin>Stechert</margin>
We also indicate the sources of the texts we have gathered; we acknowledge the primary works that proved useful for this portion of our edition, while emphasizing the controversies sparked by his physical research <note>Pascal made significant contributions to the study of fluids, pressure, and vacuum</note>, whether in the 17th century regarding Descartes <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the famous philosopher and mathematician who disputed Pascal's findings on the vacuum</note>, or more recently regarding Auzoult <note>Likely referring to Adrien Auzout (1622–1691), a French astronomer and physicist</note>.

<margin>119551</margin>

<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

In the execution of this edition, the mathematical portion was reserved for Mr. Pierre Boutroux <note>The son of philosopher Émile Boutroux and a noted historian of mathematics</note>: he has published and provided commentary on the documents concerning the letter from Étienne Pascal <note>Blaise Pascal's father</note> and Roberval <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval, a renowned mathematician who held the chair at the Collège Royal</note> to Fermat <note>Pierre de Fermat, the famous lawyer and mathematician known for his work in number theory</note> (I); the *Essay on Conics* <note>original: *Essai pour les coniques*</note> (V); the *Generation of Conic Sections* <note>original: *Generatio conisectionum*</note> (XXIII); the *Dedication* with the *Notice*, and the *Privilege* <note>A legal grant from the King giving exclusive rights to publish or invent</note>, of the *Arithmetic Machine* <note>original: *Machine arithmétique*; Pascal's mechanical calculator, often called the Pascaline</note> (XI and XXXII); and finally the various mathematical treatises of 1654, the Address to the Parisian Academy of Mathematics, and the Correspondence with Fermat (LIV-LXIV).

Mr. Strowski, who has recently published an excellent psychological monograph on Pascal covering the period we are studying, has provided us with countless remarks and advice; he obtained for us the photograph of the dedication of the *Machine*, the reproduction of which Mr. Bougouin has very graciously authorized. — Mr. Gazier <note>Augustin Gazier, a professor at the Sorbonne and a leading expert on the history of Jansenism and Port-Royal</note>, a professor at the Sorbonne, was kind enough to review the proofs of our edition; we cannot say enough regarding what we owe to the inexhaustible kindness and the inexhaustible erudition that he insisted on placing at the service of this edition of Pascal; we cannot express our gratitude to him enough.

### GENERAL PLAN OF THE EDITION

We must now enumerate the successive publications that have constituted the collected works of Blaise Pascal.

Before his second conversion <note>Pascal experienced two major spiritual renewals; the first in 1646 (the "Year of the First Conversion") and the second in 1654</note>, Pascal had published only two booklets, one of 30 pages (with VI pages of preface): *New Experiments Concerning the Void* <note>original: *Expériences nouvelles touchant le vuide*, published in October 1647</note>, the other of 20 pages: *Account of the great* <note>This refers to the "Account of the Great Experiment on the Equilibrium of Liquids," describing the 1648 experiment on atmospheric pressure at the Puy-de-Dôme</note>

<page-num>III</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

...periment on the *Equilibrium of Liquids*, toward the end of 1648¹.
After his final conversion <note>Pascal's "Second Conversion" in 1654 led him to abandon most scientific work for a life of religious devotion at Port-Royal</note>, there appeared anonymously the series of *Provincial Letters*, the collection of *Briefs* <note>original: *Factums*; these were legal statements or memoirs written during the controversy over Jansenism</note> and mandates for which Pascal was one of the principal editors, and finally, under the pseudonym Amos Dettonville, the letters and treatises on the Cycloid <note>original: *Roulette*; the curve traced by a point on a rolling wheel</note> and related problems.

The year following Pascal’s death, Perier <note>Florin Périer, Pascal’s brother-in-law</note> published the *Treatises on the Equilibrium of Liquids and the Weight of the Mass of the Air*; with the same printer, Desprez, the *Treatise on the Arithmetical Triangle* was put on sale without the family’s knowledge, along with several other small treatises on the same subject. Finally, in 1670, the *Pensées* <note>original: *Thoughts*; Pascal’s most famous work, a posthumous collection of fragments defending Christianity</note> appeared, along with some shorter works, such as the *Prayer for the Good Use of Illness* (already published in 1666, in Cologne, at the beginning of a small work entitled *Various Treatises on Piety*²) and the *Letter on the Death of Mr. Pascal the Father*. By this date, therefore, and despite the revisions of all kinds that the original text had been subjected to, the essential body of the scientist’s and the writer’s work had been brought to light.

But beyond this work, there were many documents found in various collections—particularly those that Father Jean Guerrier and Father Guerrier <note>Oratorian priests who devoted themselves to preserving Pascal's legacy</note> had piously compiled or copied—which provided more direct insight into Pascal’s thought and life. Of these documents, all those whose content presented a general interest and scope found a place in the edition of the *Works of Pascal* which Father Bossut <note>Charles Bossut (1730–1814), a mathematician who produced the first major "complete" edition of Pascal</note>

2. Gazier, *Pascal’s Thoughts on Religion*, 1907, p. 517.

<page-num>IV</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

...was published in 1779 <note>This refers to the edition by the Abbé Bossut, which significantly expanded the published corpus of Pascal's works</note>: the documents relating to the Arithmetical Machine <note>The Pascaline, a mechanical calculator invented by Pascal to assist his father’s tax accounts</note>, including the letter to Queen Christina—the polemic with Father Noël <note>Etienne Noël, a Jesuit scientist who challenged Pascal's experiments regarding the vacuum</note>—the exchange of letters with Mr. de Ribeyre—the correspondence with Fermat (which had already appeared in the edition of Fermat's works published in Toulouse in 1679)—the *Reflections on Geometry*—the *Fragment of a Preface for the Treatise on the Void*, which became *On Authority in Philosophical Matters*—the theological pamphlets, such as the *Discourse Showing that There is Not a Necessary Relation Between Possibility and Power*, or the *Questions on Miracles*—and even pages written by Nicole and Fontaine <note>Pierre Nicole and Nicolas Fontaine, Pascal’s colleagues at the Port-Royal monastery</note> based on their memories of Pascal's conversations: the *Discourses on the Condition of the Great*, published in 1670 in the *Treatise on the Education of a Prince*—the *Conversation with Mr. de Saci on Epictetus and Montaigne*, which Desmolets had inserted in 1728 in the *Continuation of Memoirs of Literature and History*, Volume V.

It was reserved for Victor Cousin and Prosper Faugère, between the years 1841 and 1846, to add to all these writings—whose authentic text they restored to us—the intimate letters and two manuscripts of great interest attributed to Pascal: the *Discourse on the Passions of Love* and the *Summary of the Life of Jesus Christ*¹.

Such are the materials of which an edition is composed

The study of the Huygens collection, undertaken for the edition of the *Works of Christiaan Huygens* provided by the *Society of Natural Sciences*, allowed for the discovery in Leiden of an autograph letter from Pascal dated January 5, 1659. The study of the writings of Father Lalouère provided two fragments of letters written by Pascal (*Review of Scientific Questions of Brussels*, April 1879). We found at the National Library <note>original: *Bibliothèque Nationale*</note> two small pieces of verse which may date from Pascal's youth (Vol. I, pp. 140-141).

<page-num>V</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

...of the works of Pascal. From these materials, we have created two parts. The fragments of the *Pensées* <note>Pascal’s most famous work, a collection of posthumously published "Thoughts" on religion and philosophy</note>, gathered in the original manuscript along with the supplement provided by the *Copies* <note>Several manuscript copies made by Pascal’s family and colleagues at Port-Royal shortly after his death to preserve his notes</note>, form a whole from which we could not separate any part without making an arbitrary division. We have published them by viewing them less as a sketch for the *Apology* <note>Pascal's intended, but unfinished, defense of the Christian religion</note> than as a sort of personal journal, a summary of Pascal's intellectual life during his final years. Although they were the first to appear in print, they actually form the conclusion of Pascal’s entire body of work. As for the mass of other writings that have come down to us as distinct pieces and whose varied nature we have just recalled, they require classification and distribution according to a general principle.

The Abbé Bossut <note>Charles Bossut (1730–1814), a mathematician and physicist who produced the first major edition of Pascal’s complete works in 1779</note>, followed very closely by the first two editors of the 19th century—Lefèvre (1819) and Lahure (1858)—had organized Pascal’s writings by subject matter. However, this was because he treated the *Pensées* and the various <term>opuscules</term> <note>Small or minor literary works; in this context, Pascal’s shorter essays and pamphlets</note> as a single block; he left aside the personal letters, and was ultimately only concerned with preserving the texts without acting directly as a historian or critic. If we, in our turn, had wished to remain faithful to the tradition established for Pascal, we would have encountered several practical difficulties. For example, we would have had to decide whether the *Reflections on the Geometric Spirit* or the *Fragment of a Preface for the Treatise on the Vacuum* <note>Pascal’s defense of scientific experimentalism over ancient authority</note> should be attached to the philosophical group or the scientific group. We would have inserted into the *Mathematical Correspondence*, as Bossut did, either the letter to Queen Christina <note>Queen Christina of Sweden, a notable patron of 17th-century intellectuals</note> from 1652, or the letter to Fermat <note>Pierre de Fermat, the mathematician with whom Pascal developed the foundations of probability theory</note> dated August 10, 1660. We would have had to create—in order to relegate some of the most significant writings—a category

...of *various* minor works <term>opuscules</term> <note>Small or minor literary works; in this context, Pascal’s shorter essays and pamphlets</note>, etc.; but above all, we would have divided Pascal into a theologian and a philosopher, into a mathematician and a physicist, to the detriment of the *cultivated gentleman* <term>honnête homme</term> <note>A 17th-century French social ideal of a person who is knowledgeable, well-mannered, and adaptable, rather than a narrow specialist</note> that he wished to be, and also to the detriment of the *cultivated gentleman* he wished to have as a reader.

Chronological order, which in the current state of our information does not present insurmountable difficulties¹, offers on the contrary this essential advantage: it relates each of the writings to the precise state of mind at the moment it was composed, and thereby implicitly provides the most accurate commentary. It is this chronological order that will be followed in the present edition.

Adopting this order gave us the opportunity—which seemed particularly valuable to us—to print at their respective dates, instead of accumulating them in commentaries or appendices, the documents necessary for understanding Pascal's various writings. Thus, one will find, starting in November 1646, the original text of the letter in which Pierre Petit <note>A mathematician and engineer who collaborated with Pascal on scientific experiments</note> describes in detail the experiment on the vacuum that he had performed in Rouen the previous month in the company of the Pascals. Similarly, Pascal's letter to Perier <note>Florin Perier, Pascal’s brother-in-law, who performed the famous barometric experiment on the Puy-de-Dôme mountain at Pascal's request</note> regarding the Puy-de-Dôme experiment—detached from the *Account* <note>The *Récit de la grande expérience de l'équilibre des liqueurs*, published in 1648</note> where it was originally published and restored to its date of November 15, 1647, when it was written—will be found included...

## II

### BLAISE PASCAL UNTIL 1654.

The works forming the first series of our chronological publication extend to that decisive date of November 23, 1654, when the *Memorial* <note>A brief, intense record of a mystical vision that Pascal kept sewn into the lining of his coat for the rest of his life</note> was written. This event, along with Pascal’s submission to his spiritual director and his retreat to the outskirts of Port-Royal <note>The Cistercian abbey that served as the intellectual and spiritual center of Jansenism</note>, marks both the internal and external transformation of his life.

Without entering into every detail that the original text of the documents will provide, we intend to sketch in a few strokes the context of the pieces we are publishing.

First of all, we see Pascal’s education, beginning in Clermont within the austere environment of the <term>nobility of the robe</term> <note>French: *noblesse de robe*; a class of French aristocrats whose status came from holding high judicial or administrative offices</note>, a household saddened early on by the death of Antoinette Pascal <note>Blaise’s mother, who died when he was only three years old</note>. Then, from 1631 in Paris, he was immersed in a circle of men of science and free criticism, including Le Pailleur, Roberval, and Desargues; in 1636, Étienne Pascal <note>Blaise’s father</note> intervened alongside Roberval in a controversy against Fermat concerning gravity. It was at this moment that the children drew attention through the precocity of their intelligence: barely had Blaise cast his eyes upon a copy of Euclid than he felt himself living in the world of geometry, demonstrating to himself the first theorems of the *Elements* <note>The foundational mathematical treatise by the Greek mathematician Euclid</note>; the first verses by Jacqueline <note>Blaise’s younger sister, a gifted poet and later a nun</note> that have reached us are dated May 1637.

The following year, at the moment when Étienne Pascal was engaged with Roberval in a polemic against Descartes, he became compromised in a tumul- <note>Likely "tumultuous" (*tumultueuse*); the sentence is interrupted by the page break</note> protest...

At the end of 1639, Étienne Pascal went to settle in Rouen. Blaise printed the *Essay on Conics*, as if to mark his place among the scholars of Paris whom he was leaving. He closely followed his father’s work in a challenging post where it was necessary to struggle, from an administrative point of view, against the <term>Parlements</term> <note>In this period, French Parlements were powerful regional courts, not legislative bodies</note> stripped of their provincial liberties, and from a fiscal point of view, against populations overwhelmed by ever-increasing taxes. While Jacqueline, crowned at the <term>Palinods</term> <note>An annual poetic competition in Rouen held in honor of the Virgin Mary</note>, saw her name associated for a day with that of Pierre Corneille, Pascal invented the arithmetic machine <note>Now known as the Pascaline, one of the earliest mechanical calculators</note>. For several years, he applied his ingenuity to the practical realization of his invention. Finally, when success was achieved, he wished to use it—in accordance with the same purpose that had inspired Jacqueline—to strengthen his father’s standing. This purpose is evident, if not from the visit Pascal made in 1644 to the Hôtel de Condé in Paris, then at least from the dedication he sent the following year to Chancellor Séguier. Such was the youth of Blaise and Jacqueline Pascal: serious, diligent, always stretched toward efforts that exceeded the normal strength of their age, yet crossed and warmed by the...

...the most beautiful hopes of glory that have ever accompanied the imperious ardor of a vocation.

Starting in the year 1646, a new period opens in the life of Blaise Pascal, following two accidental circumstances. The first—in which the entire family would see an express intervention of Providence—was Étienne Pascal's fall on the ice in the month of January. This accident led his volunteer physicians, Messrs. des Landes and de la Bouteillerie, to introduce the family to the "Catholic restoration" <note>This refers to the religious movement known as Jansenism, a rigorous and austere reform movement within the Catholic Church</note>—and to lead them all to embrace it with fervor. This movement was initiated by Jansenius, Saint-Cyran, and Antoine Arnauld, and was being propagated in Normandy by Mr. Guillebert, the priest of Rouville. The other circumstance was the visit to Rouen in October of Pierre Petit, who had received word from Father Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a monk and mathematician who acted as a central hub for scientific correspondence in Europe</note> regarding Torricelli’s experiment <note>Evangelista Torricelli’s 1643 experiment used a mercury-filled tube to prove the existence of a vacuum and atmospheric pressure, challenging the traditional Aristotelian view that "nature abhors a vacuum"</note>.

From then until the end of 1651, Pascal's writings manifest a sort of perpetual alternation between scientific ardor and religious faith—an alternation all the more curious because, by the very nature of Jansenism, the latter seemed destined to exclude the former. At Rouen, Pascal took the experiment repeated by Petit as a starting point to carry out a series of new experiments. He presented these in public lectures as early as October, if we are to believe the printed dissertation by Pierius. From February to May 1647, he engaged in a stubborn struggle that mobilized the political and religious factions of the city of Rouen, in order to prevent the appointment of a former Capuchin <note>Jacques Forton, also known as the Sieur de Saint-Ange; Pascal accused him of trying to demonstrate the mysteries of faith, such as the Trinity, through purely human reason</note> to a parish in Normandy, as the man was suspected of introducing a "fanciful philosophy" into religious dogma. In Paris, where his doctors sent him to consult for his health—which was by then irremediably compromised—Pascal belonged to two different worlds. With his sister

Along with his sister Jacqueline, he is a regular attendee at the sermons of **Mr. Singlin** in the church of **Port-Royal** <note>The spiritual center of Jansenism in Paris</note>; through the mediation of **Mr. Guillebert**, he places himself under the counsel, if not the direct spiritual guidance, of **Mr. de Rebours**. In October 1647, **Pascal** publishes the *New Experiments Touching the Vacuum*; a letter from one of the most authorized representatives of scholastic physics <note>The traditional school of thought based on Aristotle, which argued that "nature abhors a vacuum" and sought explanations in metaphysical essence rather than physical measurement</note>, **Father Noël**, provides him with the opportunity to define—in opposition to an outdated and now dying metaphysics—the caution and clarity of the young experimental method. His conclusions, already suggested by the debate that the first experiments had sparked between two professors in **Rouen**, **Jacob Pierius** and **Pierre Guiffart**, and strengthened by **Roberval's** opposition to **Descartes**, find their expression in a fragment of a *Preface* that **Pascal** wrote, probably around this time, for his great *Treatise on the Vacuum*. Finally, in November—out of so many confused discussions regarding the vacuum and "subtle matter" <note>original: "matière subtile," a hypothetical substance Descartes believed filled all space to prevent a vacuum</note>, the column of air, attraction, rarefaction, or condensation, and from the meditation on the letters from **Torricelli** to **Ricci** which are, like the experiment itself, the imperishable foundation of the doctrine—one idea emerges with particular sharpness, having already been debated in the presence of **Descartes** and **Father Mersenne**: **Pascal** dictates to **Perier** <note>Florin Périer, Pascal’s brother-in-law</note> the experiment that his brother-in-law was to carry out on the **Puy-de-Dôme** <note>A high volcanic peak in central France used to prove that air pressure decreases with altitude</note> ten months later.

<page-num>XIV</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

The death of their father was to open a new chapter in the lives of Blaise and Jacqueline Pascal. During the three following years, the spiritual unity in which they had lived until then—and in which they would live again later—was broken. Jacqueline was entirely devoted to Port-Royal <note>A Cistercian abbey near Paris that was the center of the Jansenist movement, a rigorous and controversial Catholic reform group</note>, eager to fulfill what had been her sole desire for four years, yet pained to find an obstacle in her brother and to feel that this resistance was tied to financial interests. Pascal was fully immersed in the world; he sent his arithmetic machine <note>The "Pascaline," one of the first mechanical calculators, which Pascal invented to help his father with tax calculations</note> to Queen Christina of Sweden; at the Petit-Luxembourg, in the home of the Duchess of Aiguillon—who played a major role in the movement of the Fronde <note>A series of civil wars in France between 1648 and 1653 involving the nobility's opposition to the crown</note>—he demonstrated experiments in hydrostatics <note>The branch of physics that deals with the pressure and equilibrium of fluids</note>. A few months later, after the ceremony of his sister’s taking of the habit <note>The "vêture" ceremony where a novice officially enters a religious order and receives its dress</note>, he accompanied the Duke of Roannez to his governorship in Poitou; there, he was initiated by the Chevalier de Méré into the new code of "perfect honesty" <note>original: "l'honnêteté"; in the 17th century, this referred to the social ideal of the "honnête homme"—a refined, cultured, and socially adept gentleman who was well-versed in all subjects without being a specialist</note>. He did not return from Poitou until after a prolonged stay with Monsieur and Madame Périer <note>Pascal's sister Gilberte and her husband Florin Périer</note>; in May 1653, he returned to Paris, where he somewhat begrudgingly withdrew the final objections that they, from Clermont, had all three raised against Jacqueline’s formal profession of vows.

This was the critical moment of his life; Jacqueline was henceforth Sister Saint-Euphémie. Gilberte Périer was dangerously ill. He moved more closely within the brilliant and dissipated society surrounding the Duke of Roannez, including figures such as Méré, Miton, and Des Barreaux <note>Well-known wits and "libertines" (free-thinkers) of the era</note>. It was therefore impossible to give our edition a sufficiently uniform appearance without taking one of the two following paths: either uniformly transpose all the texts into the spelling system used in the 20th century, or preserve the spelling provided by the original documents as they are, and for the other texts, restore the spelling contemporary to Pascal. It seemed to us that hesitation was not possible; we have adopted the second path; the arbitrary nature it inevitably involves—and on which there is no need to insist further—is, in our eyes, mitigated to a large extent by the uncertainty and indifference of the 17th century regarding spelling. It is useless to add that we did not feel enslaved to the typographic habits of the 17th century; we do not believe that respecting the two forms of the *s* <note>In the 17th century, a "long s" (appearing similar to an f) was used alongside the standard s</note>, or the confusion of the characters *u* and *v*, or *i* and *j*, are linked to the reproduction of spelling contemporary to Pascal. Finally, the punctuation has been brought closer to modern habits whenever the interest of clarity seemed to us to require it.

In the 19th century, the history of science was understood in an entirely different way. the common view <note>The author uses "le vulgaire" to refer to the uninformed public who view history as a series of disconnected miracles rather than a continuous process.</note>, is a monstrosity for the philosopher. The philosophical conception or, as it has become customary to say for greater precision, the <term>sociological conception of history</term> <note>A method of historical analysis that views intellectual progress as the result of social and environmental factors rather than just individual brilliance.</note>, traces scientific production back to its natural and human conditions. Far from diminishing the individual work, it enlarges it by the full perspective of the past and the entire extension into the future that it can connect to it. In any case, to approach a particular debate that has stirred up so many passions and given rise to so many errors (and it was important to warn the reader, who wishes to be informed from the outset on the spirit of our edition), this philosophical or sociological conception will be the only one that allows us to avoid narrowness and partiality. It allows us to understand at once Pascal's impression of Descartes and Descartes' impression of Pascal—just as the astronomer understands both the appearance of solar motion seen from the earth and the appearance of terrestrial motion seen from the sun. It is the only view, finally, that gives hope of escaping the deafening noise of "judicial eloquence" <note>This refers to a style of historical writing that acts like a lawyer in a courtroom, trying to "win" a case for one side rather than seeking objective truth.</note> and of achieving, in the handling of texts, the disinterestedness and penetration necessary for the understanding of historical truth.

# INTRODUCTION

# INTRODUCTION

Pierre Duhem’s historical account of Pascal’s Principle <note>original: "historique de P. Duhem sur le Principe de Pascal"; this refers to the fundamental law of hydrostatics which states that pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished in every direction.</note> (*General Review of Pure and Applied Sciences*, July 15, 1905). It was an exceptional stroke of good fortune for us, at the moment we agreed to edit Pascal’s physical treatises, to find a large part of the task we had assumed already accomplished by such a master of method, science, and erudition. The faithfulness with which we have followed Duhem’s indications in our commentary on the *Treatise on the Equilibrium of Liquids* makes further elaboration unnecessary; we have merely taken it to heart to record our debt of personal gratitude here.

In the same *Review*, on the dates of September 15 and 30, 1906, Duhem provided a contribution no less thorough and no less original to the history of experiments on the vacuum. In these two articles titled *Father Marin Mersenne and the Weight of Air*, Duhem recounts the first attempts to determine the specific weight of air. He shows how, around the year 1630, Jean Rey at Le Bugue in Périgord, Isaak Beeckman in Dordrecht, René Descartes in Amsterdam, and Jean-Baptiste Baliani in Genoa, established the principle of the weight of air with irreproachable clarity. He demonstrates how they followed the consequences of this principle with such admirable sharpness (this is particularly striking in the letter Baliani sent to Galileo <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), the Italian astronomer and physicist whose work on motion and mechanics laid the groundwork for the next generation of scientists.</note> on October 26, 1630) that they deduced from it the principle of the experiments that would eventually become the Torricelli experiment and the Puy-de-Dôme experiment. Finally, we will highlight the very insightful and thorough studies published by two writers to whom Pascal also owes much: Mr. Petitot, *Where and When Was the Discourse on the Passions of Love Composed?* (*Revue des Jeunes*, January 10, 1921) and Mr. G. Michaut: *Pascal and the Problem of the Discourse on the Passions of Love* (*Revue Bleue*, February 3 and 17, March 3, 1923). It is not absolutely certain that the *Discourse* is by Pascal; however, it is the only hypothesis worth considering, given the current historical data. It remains to be seen what light the *Discourse* will shed on Pascal's inner life. The romantic episode <note>This likely refers to the long-standing scholarly speculation regarding Pascal's supposed romantic interest in Charlotte de Roannez, the sister of his friend the Duke of Roannez.</note> whose secret some historians have tried to uncover escapes us entirely. The *Discourse* will at least show how deeply Pascal was influenced by that elegant and delicate culture which, toward the middle of the 17th century, culminated in the ideal of the *honnête homme* <term>honnête homme: The 17th-century French social ideal of a "gentleman"—a person of refined taste, social grace, and versatile knowledge, as opposed to a specialized scholar or "pedant."</term>, as conceived by a La Rochefoucauld or a Méré <note>The Chevalier de Méré was a theorist of social refinement who famously influenced Pascal's transition from pure mathematics to "worldly" philosophy.</note>.

In the series of documents concerning Pascal up to the critical date of 1654 <note>November 23, 1654, was the night of Pascal's "Memorial" or definitive religious conversion.</note>, we would therefore reserve an important place for the *Discourse on the Passions of Love*. It completes the definition of the trait characterizing his formative years: this *lust for excellence* <note>original: "libido excellendi"</note>, this passion for superiority in which Pascal would later recognize—under its most refined guise—the spirit that is opposed to the spirit of Christianity. In the sciences, Pascal seeks out those who were not systematic philosophers, but pure scientists: he treats as an equal Roberval <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675), a prominent mathematician and physicist known for his work on the "method of indivisibles."</note>, who aligns so remarkably with contemporary ideas through his distrust of theoretical speculation <term>theoretical speculation: original: "spéculation a priori"—reasoning based on theory or logic alone rather than experimental evidence.</term>,

->XXX<-

# INTRODUCTION

his concern for experimental rigor, he stands alongside Fermat who was, in the opinion of a particularly authoritative judge, "the greatest of the mathematicians born in France until the end of the 18th century<sup>1</sup>." In religion, his heart is with those who, moving beyond the abstractions of scholastic theology <term>scholastic theology: A traditional method of medieval thought that emphasized logic and systematic categorization of faith, which Pascal and his circle often found too detached from personal experience.</term>, renew the drama of Redemption in their own lives and fight to return the Catholic Church to the law of self-denial and asceticism; the conversion of his sister Jacqueline showed him the nature and effect of the absolute gift of a soul to God. Finally, with Méré<sup>2</sup>, he came to understand one of the most original creations of the French spirit: social life transformed into an art form with its own rules and codes—the subject of aesthetic enjoyment that satisfies both the deepest needs and the most delicate refinements of the human heart. Through periods of oscillation and futile attempts at reconciliation, this triple experience—the scientific, the spiritual, and the social—continues until the day of his final choice <note>This refers to Pascal’s "Night of Fire" in 1654, his definitive religious conversion.</note>. But after that day, the excellence of the mathematician and the "man of the world" would serve to arm the Christian for action and meditation; it would provide the unique tone and depth to his *Provincial Letters* <note>original: "Provinciales"</note> and his *Thoughts* <note>original: "Pensées"</note>.

Following the conventions we adopted in the edition of the *Thoughts* <note>original: *Pensées*</note>, we have printed in the standard typeface—while placing them within brackets—those words which are crossed out in the original manuscript. Conversely, for the corrections we found it necessary to introduce into the text, the words (also placed in brackets) appear in italics if the surrounding text is in regular type, or in regular type if the surrounding text is in italics. The words found within brackets in the footnotes, printed in **bold**, represent the variant readings <term>variant readings: Alternative versions or word choices found in the original manuscript that differ from the final or primary text.</term> from the original manuscript.

# BIOGRAPHIES

In 1638, while my grandfather was in Paris, it happened that the government made large reductions to the annuities <term>annuities: *rentes*, a form of investment where an individual pays a lump sum to the state or city in exchange for a regular income</term> paid by the City Hall <term>City Hall: the *Hôtel de Ville*, which managed these public funds</term>; and as his primary wealth was of that nature—having sold his offices, his house, and all his other assets in Auvergne to convert them into this kind of property, which he found more convenient for his plan to remain in Paris and raise his family, a duty with which he was entirely charged after having lost his wife—he found himself very much affected by these affairs.

Many other people in Paris were in the same situation; and meetings were held regarding this subject at the home of Mr. Chancellor Séguier¹, where these individuals gathered. It happened one day, when a very significant reduction had been decided upon, that some of the gentlemen present lost their tempers; this incited others and caused a general commotion and an uproar that troubled the ministers². That very day, once everyone had left, the authorities (who had carefully noted those in attendance) sent orders to arrest and imprison in the Bastille two of my grandfather’s friends who had been at that assembly³. <meta>This page continues the account of Étienne Pascal’s flight from Paris following the 1638 tax riots. <page-num>9</page-num>
# ETIENNE PASCAL

Having been warned, he feared for himself; and although he was quite certain of having said or done nothing that could bring this disgrace upon him—as he was not capable of such things, being very moderate and very wise—nevertheless, knowing well that on such occasions one can hardly distinguish those who are in the wrong from those who are not, he believed the safest course was to withdraw to Auvergne, where he judged correctly that they would not go looking for him; and he left his three children in Paris. My mother <note>Gilberte Pascal, the author of this biography</note>, who was the eldest, might have been fifteen or sixteen years old; Mr. Pascal my uncle <note>The famous scientist and philosopher Blaise Pascal</note>, twelve or thirteen; and my aunt <note>Jacqueline Pascal, who later became a nun at Port-Royal</note>, nine or ten.

Some time later, it happened that Cardinal Richelieu, who passionately loved theater, took a whim—

---

treasurer-payer of the Treasurers of France, to whom Father Mersenne <note>A significant mathematician and monk who acted as a "clearinghouse" for scientific ideas in Europe</note> dedicated the *Preludes to Universal Harmony* (1634), Chenu and Celoron, all three, wrote Guy Patin (*Letters*, edited by Triaire, 1907, vol. I p. 134), were <note>original: "boni viri optimeque mihi noti"</note> "good men and very well known to me." Regarding the impact of these disturbances on the Parliament of Paris, we borrow the following note from the edition of the *Memoirs of Mathieu Molé*, by Aimé Champollion-Figeac (Paris, 1855, vol. II, p. 397):

> "During the hearing of March 26, 1638, the two lieutenants of Paris came to tell the Court that: last Wednesday (March 24) a quantity of people gathered again and committed several insolences and acts of violence, following meetings held regarding the non-payment of the city's annuities <term>annuities: *rentes*, state-backed investments that provided income to the middle class</term>, which tends toward sedition and emotion; and that they have caused to be imprisoned three people who are said to have given occasion for such actions. The Court ordered that the investigation and judgment of the arrested persons proceed, and issued an inhibition and prohibition to all persons, of whatever quality and condition they might be, from gathering and holding any assembly, under the pretext of payment of annuities or otherwise, under penalty of being taken as disturbers of the public peace, except for the annuitants to address the Provost of Merchants."

The Grand Chamber <note>A senior judicial body within the Parliament</note> had called for a stay of the decree; on March 29 a royal warrant <term>royal warrant: *lettre de cachet*, a private order from the King that could bypass legal courts</term> forbade the Grand Chamber from deliberating on the refusal to pay the annuities. The parliamentarians who resisted were exiled; Barillon, the elder brother of Mr. de Morangis, had to withdraw to Tours (See the *Memoirs* of Omer Talon, coll. Michaud and Poujoulat, p. 59).

My mother <note>Gilberte Pascal, acting as head of the family</note> consented to it and gave her little sister <note>Jacqueline Pascal</note>, who was made to learn her role. She performed it so perfectly in the rehearsals—at which Madame d’Aiguillon was always present—that there was no doubt they could risk having her ask for my grandfather’s <note>Étienne Pascal</note> return.

The day having arrived when the play was to be performed before the Cardinal, Madame d’Aiguillon agreed with my mother that as soon as the comedy was over, she would take her little sister and present her to the Cardinal; and that after the first friendly greetings the Cardinal offered her, she would speak to him of the matter. To make the outcome more certain, Madame d’Aiguillon notified the Chancellor <note>Pierre Séguier, the high judicial officer of France</note> and begged him to be present, and not to leave until the deed was done, and to offer his assistance¹.

The play was thus performed². The young Pascal girl <note>Jacqueline Pascal, then ten years old</note> played her character in such a surprising manner that she received extraordinary applause; for although she was ten years old, she did not look even six, because she was very small and very beautiful; and this air of youth, or rather of a child, which she possessed, was the reason that people admired her all the more, seeing her enter into all the emotions she had to express: for she was seen, for example, appearing suddenly on the stage, out of breath, overcome and frightened as if she had just learned some bad news that surprised her²; at other times weeping and distressed, and lamenting a misfortune; in short, she was the best actress in the entire play. <meta>This page continues the narrative of Étienne Pascal’s official appointment following his reconciliation with Cardinal Richelieu. It describes his administrative mission to Normandy, a province then in the throes of violent tax revolts known as the "Nu-pieds" (Barefoot) rebellion.</meta>

# ÉTIENNE PASCAL

This was, therefore, what gave my grandfather the occasion to enter this employment; and he carried it out amidst very great troubles. The tax offices had been pillaged and the collectors killed. The Parliament, which had not done its duty, was suspended, and officers from the Parliament of Paris were sent to administer justice. Troops were also sent under the command of Marshal de Gassion, who departed with my grandfather. The King then placed two *intendants* <term>Intendant: a high-ranking administrative official representing the King's authority in a province</term> in Normandy: one for the military, who was Mr. de Paris, Master of Requests, and the other for the *tailles* <term>Taille: a direct land tax from which the French nobility and clergy were exempt, placing the burden on the commoners</term>, who was my grandfather. He found matters in such great disorder that he was obliged to reform the tax rolls of every parish in the district. He remained in Normandy for nine or ten years, leaving only in 1648 when the Parliament of Paris, during the War of the Princes <note>original: "guerre des Princes," referring to the Fronde, a series of civil wars in France between 1648 and 1653</note>, demanded the recall of all *intendants*.

> “Mr. Pascal performed his duty with all possible uprightness and equity; he would not suffer his servants to receive presents, to the point that the secretary he had first taken and brought from Clermont because he was a relative, having once received a *louis d’or* <note>A gold coin introduced by Louis XIII in 1640</note> from someone, he dismissed him and would hear no more of it.

> “He possessed piety; but it was not yet sufficiently enlightened; he did not yet know all the duties of the Christian life. Like those honest men of the world, he thought he could combine ambitions of fortune with the practice of the Gospel. But God, who had designs of mercy for him and his family, permitted an accident to befall him which was the cause of his conversion.”

The details given here by Marguerite Perier <note>Étienne Pascal's granddaughter and Blaise Pascal's niece</note> are completed—and corrected—by Mr. Ch. de Beaurepaire in a scholarly memoir: *Blaise Pascal and his family in Rouen, from 1640 to 1647. Analytical summary of the works of the Academy of Sciences, Belles Lettres, and Arts of Rouen, 1901-1902.* During his stay in Rouen, Étienne Pascal was likely only the assistant to Mr. de Paris, and later to Mr. de Miromesnil, who alone held the title of Intendants of the *Généralité* <term>Généralité: a primary administrative district of pre-revolutionary France</term> of Rouen. His exact status is given to him in the account of the conferences with Jacques Forton Saint-Ange: he is the “commissioner appointed by His Majesty in Upper Normandy for the tax and collection of the *tailles*, and for the matter of the subsistence and supply-stops of the troops, and other affairs concerning His Majesty's services in the said province.”

XXVII. The Lords Intendants of justice, commissioners, are not officers of the ordinances of your State, nor the judges established by the laws of your kingdom, but ministers sent for the execution of orders conceived in Your Majesty's name to more easily provide for the account of the tax-farmer in the Generality <term>Generality: an administrative district used for tax collection</term> of Rouen.*" The funeral oration that the *Burlesque Courier of the War of Paris* <note>A satirical periodical published during the Fronde, a series of civil wars in France</note> made of it gives a fair measure of the popularity of the Intendants:

> ->Plundering in the countryside,<-
> ->Cursed little tyrants, half-princes.<-

He was a close relative of my grandfather <note>Étienne Pascal</note>, the son of his first cousin, and my grandfather loved him dearly because he had recognized in him from his youth a very great mind and a strong love and aptitude for all the sciences. Having this opportunity to bring him to his side, he gave him this commission <note>a temporary administrative post</note> which was only for a few years. And when he arrived at his home, he found in him all the qualities he could wish for in a son-in-law; thus, he married him to my mother<sup>1</sup>. He obtained a dispensation; for they were second cousins <note>original: "cousins issus de germains"</note>, and he did not pay much attention to the kinship, which later caused him some scruples, as it did my father and mother, since there was no necessity or reason to request it.

But God, through His Providence, created another occasion which allowed my grandfather and his whole family to know God and true piety. There was a priest in Normandy, in a village named Rouville, who was a very great servant of God, who governed his parish with a very solid piety, and who preached there—

they knew how to set broken or dislocated limbs; and as they were men of great wit and honor, they had studied anatomy and medicine from their youth, so as not to risk making any error by relying solely on their natural skill. When these two gentlemen had resolved to give themselves entirely to God, they each had a small hospital <note>In the 17th century, a "hospital" was often a private charitable infirmary or almshouse rather than a large public institution</note> built at the end of their park, on their lands which adjoined one another. Mr. Deslandes, who had ten children, put ten beds in his hospital, and Mr. de la Bouteillerie, who had no children, put twenty. In these thirty beds, they received all the poor who presented themselves and treated them charitably for all kinds of illnesses, being good surgeons and good physicians; but they preferred those who needed their services for the setting of limbs.

During that time, it happened one day that someone came to warn my grandfather <note>Étienne Pascal (1588–1651), the father of the famous mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal</note> that there were gentlemen in a suburb of Rouen who had given a signal to fight a duel. My grandfather immediately wanted to go there; but being unable to go by carriage because the whole city was nothing but a sheet of ice and his horses were not shod for ice <note>Horses were "shod for ice" with sharpened nails or calkins to provide traction on frozen roads</note>, he risked going on foot. On his way there, he fell and dislocated his hip <note>original: "desmit la cuisse" — literally "dislocated his thigh," referring to the hip joint</note>. He had himself carried home, and at the same time sent for Mr. Deslandes, to place himself in his hands and those of his brother. These gentlemen happened to be away, ten leagues <note>A league was approximately 4 kilometers or 2.5 miles; ten leagues was a significant distance for an emergency journey in winter</note> from Rouen. Meanwhile, my grandfather, who was their friend and had confidence in them, did not want anyone else to touch him. He sent for them ten leagues away. All these delays caused this dislocation to be very difficult to set, and it forced these gentlemen—who nevertheless set it very well—to remain for three months at my grandfather’s house, not wanting any-

My father and my mother <note>Florin Périer and Gilberte Pascal, the sister of Blaise</note>, shortly after, went to Rouen to see my grandfather <note>Étienne Pascal (1588–1651)</note>; and finding the whole family devoted to God and filled with sentiments of true and solid piety, they gave themselves to it also. They conducted themselves likewise according to the advice of this holy priest who had done so much good for the others. And my mother, having absolutely left the world and all the finery and ornaments of the world, renounced them also for her children, whom she dressed very modestly and for whom she spared nothing to provide a good and holy education.

This was the origin of all the good that has been in our family. My grandfather, shortly after, left Normandy at the time of the general revocation of all the *intendants* <term>intendants: high-ranking royal officials who acted as the King's direct representatives in the provinces to oversee justice, finance, and policing</term>, during the troubles in Paris ¹. These had on one side the coat of arms of the city, which features a Paschal lamb <note>original: "agneau pascal"; this was a symbolic play on the family name, Pascal</note>, and—

the family owed a considerable sum to Mr. Perier, who, seeing that this debt was on the verge of expiring <note>original: "prescrire"—referring to the statute of limitations where a debt becomes legally uncollectible after a certain time.</note>, wished to take some legal steps to prevent the expiration. My father went to see this treasurer to beg him not to take it ill if he made some formal notification. This man lost his temper in an undignified manner and made bitter and very insulting complaints against him in public. This was reported to my father, who said: "We must forgive a man whose affairs are in such a bad state." 

About eight days later, news arrived from Paris stating that the treasurers would be required to pay a tax of ten thousand livres <note>A very large sum; the "livre" was the primary currency of France at the time. The French Crown often levied such taxes on "offices" (government positions) to raise funds.</note>, failing which their offices would be lost. My father told this to my mother and added: "There is a man ruined; I have a mind to offer him some money." My mother said to him: "Do as you wish, but you see how much is already owed to you by that household" $^1$. He said nothing more; but the very next day he went to find this treasurer, and asked him if he had heard this news, and what he had decided to do. "I must indeed," replied the treasurer, "abandon my office, for you can well see that I will not find ten thousand francs." On the 3rd day of January 1620 was baptized Gilberte Paschal, daughter of the noble Estienne Pascal, <term>elected counselor</term><note>A magistrate in the "Election," a financial administrative district of the French monarchy</note> for the King in the district of Lower Auvergne at Clermont, and the noble lady Antoinette Begon. The godfather [was] the noble Jehan Begon, elected counselor for the King in the district of Lower Auvergne at Clermont. The godmother [was] the lady Gilberte Paschal <note>Sister of Etienne Pascal, married to François Fedict.</note> — Signed: Pascal, Begon.

My mother, named Gilberte Pascal, died three years after this third of my brothers <note>This refers to the death of her brother, likely Blaise Pascal, who died in 1662; Gilberte passed away in 1687</note>. She was born on January 7, 1620, at Clermont. My grandfather retired to Paris, as I have noted, in 1630, to raise his children. My mother, who was the eldest, was ten years old. She was married at twenty-one, and she stayed in Rouen for two years with my grandfather. When she was here <note>That is to say, when she returned to Clermont.</note>, she entered <term>high society</term><note>The "grand monde," referring to the social elite and aristocratic circles of the time</note>, as did all persons of her age and status. She possessed everything required to be well-received there, being beautiful and well-formed <note>The general hospital of Clermont-Ferrand, the universal legatee of Marguerite Perier, preserves a portrait of Madame Perier which bears a striking resemblance to the portraits of her brother. Mr. Jaloustre published a reproduction of it at the beginning of his study on the *Marriage of Gilberte Pascal with Florin Perier* (*Historical and Scientific Bulletin of Auvergne*, No. 8-9, year 1904).</note>. She was highly intelligent; she had been educated by my grandfather, who, from her earliest youth, had taken pleasure in teaching her mathematics, philosophy, and history <note>The following is what Fléchier writes of the "society" of Clermont in 1665: "The person who seemed most reasonable to us was Madame..."</note>.

<meta>This page continues the biographical account of Gilberte Pascal (Madame Périer), moving from her early life and marriage to the pivotal religious conversion of the Pascal family in 1646. ### BIOGRAPHIES

In 1646, my mother having gone to Rouen to my grandfather's house, she found all his family <term>devoted to God</term><note>This refers to the family's conversion to Jansenism, a rigorous and austere movement within the Catholic Church</note>, who granted her the grace, and to my father, to enter into these same sentiments; she therefore left the world and all the pleasures she could have had there at the age of twenty-six, and has always lived in this separation until her death.

My father and she having put themselves under the guidance of M. Guillebert, who was a doctor of the <term>Sorbonne</term><note>The prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris</note>, very holy and very skillful, he moved my mother to give up all her finery and to renounce all sorts of embellishments, which she did with a good heart; and after having remained there for two years dressed very modestly, M. Guillebert, seeing that she was obliged to return here <note>To Clermont-Ferrand</note>, told her that he had an important piece of advice to give her: it was that often ladies who give up finery out of piety put them on their children, and that she should take care not to do so, because that is more dangerous for their children than for themselves, who know the evil of it and do not become attached to it, whereas children set their hearts upon it. My mother benefited so well from this advice that having returned here, at the end of 1648, she found us—my sister who was only four years and several months old, and me who was only two years and eight or ten months; my grandmother had dressed us both in dresses full of silver braid, many ribbons and laces, according to the fashion of that time. My mother first took all that away from us, and dressed us in <term>camelot</term><note>original: "camelot." A coarse, durable fabric made of wool or goat hair, signaling a rejection of silk and luxury.</note>

Périer: the praise that the Marquise de Sablé gives her, the reputation that M. Pascal, her brother, had acquired, and her own virtue, make her very distinguished in the city; and whatever glory she draws from the esteem in which she is held and from the relatives she has had, she would be illustrious even if there had never been a Marquise de Sablé and even if there had never been a M. Pascal. (*Memoirs on the <term>Grands Jours d'Auvergne</term><note>Special judicial sessions held in the provinces to restore order and address local grievances</note>*, Gonod edition, p. 41).

She forbade our governess from visiting or allowing us to visit two young ladies in our neighborhood of our own age, with whom we spent time every day, because these two children were all dressed in finery. Her strictness on this matter was so great that at the end of 1651, when my grandfather <note>Étienne Pascal, the father of Blaise and Gilberte</note> died, she was obliged to go to Paris to settle the <term>division of the estate</term><note>The legal distribution of an inheritance among heirs</note> with my uncle and my aunt; she feared that, in her absence, my grandmother might put finery back on us, and she preferred to go to the expense of taking us to Paris with her rather than leaving us here, and she then brought us back at the beginning of 1652. She died in Paris on April 25, 1687, aged sixty-seven years and four months, and was buried at Saint-Étienne-du-Mont, with my uncle and my brother¹.

# INTRODUCTION

The biography of Pascal by Madame Perier <note>Gilberte Perier (1620–1687) was the elder sister of Blaise Pascal and his first biographer.</note> has a history, and a rather complicated one at that. In this *Introduction*, we have gathered the various documents that shed light on it.

->I<-

According to the testimony of Madame Perier, in a letter from 1682 which we publish on page 43, the first draft of the *Life* <note>Referring to *La Vie de Monsieur Pascal* (The Life of Mr. Pascal)</note> dates back to the year following the death of Blaise Pascal; it seems to have been immediately utilized in the *Preface*, likely written by Mr. Perier <note>Florin Perier, Gilberte’s husband and Pascal’s brother-in-law.</note>, for the *Posthumous Treatises* of 1663 (see below <note>original: *infra*</note>, volume III, page 267). Madame Perier adds that it was also at this time that one of the copies then circulating among Pascal’s friends was stolen; it is likely this incident that is recounted in the following letter addressed to Mr. Perier. It is signed by Bridieu. Its author was either—according to the Troyes manuscript¹—a close associate of the Duke of Liancourt, the Archdeacon of Beauvais, who was a faithful friend of Port-Royal <note>Port-Royal was a Cistercian abbey that became the center of the Jansenist religious movement, with which Pascal was deeply involved.</note>, or rather a gentleman from Limousin, a former squire to the Duke of Guise, who had defended the town of Guise against the Spaniards in 1650. He was naturally in contact with the close friend of Pascal and the Duke of Roannez, Mr. du Bois (“he was called Mr. du Bois of the Hôtel de Guise: he lived there until the death of Mademoiselle de Guise, having first been a dancing master, then tutor and governor to the Duke of Guise.” Sainte-Beuve, *Port-Royal*, 5th edition, volume V, page 469, note 1). Bridieu's letter to Mr. Perier is only dated July 28th, without mentioning a year; it must be from 1663.

1. See the Troyes manuscript, in <note>original: *apud*</note> Jovy, *Some Notes on Pascal*, page 19.

### LETTER FROM MR. BRIDIEU TO MR. PERIER.

> “I believe that you have already been spoken to on my behalf regarding the life of Mr. Pascal written by your wife <note>Gilberte Perier (1620–1687), Blaise Pascal's elder sister and his first biographer.</note>, and that you have been urged to consent to its publication; we have found it so beautiful and so edifying that we all here have judged that it would be wrong not to do so, and those who saw it in Paris have made the same judgment; and Mr. Du Bois will tell you that Mademoiselle de Guise found it admirable, both for the subject matter and for the manner in which it is written; some minor corrections have been made here which we believe you will not disapprove of once you know that they spoil nothing. If the work is not yet perfect, it will be worked on further if you so desire, and you shall be the judge and master of everything, so that it is to you and not to others that the public owes the obligation for this treasure.
> 
> “Furthermore, Monsieur, I must tell you that I had given a copy to a young man who was going to Paris, whom I believed to be a reliable man, but who was not, so that I do not know what has become of it, nor does he. It might have fallen into such hands that it could be printed without us. Would it not, therefore, be more appropriate to have the version currently in the hands of Mr. Du Bois printed, after having reviewed it and brought it to as much perfection as possible? I ask your permission for this, Monsieur, and I do so with such confidence that I hope you will not refuse me. Mr. de Roannez <note>Artus Gouffier, Duke of Roannez (1627–1696), a close friend of Pascal who shared his interest in both mathematics and the Port-Royal movement.</note> wishes it very much, as does Mr. Du Bois, to whom much deference must be given, it seems to me, in everything regarding Mr. Pascal.
> 
> “I am,
> 
> *Signed*: DE BRIDIEU.”

On October 22 [1668, in all likelihood], he wrote from Aleth, where Nicolas Pavillon <note>The Bishop of Aleth, known for his rigorous piety and support of the Jansenists.</note> resided, as is well known: "He [*the Bishop of Aleth*] has a singular veneration for Mr. Pascal, and he wanted me to tell him his entire life story, and everything I knew of him¹."

On November 4, 1668, Barillon’s intimate friend, M. Feret, the priest of Saint-Nicolas du Chardonnet, also wrote regarding Pavillon, to whom he had shared some of Pascal's fragments:

> "As he is currently still reading a dozen fragments by the late Mr. Pascal, he told me... that he had never seen anything so beautiful, and even so touching. He expressed a great desire to see them, and upon my telling him that I would ask you for them, he replied that I would be doing him a pleasure, and furthermore to give him a copy of the *Life of Mr. Pascal* which someone told him had been composed by Mme Perier²."

In 1669, M. Féret wrote from Paris:
> “A few days before leaving Aleth, the son of President Caulet <note>A high-ranking magistrate; his father was the President of the Court of Aids in Montpellier and a close associate of the Jansenist bishops.</note> sent us the manuscript of the *Life of Mr. Pascal*. ### III

These praises should have been a powerful encouragement to publish the *Life* at the beginning of the collection of the *Thoughts* (*Pensées*), the edition of which was being prepared at that time. But we know the conditions under which this first edition was produced; we know that one of the members of the “Committee” established by Port-Royal <note>The intellectual and religious center of the Jansenist movement, located southwest of Paris.</note>, Filleau de la Chaise, had written a *Preface* for the *Thoughts*, and we know the reception given to it by Madame Perier <note>Gilberte Perier (1620–1687), Blaise Pascal's elder sister and biographer.</note>:
> “We were quite surprised, when we saw it, that it contained nothing of all the things we wanted to say, and that it contained several that we did not want to say.”

Finally, we know how Étienne Perier <note>Pascal's nephew, Gilberte's son.</note> substituted for it a second *Preface*, presented as coming from Clermont, the final pages of which are borrowed from the manuscript version of the *Life*<sup>1</sup>. Furthermore, the publication of the *Thoughts* was bound to result in the renewal—under particularly delicate circumstances due to the intervention of the Archbishop of Paris <note>Hardouin de Péréfixe, who was actively pressuring the Jansenists to sign a formulary condemning their beliefs.</note>—of the matter of Pascal’s alleged retraction<sup>2</sup> <note>A controversial claim by Pascal’s enemies that he had renounced Jansenism and his previous criticisms of the Jesuits on his deathbed.</note>; this created a new obstacle to the printing of the biography written by Madame Perier.

And indeed, in 1677, when Madame Perier insisted once more on this publication, here is the curious response that her sons conveyed to her:

### LETTER FROM MESSRS. LOUIS AND BLAISE PERIER TO MADAME THEIR MOTHER.

->from Paris, March 8, 1677.<-

"It has already been some time since we spoke of the *Life* <note>The biography of Blaise Pascal written by his sister, Gilberte Perier.</note> to these gentlemen; but to each of them separately. They had given us no positive response on the matter; but they had testified to us that it was a thing of great consequence and one which required much thought. Since that time, having all found themselves together at the home of Mr. du Bois, they examined this affair closely, and concluded not to print it at all, for several reasons that Messrs. de Roannés and Nicole <note>The Duke of Roannez was a close friend of Pascal; Pierre Nicole was a prominent theologian and polemicist of Port-Royal.</note> reported to us. They all agreed that the *Life* should not be printed without including the article that we intend to add to it, and which they found very good; but they believe that this very thing must be a reason not to make it appear at present, and in the current state of affairs. This is because, although one does not speak openly of this matter, it would nevertheless signify in the minds of everyone that one maintains that Mr. Pascal did not at all retract from Jansenism <note>A controversial theological movement within the Catholic Church that emphasized original sin and divine grace; it was frequently condemned by the Pope and the French Crown.</note>, which would be making a profession of faith that would not be well received in these times, and which could even bring about the suppression of the book. But as things may one day be in such a state that all these inconveniences will no longer exist, they believe it would be good to work on the *Life* from this hour, to put it into the state in which one would wish it to appear. And for the declaration of Mr. of St. Etienne <note>Referring to Paul Beurrier, the priest of the parish of Saint-Étienne-du-Mont who attended Pascal on his deathbed.</note> one would no longer speak of it in the manner that had been projected, because apparently it will no longer be during the lifetime of Mr. the Priest of St. Etienne¹, but one could put the

### IV

The privilege <note>In this context, a "privilege" refers to a royal publishing license that granted exclusive rights to print and sell a specific book, protecting it from piracy.</note> obtained by Madame Périer for the publication of the *Life* of her brother proves that she has not given up on her project. She is waiting for a more favorable opportunity; her state of mind is revealed in three letters from 1682, preserved for us in the *Guerrier Collections* <note>The *Recueils Guerrier* are a famous set of manuscripts compiled by the Abbé Guerrier in the 18th century, containing vital documents for the history of Pascal and the Port-Royal movement.</note>.

### LETTER FROM MADAME PÉRIER TO MR. AUDIGIER.

> "I was very surprised, sir, to learn that a small memoir I wrote twenty years ago concerning several details of my brother's life, and which was stolen from me at that time, has fallen into your hands and that you have had the thought of having it printed. I am convinced, sir, that being friends as we have been for so long, you did not believe you were displeasing me in this. Thus, I have not hesitated to tell you my feelings directly, knowing well that as soon as you are aware of them, you will change your mind. It is a small work that I wrote for my family and for a few private friends who had requested it of me. However, since several copies have been published against my intention, it has often happened that people who knew me—and others who did not—believing that the public could be edified by this reading, have taken the same design as you; but as neither the former nor the latter wished to do so without my participation, I have asked them to excuse themselves from this trouble. This is because, if I wanted this piece to appear, I would do it myself and I would put it into a different state than it is currently in. Thus, no one has done it yet. But as I saw that I was often in this danger, I obtained a very ample privilege <term>privilège: A legal permit granted by the king or authorities giving an author or publisher the exclusive right to print a work for a certain number of years.</term> to use whenever I wished to print this work in the manner

### LETTER FROM MADAME PÉRIER TO MONSIEUR DE LA TARTIÈRE, LORD OF LA SERVE.

> "You are so obliging, Sir, that people have recourse to you on every occasion. Here is one that affects me deeply, and in which I most humbly ask for your help. Mr. Audigier has had the idea to print a small memoir that I wrote twenty years ago regarding some details of my brother’s life, and to add a Preface where he wants to insert things that are very false and which are against my brother’s honor. These are calumnies <note>False and malicious statements intended to damage a person's reputation.</note> that have been circulating for a long time and about which you have no doubt heard. You well understand, Sir, that I cannot suffer it; thus I would be obliged to act against him by every possible means to prevent it. He is a person for whom I have always had much consideration and a particular attachment for his whole family. I would take very great displeasure in coming to that <note>Meaning, resorting to legal action or a public quarrel.</note>; this is why, Sir, I take the liberty of addressing you to earnestly beseech you to intervene in a matter that would have troublesome consequences. I have a privilege <term>privilège: a legal license from the King giving an author or publisher the exclusive right to print a specific work</term> that I would certainly make good use of. I know your prudence; therefore I expect everything from you. You will thereby render a service to Mr. Audigier and you will acquire from me a very close obligation; I will add it to so many others for which I am indebted to you. I am waiting for the conclusion of my affairs to express to you all at once my sentiments and a very humble gratitude; but these are only words that I beg you to regard as very sincere, and to do me the grace of believing that one cannot be more perfectly and with more respect than I am,
->Sir,<-
->yours, etc.<-
->G. PASCAL.<-

With your permission, I will here assure your sister of my very humble service (*Copied from the original*).

> “You will perhaps be surprised by the liberty I take in writing to you on the same subject about which Madame Perier <note>Gilberte Périer, Blaise Pascal's sister and author of the memoir in question.</note> is also writing to you; for the consideration I know you have for her merit, and for the great interest that obliges her to make this request of you, should persuade me that nothing from me could move you as much as her plea and her reasons. ### V

In 1684, finally, a 49-page pamphlet and a reprint of the *Thoughts* <note>Pascal’s *Pensées*, his famous unfinished defense of the Christian religion.</note>, both published by the bookseller A. Wolfgang of Amsterdam—or at least bearing that name—offered to the public the *Life of Blaise Pascal*, without raising any of the unfortunate incidents that had been feared. On the contrary, a remarkable article that Pierre Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a prominent philosopher and pioneer of the Enlightenment, known for his critical and skeptical approach.</note> inserted in the month of December in the *News of the Republic of Letters* <note>Original title: *Nouvelles de la République des Lettres*, one of the first major scholarly and literary journals.</note> confirmed the edifying character the biographer had intended to give to his narrative:

> “A hundred volumes of Sermons,” he wrote, “are not worth that life, and are much less capable of disarming the ungodly. The extraordinary humility and devotion of Mr. Pascal mortify the libertines <term>libertine: in the 17th century, this term referred to "free-thinkers" or skeptics who rejected traditional religious morality and dogma.</term> more than if a dozen Missionaries were unleashed upon them. They can no longer tell us that only small minds have piety; for they are shown the most advanced piety in one of the greatest Geometers, one of the most subtle Metaphysicians, and one of the most penetrating minds to have ever been in the world. The piety of such a Philosopher should make the irreligious and the libertines say what a certain Diocles <note>A philosopher mentioned in ancient texts as a contemporary of Epicurus.</note> said one day upon seeing Epicurus <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who founded Epicureanism; his presence in a temple was seen as surprising given his views on the gods.</note> in a temple: ‘What a festival,’ he cried out, ‘what a spectacle for me, to see Epicurus

> "...in a temple! From 1687 onwards, the successive editions of the *Thoughts* <note>Pascal's *Pensées*, his famous posthumous collection of reflections on religion and philosophy.</note> published by Desprez all contain the *Life* as it had been printed, without the additions that the family still intended to make to it, and also without the corrections required by the faulty Amsterdam printing. It was only in 1898 that Mr. Gazier gave us a correct text of the printed version. See the article in the *Review of French Literary History*, October 1898, and the edition of the *Thoughts* at the French Society of Printing and Bookselling, Paris, 1907.

IV, p. 469), that there existed another manuscript draft of the *Life of Blaise Pascal*. <meta>This page transitions from the editor's bibliographical introduction to the primary text of the biography. It begins with the official record of Blaise Pascal’s baptism followed by the opening of the "Life of Blaise Pascal" written by his sister, Gilberte Périer.</meta>

*On the 27th day of June, 1623, was baptized Blaise Pascal, son of the noble Etienne Pascal, elected councilor for the King in the district of Auvergne, at Clermont; and of the noble lady Antoinette Begon; the godfather, the noble Blaise Pascal, councilor to the King in the seneschal's jurisdiction and presiding court of Auvergne, in the said Clermont¹, the godmother, Lady Antoinette de Fontfreyde².*

*In the register, Pascal and Fontfreyde have signed³.*

My brother was born at Clermont, on the 19th of June in the year sixteen hundred and twenty-three. My father was named Etienne Pascal, President of the <term>Court of Aides</term> <note>A sovereign financial court of the Old Regime that handled cases related to taxes and customs.</note>; and my mother, Antoinette Begon. As soon as my brother reached an age where one could speak to him, he gave signs of a quite extraordinary mind through the little witty repartees he made so aptly, but even more so by the questions he asked regarding the nature of things, which surprised everyone. This beginning, which gave such great hope, never wavered; for as he grew, he always increased in the strength of his reasoning, such that he was always far beyond his age.

However, my mother died as early as the year 1626, when my brother was only three years old; my father, finding himself alone, applied himself more strenuously to the care of his family; and

### BLAISE PASCAL

He decided from then on to instruct him himself, as he did; my brother never attended a **college** <note>In 17th-century France, a *collège* was a secondary school, typically run by religious orders like the Jesuits, where boys studied the humanities.</note>, and never had any other master but my father.

In the year 1631, my father retired to Paris, where he brought us all and established his residence. My brother, who was then only eight years old, received a great advantage from this retreat in view of the plan my father had for raising him; for there is no doubt that he could not have taken the same care in the Province <note>Referring to Auvergne, where the family lived previously.</note>, where the duties of his office and the constant company of those who visited him would have greatly distracted him. But, as he was in Paris with complete freedom, he applied himself entirely to it; and he had all the success that could come from the care of a father as intelligent and affectionate as one could possibly be.

His principal maxim in this education was to keep this child *above his work*; it was for this reason that he did not want to teach him Latin until he was twelve years old, so that he might do so with greater ease. During this interval, he did not leave him idle; for he conversed with him about all the things of which he saw him capable. He showed him in general what languages were; he showed him how they had been reduced to grammars under certain rules; that these rules also had exceptions that had been carefully noted; and that thus a means had been found through this to make all languages communicable from one country to another. This general idea cleared his mind and showed him the reason for the rules of grammar; so that, when he came to learn it, he knew why he was doing so.

After this knowledge, my father gave him more; he often spoke to him about the extraordinary effects of nature, such as gunpowder and other things that are surprising when one considers them. My brother took great pleasure in these conversations, but he wanted to know the reason for all things; and as reasons are not all known, when my father did not tell them to him, or told him only those commonly cited—which are properly nothing but excuses <note>The original French word *defaittes* (défaites) here refers to "evasions" or "poor excuses" used to dodge a difficult question.</note>—this did not satisfy him. For he always possessed an admirable clarity of mind for discerning the false; and one can say that always and in all things, truth was the only object of his mind, since nothing ever could or did satisfy him except the knowledge of it. Thus from his childhood, he could yield only to what appeared evidently true to him; so that when he was not given good reasons, he sought them himself; and once he had applied himself to something, he would not leave it until he had found a reason that could satisfy him.

Once, among other instances, someone at the table happened to strike a ceramic <term>fayence</term> <note>A type of glazed earthenware or pottery.</note> dish with a knife. He noticed that it made a loud sound, but as soon as a hand was placed upon it, the sound stopped. He wanted to know the cause at that very moment, and this experience led him to perform many others regarding sounds. He noticed so many things that he wrote a treatise on the subject at the age of eleven, which was found to be quite well-reasoned¹.
