# BLAISE PASCAL

His genius for geometry began to appear when he was only twelve<note>The original French text notes a transcription error in the Mazarine manuscript which incorrectly listed his age as twenty-two.</note> years old, and by an occurrence so extraordinary that it seems to me well worth being detailed in particular.

My father was learned in Mathematics, and through that, he was acquainted with all the skilled people in that science, who were often at his house; but as he intended to instruct my brother in languages, and as he knew that mathematics is something that fills and satisfies the mind a great deal, he did not want my brother to have any knowledge of it, for fear that it would make him negligent in Latin and the other languages in which he wished him to become perfect. For this reason, he had locked away<note>The original manuscript uses "serré" (locked away), though some transcriptions mistakenly read "fermé" (closed).</note> all the books that dealt with it, and he refrained from speaking of it with his friends in his presence. However, this precaution did not prevent the child's curiosity from being excited; so much so that he often begged my father to teach him Mathematics; but he refused him, offering it only as a reward. He promised him that as soon as he knew Latin and Greek, he would teach it to him. My brother, seeing this resistance, asked him one day what this science was, and what it dealt with. My father told him in general that it was the means of making accurate figures, and of finding the proportions they have between one another, and at the same time forbade him to speak of it any further, or to ever think of it. But that mind, which could not remain within those boundaries, as soon as it had this simple opening,

Since <term>Mathematics</term> provided the means to create figures that were infallibly accurate, he began to dream of it himself during his hours of recreation. Being alone in a room where he was accustomed to amuse himself, he would take pieces of charcoal and draw figures on the floor tiles, seeking the means, for example, to make a perfectly round circle, or a triangle whose sides and angles were equal. He discovered all of this on his own; then he sought the proportions of the figures between one another. 

But as my father’s care had been so great as to hide all these things from him, he did not even know their names. He was constrained to invent them for himself: he called a circle a "round," a line a "bar," and so on for the others. After these names, he created <term>axioms</term> <note>self-evident truths that require no proof</note>, and finally, he constructed perfect demonstrations. As one proceeds from one thing to another in these matters, he pushed his research so far that he reached the thirty-second proposition of the first book of Euclid. 

While he was occupied with this, my father happened to enter the room where he was, without my brother hearing him. He found him so intensely focused that it was a long time before he noticed his arrival. It is hard to say who was more surprised: the son, to see his father because of the express prohibition he had been given; or the father, to see his son in the midst of all these things. But the father’s surprise was much greater when, having asked him what he was doing, the boy told him he was seeking a certain thing, which was the thirty-second proposition of the first book of Euclid. <margin>This is the proposition often used as the standard example of a geometric theorem: *The sum of the angles of a triangle is equal to two right angles.* <note>original: "La somme des angles d’un triangle est égale à deux angles droits."</note></margin> My father asked him what had made him think of seeking that. Consequently, it took him two years to bring it to the perfection in which it now exists.

But this fatigue, combined with the delicate state of his health for several years, threw him into infirmities that never left him; so much so that he told us sometimes that since the age of eighteen, he had not passed a single day without pain. Nevertheless, as his infirmities were not always of equal violence, as soon as he had a little rest and relief, his mind immediately turned to seeking something new.

Thus this mind, so great, so vast, and so filled with curiosity, which sought with such care the cause and the reason for everything, was at the same time submissive to all matters of Religion like a child; and this simplicity reigned in him all his life: so much so that, even from the time he resolved to pursue no other study than that of religion, he never applied himself to the curious questions of Theology <note>referring to speculative or abstract academic debates</note>, and he put all the strength of his mind into knowing and practicing the perfection of Christian morality, to which he consecrated all the talents that God had given him, having done nothing else in all the rest of his life but meditate on the law of God day and night.

But although he had not made a particular study of Scholasticism <note>the formal, logic-based system of theology and philosophy taught in medieval European universities</note>, he was nevertheless not ignorant of the Decisions of the Church against the heresies which have been invented by the subtlety and the wandering of the human mind; and it was against these sorts of inquiries that he was most animated; and God gave him from that time an occasion to show the zeal he had for Religion.

He was at that time in Rouen, where my father was employed in the service of the King <note>Pascal's father, Étienne, was a high-ranking tax administrator</note>, and there was also at this same time a man¹ who was teaching a new philosophy that attracted all the curious. My brother, having been urged by two young men who were his friends, went with them; but they were quite surprised, in the conversation they had with this man, that while explaining the principles of his philosophy to them, he drew conclusions regarding points of faith that were contrary to the decisions of the Church. He proved through reasoning that the body of Jesus Christ was not formed from the blood of the Holy Virgin, but from another matter created specifically for that purpose, and several other similar things. They tried to contradict him, but he remained firm in his opinions. Consequently, having considered among themselves the danger there was in allowing a man with such erroneous views the freedom to instruct the youth, they resolved to first warn him, and then to denounce him if he resisted their advice. That is exactly what happened, for he looked upon their advice with contempt; so they believed it was their duty to denounce him to My Lord of Belley², who was at that time performing Episcopal functions in the Diocese of Rouen, by commission of the Archbishop. Mr. de Belley sent for this man, and, having questioned him, was deceived by an equivocal confession of faith that the man wrote and signed with his own hand; furthermore, the Bishop made little of a warning of such importance given to him by three young men.

It was also quite true that there had been no design to harm him, nor any other views than to disabuse him and prevent him from seducing young people who would not have been capable of discerning the true from the false in such subtle questions.

As she possessed great wit, as soon as God had turned her heart, she understood—just as my brother did—everything he said regarding the holiness of the Christian Religion; and being unable to endure the imperfection in which she believed herself to live while in the world, she became a nun in a very austere house at Port-Royal-des-Champs <note>A famous Cistercian abbey and center of the Jansenist movement, known for its rigorous devotion</note>. She died there at only thirty-six years of age, after having served in the most difficult offices and thus exhausting herself in a short time through a merit that others would only acquire after many years.

My brother was then twenty-four years old. His infirmities had always increased significantly, and they reached the point where he could no longer swallow any liquid unless it was hot, and even then, he could only do so drop by drop. But as he suffered, in addition to this, an almost unbearable headache, a burning in his intestines, and many other ailments, the doctors ordered him to take a purgative every other day for three months. Consequently, it was necessary to take all the medicines in the only manner he was capable: that is, to have them heated and to swallow them drop by drop. This was a true torture, and those who were near him were horrified just by seeing it; but my brother never complained of it; he looked upon all of this as a gain for himself. For as he no longer recognized any science other than that of virtue, and as he knew that virtue is perfected in infirmities <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:9: "My strength is made perfect in weakness"</note>, he joyfully made a sacrifice of his penance out of all his pains; re—

Highlighting in all things the advantages of Christianity, he often said that in former times his ailments diverted him from his studies, which caused him great distress; but that a Christian finds value in everything, and in suffering even more particularly, because therein one comes to know Jesus Christ crucified <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:2, emphasizing spiritual wisdom over worldly knowledge</note>, who must be the entirety of a Christian’s knowledge and the sole glory of his life.

The continuation of these remedies, along with others he was made to practice, brought him some relief, but not perfect health; so much so that the physicians believed that to recover entirely, he must renounce all mental occupation that required sustained focus, and that he should seek as much as possible opportunities to divert himself with something that would occupy him and be agreeable to him; that is to say, in a word, the ordinary conversations of the world. For there were no other diversions suitable for my brother, but what means is there for a man as moved by grace as he was to resolve to do so! Indeed, there was much difficulty at first; but he was so pressed from all sides that he finally yielded to the specious reasoning of restoring his health; they persuaded him that health is a trust of which God wishes us to take care.

This was the time of his life most poorly spent; for, although by the mercy of God he was preserved from vices, nonetheless, it was always the atmosphere of the world, which is very different from that of the Gospel. God, who demanded of him a greater perfection, did not wish to leave him there any longer, and for that purpose He used my sister <note>Jacqueline Pascal, who had entered the convent at Port-Royal</note> to withdraw him, just as He had formerly used my brother to withdraw my sister from the engagements she had in the world.

Ever since she had entered the Religious life <note>referring to Jacqueline Pascal entering the convent of Port-Royal</note>, she had increased in fervor every day, and all her sentiments breathed nothing but an unreserved holiness; this is why she could not endure that the one to whom she was indebted, after God, for the graces she enjoyed, should not himself be in possession of those same graces. As my brother saw her often, she also spoke to him often, and finally she did so with such force that she persuaded him of what he had first persuaded her: to leave the world and all worldly conversations, of which even the most innocent are but continual vanities, entirely unworthy of the holiness of Christianity to which we are all called and of which Jesus Christ has given us the example.

The excuse of his health, which had influenced him previously, appeared so pitiful to him that he was ashamed of it himself. The light of true wisdom made him see clearly that Salvation must be preferable to all things, and that it was false reasoning to dwell upon a passing good of our body when it concerned the eternal good of our soul.

Finally, he always acted by principles in all things; his mind and his heart, fashioned as they were, could not have any other conduct. Thus, those principles which he set for himself in his retreat were the solid maxims of true piety: one being to renounce all pleasures, and the other to also renounce all kinds of superfluities <note>excesses or luxuries beyond what is necessary for survival</note>.

To begin the practice of the first maxim, he started from that moment—as he always did thereafter <gloss>original: "du depuis" in manuscript F</gloss>—to do without the service of domestic servants as much as he possibly could. He made his own bed, he went to fetch his own dinner in the kitchen, he brought back his own dishes, and finally, he only made use of his staff <gloss>The printed text adds: "only to do the cooking, to go into town, and for other things..."</gloss> for those things which he absolutely could not do himself.

It was not possible for him to avoid using his senses; but, when he was obliged by necessity to give them some pleasure, he possessed a marvelous skill for diverting his mind so that it took no part in it. We never heard him praise the food served to him while eating; and when care had been taken at times to serve him something more delicate <gloss>The 1684 text reads: "new according to the seasons"</gloss>, if he was asked if he had found it good, he said simply:

> "You should have warned me beforehand, for now I no longer remember it, and I confess to you that I did not pay it any attention."

Although he only engaged in these conversations for reasons of pure charity, and although he kept a close watch over himself so as not to lose anything of what he endeavored to acquire in his retreat, he nevertheless felt some distress. He feared that self-love <note>original: "l'amour propre"; in 17th-century spirituality, this refers to a prideful or ego-driven attachment to oneself</note> might cause him to take some pleasure in these conversations, and his rule was to take part in nothing where this principle had the slightest share. He rightly apprehended that this lack of occupation, which is the root of all evil, might turn him away from his spiritual goals; and to keep himself always alert, he had, as it were, incorporated this voluntary enemy which, by stinging his body, incessantly excited his spirit to remain in fervor, and thus gave him the means of an assured victory. But all this was so secret that we knew nothing of it at all, and we only learned of it after his death from a person of very great virtue whom he loved and to whom he had been obliged to tell it for reasons that concerned her personally.

This was like the center of his heart, and where he found his joy and all the rest of his retreat. # BLAISE PASCAL

Holy Scripture was not a science <insert>of the</insert> mind, but of the heart, and that it was only intelligible to those who have a righteous heart, while all others found nothing but obscurity within it. He believed that the veil which covers the Scriptures for the Jews is also there for bad Christians; and that charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to *caritas*, or divine love, rather than just almsgiving.</note> was not only the object of the Scripture, but was also its gateway. He went further, saying also that one was well-disposed to understand the Holy Scriptures when one hated oneself and loved the mortified life of Jesus Christ. It was with these dispositions that he <insert>read the Holy Scripture,</insert> and he had applied himself to it so strongly that he knew almost all of it by heart. Consequently, one could not misquote it to him; he would say positively, "that is not from Scripture" <insert>or: "*that is from it*"</insert> and would precisely mark the location. Generally, he mastered everything that could serve to give him a perfect understanding of all truths, both of faith and of morality.

He possessed such an admirable turn of mind that he embellished everything he said. Although he learned many things from books, once he had digested them in his own manner, they appeared entirely different, because he always knew how to express them in the exact way necessary for them to enter into the human mind.

<meta>This page continues a biographical sketch, focusing on the subject's unique rhetorical philosophy and psychological approach to communication.</meta>

# BIOGRAPHIES

He possessed a naturally extraordinary turn of mind; but he had established for himself quite particular rules of eloquence <note>The art of persuasive speaking or writing</note>, which further enhanced his talent. It was not at all what one calls "beautiful thoughts," which possess only a false brilliance and signify nothing; never great, empty words; and few metaphorical expressions, nothing obscure nor harsh, nor overbearing, nor omitted, nor superfluous. Instead, he conceived of eloquence as a means of saying things in a manner that all those to whom one speaks might understand them without difficulty and with pleasure. He understood that this art consisted of certain arrangements that must exist between the mind and the heart of those to whom one speaks on one side, and the thoughts and expressions one employs on the other; but that these proportions only adjust themselves properly through the specific "turn" or phrasing one gives them.

It was for this reason that he had deeply studied the human heart and mind; he knew all their inner workings <note>original: "ressorts" — literally the springs or mechanisms of a machine</note> perfectly well. When he thought of something, he would put himself in the place of those who were meant to hear it; and examining whether all the proportions were present, he would then see what "turn" he needed to give them. He was never satisfied until he saw clearly that the one was so perfectly made for the other—that is to say, that what he had thought was so suited to the mind of the person he was to see—that when the two were joined by the application of his words, it would be impossible for the human mind not to surrender to it with pleasure.

What was small, he did not make large; and what was large, he did not make small. It was not enough for him that a thing appeared beautiful; it had to be appropriate to the subject, having nothing superfluous, but also nothing lacking. Finally, he was such a master of his style that he said everything he wished, and his discourse always achieved the effect he had intended. And this manner...

# BLAISE PASCAL

His way of writing—simple, precise, pleasing, powerful, and natural all at once—was so uniquely his own that as soon as the *Provincial Letters* <note>A series of eighteen letters published by Pascal under the pseudonym Louis de Montalte, defending Jansenist doctrines against the Jesuits.</note> appeared, people judged correctly that they were by him, despite the great care he took to hide this even from his closest relatives.

It was at that time that it pleased God to heal my daughter of a lacrimal fistula <note>A chronic, painful abscess of the tear duct.</note>, from which she had suffered for three and a half years. This fistula was of such a malignant nature that the most skilled surgeons in Paris judged it incurable. In the end, God reserved her healing for the touch of a Holy Thorn <note>A relic believed to be a thorn from the crown of Jesus, kept at the convent of Port-Royal.</note> which is at Port-Royal; and this miracle was attested to by several surgeons and physicians, and authorized by the solemn judgment of the Church.

My daughter was my brother’s goddaughter; but he was more deeply moved by this miracle because God was glorified by it, and because it occurred at a time when faith in most of the world was mediocre. The joy he felt was so great that he was completely permeated by it¹; and as his mind never occupied itself with anything without much reflection, this particular miracle gave rise to several very important thoughts on miracles in general.

<margin>¹ The 1684 text contains, instead of the development on the *Pensées*, these simple lines: "so that with his mind entirely occupied by it, God inspired in him an infinite number of admirable thoughts on miracles, which, giving him new light on religion, redoubled the love and respect he had always held for it. 
'And this was the occasion that gave birth to an extreme desire he had to work on refuting the principal and strongest arguments of the atheists. He had studied them with great care, and had employed his whole mind in seeking the means to convince them. This is what he had devoted himself to entirely, and the last year of his work was spent collecting various thoughts on this subject; but God, who had inspired this design and all these thoughts, did not permit him to bring it to perfection, for reasons unknown to us."</margin>

<meta>This page continues the biographical account of the subject's intellectual and spiritual defense of Christianity, specifically focusing on his logical proofs for the existence of God and the divinity of Christ through miracles.</meta>

general, as much of the Old as of the New Testament. If there are miracles, there is therefore something above what we call nature; the consequence is one of common sense; one only has to ensure the certainty and the truth of the miracles. Now, there are rules for this, which are also rooted in common sense, and these rules are found to be accurate for the miracles found in the Old Testament. These miracles are therefore true. There is, therefore, something above nature.

But these miracles also bear marks showing that their principle is God; and those of the New Testament in particular, show that he who performed them was the Messiah whom men were to expect. Therefore, just as the miracles of both the Old and the New Testament prove that there is a God, those of the New in particular prove that Jesus Christ was the true Messiah.

He disentangled all of this with an admirable light, and when we heard him speak, and as he unfolded all the circumstances of the Old and New Testaments where these miracles were reported, they appeared clear to us. One could not deny the truth of these miracles, nor the consequences he drew from them for the proof of God and the Messiah, without clashing with the most common principles upon which all things regarded as indubitable are assured. Some of his thoughts on this have been collected, but it is little, and I would believe myself obliged to expand further to shed more light on it, according to all we heard him say, if one of his friends had not given us a dissertation on the works of Moses, where all this is admirably well disentangled and in a manner that would not be unworthy of my brother¹.

->BLAISE PASCAL<-

I refer you, therefore, to that work, and I add only what is important to report here: that all the various reflections my brother made regarding miracles gave him much new enlightenment concerning religion. Since all truths are drawn from one another, it was enough that he applied himself to one; the others came to him in a crowd, and unfolded in his mind in a manner that—as he often told us—carried him away. It was on this occasion that he felt so moved against the atheists that, seeing in the insights God had given him the means to convince and confound them without recourse, he applied himself to this work. The fragments of it that have been collected <note>A reference to the posthumous collection known as the *Pensées*.</note> cause us much regret that he was not able to assemble them himself and, with all that he could have added further, create a composition of perfect beauty. He was certainly very capable of it; but God, who had given him all the intellect necessary for such a great design, did not give him enough health to bring it to such perfection.

He intended to show that the Christian Religion had as many marks of certainty as the things received in the world as the most indubitable. He did not use metaphysical proofs for this purpose; it was not that he believed them to be contemptible when they were properly brought to light, but he said that they were too far removed from the ordinary reasoning of men; that not everyone was capable of them, and that for those who were, they served only for a moment, for an hour later they would not know what to say of them and they feared—

He also said that these kinds of proofs can only lead us to a speculative knowledge of God; and that to know God in this manner was the same as not knowing Him at all. Nor did he feel he should make use of the ordinary arguments taken from the works of nature; he respected them, however, because they were consecrated by Holy Scripture and conformed to reason, but he believed that they were not sufficiently suited to the spirit and the disposition of the heart of those whom he intended to convince. He had noticed through experience that far from winning them over by this means, nothing was more capable, on the contrary, of repelling them and stripping them of the hope of finding the truth, than to claim to convince them only by these kinds of reasonings against which they have so often <gloss>stiffened themselves</gloss> <note>The original French "roidis" implies a stubborn or rigid resistance.</note> that the hardening of their hearts has rendered them deaf to this voice of nature; and that finally, they were in a blindness from which they could not emerge except through Jesus Christ, outside of whom all communication with God is taken away from us, because it is written: *that no one knows the Father except the Son and he to whom it pleases the Son to reveal Him.* <note>original: "que personne ne connoist le Pere que le Fils et celui à qui il plaist au Fils de le reveler." A translation of Matthew 11:27.</note>

The Divinity of the Christians does not consist merely in a God who is simply the author of geometric truths and the order of the elements; that is the portion of the pagans. It does not consist in a God who exercises his providence over the lives and the goods of men, to give them a happy succession of years; that is the portion of the Jews. But the God of Abraham and of Jacob, the God of the Christians, is a—

<meta>This page continues Pascal's reflections on the nature of the Christian God, contrasting true spiritual knowledge with mere intellectual recognition.</meta>

<page-num>77</page-num>
# BLAISE PASCAL

A God of love and consolation: this is a God who fills the soul and the heart of those whom He possesses. He is a God who makes them feel inwardly their own misery and His infinite mercy; who unites Himself with the depths of their soul; who fills them with humility, faith, confidence, and love; who renders them incapable of any other end but Himself. The God of the Christians is a God who makes the soul feel that He is its only good; that all its rest is in Him, that it will have no joy except in loving Him; and who at the same time makes the soul abhor the obstacles that hold it back and prevent it from loving Him with all its strength. Self-love <note>original: "l'amour-propre," referring to the theological concept of prideful self-interest</note> and concupiscence <note>term: concupiscence (the inclination toward earthly desires rather than spiritual ones)</note> which arrest the soul are unbearable to it, and God makes it feel that it has this depth of self-love and that He alone can cure it.

This is what it means to know God as Christians do. But to know Him in this manner, one must know at the same time one's own misery and unworthiness, and the need one has for a Mediator <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the bridge between humanity and the Divine</note> to approach God and to be united with Him. One must not separate these forms of knowledge¹, because when separated, they are not only useless, but harmful. The knowledge of God without that of our misery produces pride. The knowledge of our misery without that of Jesus Christ produces our despair; but the knowledge of Jesus Christ exempts us from both pride and despair, because in Him we find God, the sole consoler of our misery, and the only way to repair it.

We can know God without knowing our misery, or our misery without knowing God; or even God and our misery without knowing the means to deliver ourselves from the miseries that overwhelm us. But we cannot—

We can only know Jesus Christ by knowing both God and our own misery at the same time; because he is not simply God, but a God who repairs our miseries. Thus, all those who seek God without Jesus Christ find no light that satisfies them or that is truly useful to them; for either they do not reach the point of knowing that there is a God, or if they do reach it, it is useless to them, because they create a means of communicating without a <term>Mediator</term> <note>A theological term for Jesus Christ as the bridge between God and humanity.</note> with this God whom they have known without a Mediator; so that they fall into atheism or <term>deism</term> <note>The belief in a creator who does not intervene in the universe, which the author views as insufficient for salvation.</note>, which are the two things that Religion abhors almost equally.

One must therefore strive solely to know Jesus Christ, since it is through him alone that we can claim to know God in a way that is useful to us. He is the true God of men, of the miserable, and of sinners. He is the center of everything and the object of everything; and whoever does not know him knows nothing in the order of the nature of the world, nor in themselves; for, not only do we know God only through Jesus Christ, but we know ourselves only through Jesus Christ.

Without Jesus Christ, man must be in vice and in misery; with Jesus Christ, man is exempt from vice and misery. In him is all our happiness, our virtue, our life, our light, our hope; and outside of him, there is nothing but vices, miseries, despair, and we see only darkness and confusion in the nature of God and in our own.

These words are his own, word for word, and I believed I should report them here because they show us admirably well what the spirit of his work was, and that the manner in which he wished to proceed was without <gloss>further delay or deviation</gloss> <insert>interruption</insert>.

doubt the most capable of making an impression on the hearts of men.

One of the principal points of eloquence that he had established for himself was not only to say nothing that could not be understood, but also to say things in which those to whom we spoke would find themselves interested; for he was certain that, in such cases, self-love <note>French: *l'amour propre*; in 17th-century thought, this refers to the natural instinct of self-interest and ego</note> itself would never fail to make us reflect upon them. Furthermore, since the part we take in things is of two kinds (for they either afflict us or they console us), he believed that one should never cause affliction without also providing consolation, and that managing all of this well was the secret of eloquence. Thus, in the proofs he intended to give of God and of the Christian Religion, he wished to say nothing that was not within the reach of all those for whom they were intended, and in which man would not find himself interested in taking part—either by feeling within himself all the things being pointed out to him, whether good or bad, or by seeing clearly that he could take no better or more reasonable path than to believe there is a God whom we may enjoy, and a Mediator <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the bridge between God and humanity</note> who, having come to merit grace for us, begins to make us happy even in this life through the virtues he inspires in us—far more than one could ever be by everything the world promises us—and gives us assurance that we shall be perfectly happy in heaven, if we merit it through the ways he has presented to us and of which he himself has given us the example.

But, although he was persuaded that everything he had to say on Religion in this manner would have been very clear and very convincing, he did not believe, however, that it ought to be so for those who were in a state of indifference, and who, not finding within themselves the light <note>Internal spiritual insight or divine illumination</note> that would persuade them, negle—

For he established these two truths as certain: that God has placed perceptible marks, particularly within the Church, to make himself known to those who seek him sincerely; and yet he has covered them in such a way that he will only be perceived by those who seek him with all their heart.

This is why, when he had to confer with any **atheists**, he never began with dispute, nor by establishing the principles he had to say: but he wanted to know beforehand if they sought the truth with all their heart; and he acted accordingly with them, either to help them find the light they did not have, if they sought it sincerely, or to dispose them to seek it and to make it their most serious occupation, before instructing them, if they wished his instruction to be useful to them.

It was his **infirmities** <note>Pascal suffered from chronic pain and neurological issues throughout his adult life.</note> which prevented him from working further on his design. He was about thirty-four years old when he began to apply himself to it. He spent an entire year preparing for it in the manner that his other occupations allowed him, which was to collect the different thoughts that came to him on the subject; and at the end of the year—that is to say, his thirty-fifth year, which was the fifth of his **retreat** <note>Referring to his withdrawal from worldly society to the religious circle of Port-Royal.</note>—he fell back into his ailments in such an overwhelming manner that he could do nothing more during the four years he still had to live, if one can call "living" the piteous languor in which he passed them.

This renewal of my brother’s ailments began with a toothache that absolutely deprived him of sleep. But what means is there for a mind like his to be awake and think of nothing? This is why, even during those bouts of insomnia, which are otherwise so frequent and exhausting, there came into his mind one night some thoughts on the cycloid <note>original: "roulette"; the geometric curve traced by a point on the rim of a circular wheel as it rolls along a straight line</note>; the first was followed by a second, and the second by a third, and finally by a multitude of thoughts that succeeded one another. It is incredible with what haste he put this to paper. For he did nothing but write as fast as his hand could move, and he finished it in very few days¹; he made no copy of it at all, but gave the sheets away as soon as he produced them. Another work of his was also being printed, which he provided in the same manner as he composed it, and thus he supplied the printers with two different works at once². This was not too much for his mind; but his body could not endure it, for it was this final exhaustion that finished undermining his health entirely and reduced him to that distressing state we have mentioned, where he was unable to swallow. <note>Pascal suffered from a debilitating gastrointestinal or neurological condition toward the end of his life that made eating and drinking nearly impossible.</note>

But if his infirmities rendered him incapable of serving others, they were not useless to himself; for he suffered them with such patience that there is reason to believe, and to take comfort in the thought, that God wished by this means to make him as He desired him to be before appearing in His presence. Indeed, he thought of nothing else, and having always before his eyes the two maxims he had set for himself—to renounce all pleasures and all superfluities—he practiced them with even greater fervor, as if he were pressed by the weight of charity <note>original: "charité"; in this context, it refers to the theological concept of divine love</note> which felt it was approaching the center where it was to enjoy eternal rest.

It was upon these same principles that he had such a great love for penance <note>In this context, penance refers to voluntary self-punishment as an outward expression of repentance for sin.</note>; for he said that a sinful body must be punished, and punished without reserve through continual penance, because without this it was rebellious to the spirit and contradictory to all feelings of salvation. But as we do not have the courage to punish ourselves, we ought to consider ourselves greatly obliged to God when it pleases Him to do so; this is why he blessed Him unceasingly for the sufferings He had sent him, which he regarded as a fire that burned away his sins little by little through a daily sacrifice, thus preparing himself while waiting for it to please God to send him death, which would consummate the perfect sacrifice.

He had always possessed such a great love for poverty that it was continually present to him; so much so that, as soon as he wished to undertake something, or when someone asked him for advice, the first thought that rose from his heart to his mind was to see if poverty could be practiced therein. But the love of this virtue increased so greatly at the end of his life that I could satisfy him in no better way than by speaking of it with him, and by listening to what he was always ready to tell us about it.

He never refused alms <note>Charitable donations to the poor.</note> to anyone, although he had little wealth, and the expenses he was obliged to incur because of his infirmities <note>Pascal suffered from chronic, debilitating illnesses throughout his adult life.</note> exceeded his income. He never gave except from what was necessary for himself. He had an extreme tenderness for his friends and for those whom he believed belonged to God; and one can say that if ever a person was more worthy of being loved, no one ever knew better how to love, nor ever practiced it better than he. But his tenderness was not merely an effect of his temperament; for although his heart was always ready to be moved by the needs of his friends, he nevertheless only allowed himself to be moved according to the rules of Christianity that reason and faith set before his eyes. He could no longer love anyone as he loved my sister, and he was right to do so; he saw her often, he spoke to her about all things without reserve, and he received satisfaction from her on all matters without exception; for there was such a great correspondence between their feelings that they agreed on everything. And when he saw me afflicted by it (for it is true that I felt this loss deeply), it pained him, and he told me that this was not right, and that one should not have such feelings regarding the death of the righteous; but that we should, on the contrary, praise God for having rewarded her so soon for the small services she had rendered Him.

He distinguished between two kinds of <term>tenderness</term> <note>original: "tendresse"; here meaning emotional sensitivity or affection</note>: one based on feeling, the other on reason. Admitting that the former was of little use in the ways of the world, he nevertheless said that merit played no part in it, and that honorable people should only value the "reasonable tenderness" which he defined as taking part in everything that happens to our friends in every way that reason dictates we should—at the expense of our wealth, our convenience, our liberty, and even our life, if the cause merits it; and that it always merits it if it is a matter of serving them for the sake of God, who must be the sole end of the tenderness of <term>Christians</term>.

"A heart is hard," he would say, "when it recognizes the interests of its <term>neighbor</term> <note>original: "prochain"; the biblical concept of the fellow human being</note> and resists the obligation pressing upon it to take part in them; and on the contrary, a heart is tender when all the interests of the neighbor enter into it easily, so to speak, through all the sentiments that reason dictates one should have for one another in such encounters; which rejoices when it is time to rejoice; which grieves when it is time to grieve." But he added that tenderness can only be perfect when reason is enlightened by faith and when it makes us act by the...

These were the sentiments he held regarding the service of the King: likewise, he was irreconcilable with all those who opposed it. And what demonstrates that this was not due to his temperament or an attachment to his own opinions is that he possessed an admirable gentleness toward those who offended him personally; so much so that he never made a distinction between them and others. <meta>This page continues the biographical sketch of Blaise Pascal, focusing on his moral character and temperament following his intellectual achievements.</meta>

# BIOGRAPHIES

He was not only seemingly insensitive to insults, but he was also indifferent to those things that wound all other men and which constitute their greatest passion. He certainly possessed a great soul, but one without ambition, desiring neither to be great, nor powerful, nor honored in the world, and even regarding all such things as containing more misery than happiness. He wished for wealth only to share it with others, and his pleasure lay in reason, in order, in justice, and finally in everything capable of nourishing the soul, finding little pleasure in sensory things.

He was not without faults; but one had complete freedom to warn him of them, and he yielded to the advice of his friends with a very great submission when they were just, and when they were not, he always received them with gentleness. The extreme vivacity of his spirit made him so impatient at times that it was difficult to satisfy him¹; but as soon as he was warned, or perceived himself that he had upset someone by this impatience of his spirit, he immediately repaired his fault with such honorable treatment that he never lost anyone's friendship because of it.

The self-love <note>original: "amour propre"; a key 17th-century concept referring to vanity or ego</note> of others was not inconvenienced by his own, and one would even have said that he had none at all, never speaking of himself², nor of anything in relation to himself; and

# BLAISE PASCAL

It is well known that he wished for a man of honor <note>French: "honneste homme," a 17th-century ideal of a cultivated, virtuous, and socially adept gentleman</note> to avoid naming himself, and even to avoid using the words *I* or *me*; what he was accustomed to say on this subject is that Christian piety annihilates the human *self*, and that human civility hides and suppresses it; he conceived of this as a rule, and it is precisely what he practiced.

He was not troublesome to anyone regarding their faults; but when he was engaged to speak of things, he always spoke of them without dissimulation; and as he did not know what it was to please through flattery, he was also incapable of not telling the truth when he was obliged to do so. Those who did not know him were surprised at first when they heard him speak in conversations, because it always seemed that he held the upper hand, with a certain kind of dominance; but it was the very principle of the vivacity of his spirit that was the cause of it, and one was not with him for long before seeing soon enough that in this very thing there was something lovable, and before being, in the end, as satisfied with his manner of speaking as one was with the things he said.

Furthermore, he held every kind of lie in horror, and the slightest deceptions were unbearable to him; so that, just as the character of his mind was to be penetrating and just, and that of his heart to be upright and without distraction, that of his actions and his conduct was sincerity and fidelity.

We have found a note by him where he had undoubtedly painted a portrait of himself so that, having continually before his eyes the path by which God was leading him, he could never turn away from it. This is what this note says:

> "I love poverty, because Jesus Christ loved it. I love wealth, because it gives the means to assis— <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "assister" (to assist/help the poor).</note>

One could undoubtedly add many things to this portrait, if one wished to complete it to its final perfection; but, leaving it to others, more capable than I, to add the final strokes which belong only to the masters, I will only add that this man, so great in all things, was as simple as a child regarding piety. Those who saw him regularly were surprised by it. Not only was there neither affectation nor hypocrisy in his way of acting; but just as he knew how to rise in the penetration of the highest virtues, he knew how to humble himself in the practice of the most common ones.

His principal diversion, especially in the final years of his life when he was unable to work <note>Pascal suffered from chronic, debilitating illness that eventually prevented him from pursuing his mathematical and scientific research</note>, was to go visit the Churches where relics were on display or where some solemnity was being held. For this purpose, he was specifically provided with a spiritual almanac <note>A liturgical calendar or guide to local religious festivals</note> which informed him of the places where all the various devotions were to be found. He did this so devoutly and so simply that those who saw him were surprised by it; among others, a very virtuous and enlightened person explained it with these beautiful words: *That the grace of God makes itself known in great minds by small things, and in common minds by great things.*

He had a heartfelt love for the Office (that is to say, the prayers of the Breviary <term>Breviary: A book containing the daily psalms, hymns, and prayers to be recited by clergy and devout laity at specific hours</term>) and subjected himself to reciting it as much as he was able; but especially the "Little Hours" <note>The shorter prayer services of the day: Prime, Terce, Sext, and None</note> which are composed of the hundred and eighteenth Psalm <note>Psalm 119 in modern numbering; the longest psalm, focused entirely on the beauty of God's law</note>, in which he found so many admirable things that he always felt a new joy in reciting it¹. When he conversed with his friends about the beauty of this Psalm, he was transported by it, and like himself, he carried away all those to whom he spoke of it. When he was sent a monthly devotional slip <note>original: "billet"</note>, as is the custom in many places, he read it and received it with great respect, never failing to read the sentence <note>A short spiritual maxim or verse for daily meditation</note> every day. And as we could not help but pity him at the height of his pains, he would say: "Do not pity me; illness is the natural state of Christians, because through it one is as one always ought to be: that is to say, in suffering, in hardships, in the privation of all goods and <insert>of</insert> <note>The original manuscript 'F' reads "the" instead of "of".</note> pleasures of the senses, exempt from all passions, without ambition, without avarice, and in the continual expectation of death. They lasted until his death, which occurred twenty-four hours later; namely, on the nineteenth of August, sixteen hundred and sixty-two, at one o'clock in the morning, at the age of thirty-nine years and two months.

# APPENDIX
## MR. LE PAILLEUR.

The son of a lieutenant from the district of Meulan, Le Pailleur—whose rigid integrity and jovial good humor were both praised by Tallemant des Réaux—lived in the household of the Maréchale de Thémines <note>The wife of a Marshal of France; a high-ranking noblewoman.</note> "without wages or salary, but simply as a friend of the house; it is true that he managed all her affairs." He "knew music, sang, danced, and wrote humorous verses." We see Mr. de Nemours having him admitted, "by great favor," to the private concert that Louis XIII held at his home with "all those of the Chamber Music¹" <note>The King's private ensemble of musicians.</note>. Tallemant des Réaux adds finally that he had devoted himself to mathematics since his childhood: "he learned them all by himself. He had only twenty-nine sous when he began to read books on this science, and he would exchange the books as he finished reading them. He had written a fair amount, but he did not deign to publish anything: he wrote very natural burlesque epistles."

Although Le Pailleur did not leave behind any first-rate mathematical works, he is often cited by his contemporaries as having been involved in the questions of the day. He had worked on plane loci <note>original: "lieux plans"; a geometric concept involving the set of points satisfying a specific condition.</note> (see below vol. III, p. 302), and had obtained the solution to some of the problems communicated by Fermat to the Mersenne Academy <note>The intellectual circle surrounding Father Marin Mersenne, a precursor to the French Academy of Sciences.</note> (see below p. 172: Roberval, describing the reception given to these problems, wrote to Fermat on April 4, 1637: "a man named Mr. Le Pailleur had found the specific demonstration for 3 and 4 points" (from *Works of Fermat*, Ed. Tannery-Henry, II, p. 103).

---
1. *Historiettes*, 203-207, ed. Monmerqué, Paulin-Paris, 1855, vol. V, p. 214-215. — See Strowski, *The History of Pascal*, 1907, p. 12.

### BIOGRAPHIES

Around 1644, alongside Roberval, Descartes, Mersenne, and Carcavi, Le Pailleur participated in the controversy initiated by Longomontanus <note>Christian Sørensen Longomontanus (1562–1647), a Danish astronomer</note> and John Pell regarding the squaring of the circle <note>The "quadrature of the circle" is the ancient, and ultimately impossible, challenge of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle using only a compass and straightedge.</note>. Pell even printed a letter from him (signed *D. Pallieus, Nobleman of Paris* <note>original: "D. Pallieus, Nobilis Parisinus"</note>) in his *Controversies on the True Measurement of the Circle* <note>original: "Controversiæ de verâ circuli mensurâ"</note> (See the notice by Jacoli in Boncompagni’s *Bulletin of Bibliography*, volume II, 1869, pp. 299-312. — *Cf. Works of Descartes, Adam-Tannery edition*, IV, p. 343).

Le Pailleur also occupied himself with cubic equations and sought to solve them "by the circle and by the parabola without purging them of the highest degree" (Mylon to Christiaan Huygens, June 23, 1656, *Works of Huygens*, I, p. 439). He had written a small treatise on this subject which he had entrusted to Mylon: "he gave it to me a few months before he died," said Mylon, "intending to place it in my hands along with what I was collecting from the assembly that was held at his home" <note>Le Pailleur hosted a famous scientific "academy" or informal gathering that preceded the official French Academy of Sciences.</note> (Mylon to Schooten, November 1656, *Works of Huygens*, I, p. 514). Mylon thought it best to send the treatise to Holland so that it might be examined by Huygens and also by Schooten "who testified to me," said Mylon, "that he would be very glad to have it promptly so as not to delay the printing he is doing of Mr. Descartes's Geometry and the other short works he is to join to it" (*Works of Huygens*, I, p. 439). Le Pailleur's method was indeed studied closely by the two Dutchmen (see the letters from Schooten to Mylon, *Works of Huygens*, I, p. 513, from Huygens to Mylon, *ibid.*, p. 525 and the following letters). They noted omissions in it and judged that it was not sufficiently general.

Le Pailleur informs us directly about his spirit and his philosophy in a *Response to the Bacchic Verses and Sonnets on the Movement of the Earth* that Dalibray had dedicated to him <margin>1. *See below p. 295, and vol. II, p. 44.*</margin>. From this response, which Dalibray published two years after Le Pailleur's death in his *Poetic Works*,

->From MR. LE PAILLEUR to Mr. d'Alibray, in response to several sonnets which he had sent him, by which he asked him his opinion on the theory of Galileo concerning the movement of the earth:<-

    Finally, you have provoked me too much,
    D'Alibray, I feel myself stung
    By ten sonnets with which you tease me
    And by twenty with which you threaten me.
    I can hardly endure
    This bravado without swearing.

    But do not expect me to contest
    Whether this torch <note>The sun</note> which they call celestial
    Moves, or if it moves not at all;
    My Muse is too short by a point
    To touch upon so high a mystery:
    It is enough that I revere it,
    And that by humbly suspending
    My judgment on this subject,
    I only make you understand
    What obliges me to suspend it...
    But — speaking with a healthier spirit —
    He whose powerful hand
    Made every creature from nothing,
    That great author of Nature,
    That jealous God, does not permit
    That we who are here below,
    Have knowledge of what is up there...
    After that, do you wish to constrain me
    To decipher this movement
    Which appears beneath the Firmament <term>Firmament: the heavens or the sky, traditionally viewed as a solid dome</term>?
    I, who moreover since my childhood
    Profess an entire ignorance?

-># BLAISE PASCAL<-

Jacqueline <note>Pascal's younger sister, a gifted poet and later a nun at Port-Royal</note> addressed verses to Benserade <note>Isaac de Benserade, a popular court poet</note> which were published in his *Works* (see below p. 232 ff.). In 1647, Pascal invited Dalibray <note>Charles de Dalibray, a poet and translator</note> to see Descartes at his home; in 1648, he wrote to Le Pailleur to justify himself against the attacks of Father Noël <note>Etienne Noël, a Jesuit who disputed Pascal's experiments on the vacuum</note>. We can therefore reconstruct the circle that Pascal frequented from the earliest years of his childhood; we can also, through the lightness of the tone, perceive the philosophy that reigned in this environment. The frank freedom of doubt, the hatred of Scholastic pedantry <note>The traditional, rigid academic philosophy of the medieval universities</note>, the "reverence" for religion, the praise of ignorance and of tranquility of mind¹, these are the characteristic features of Montaigne's *Essays*. It is therefore certain, as more than one clue already allowed us to suspect, that Pascal did not wait for his meeting with Méré <note>The Chevalier de Méré, who later introduced Pascal to the "worldly" circles of high society</note> and the emancipation of his social period to be initiated into the movement of the new philosophy, and in particular to the reading of Montaigne.

circumstances that were not at all ordinary: one, that he could not bear to see water without falling into fits of very great rage; and the other, much more astonishing, was that he could not bear to see his father and mother near one another. My grandfather said to her: "Oh! I would rather my son die than to cause the death of another person." She told him: "the spell can be placed upon a beast." My grandfather offered her a horse; she told him that, without going to such great expense, a cat would suffice. He had one given to her; she carried it away, and as she was going down, she met two Capuchins <note>A reform branch of the Franciscan order of friars, known for their brown robes and pointed hoods.</note> who were coming up to console my grandmother regarding the extreme illness of this child. These fathers told her that she surely intended to perform some sorcery with this cat; she took it and threw it out of a window, from which it fell only six feet and dropped dead. She asked for another, which my grandfather had given to her. The great tenderness he had for this child meant he did not pay attention to the fact that all of this was worthless, since, to transfer this spell, it required a new invocation to the Devil; this thought never entered his mind until much later, and he repented for having allowed it to happen.

In the evening, the woman came and told my grandfather that she needed a child who was not yet seven years old, and who, before sunrise, would gather nine leaves of three kinds of herbs: that is to say, three of each kind. On the contrary, he broke more and more with all his friends, no longer seeing any of those from the secular world.

During his retreat, he committed himself by an order of providence to work against the atheists; and here is how the material given to the public was collected. Mr. Pascal was accustomed, when he worked, to form in his head everything he wanted to write without almost ever making a draft on paper; and he possessed an extraordinary quality for this, which was that he never forgot anything, and he said himself that he had never forgotten anything he had wished to retain. Thus, he kept in his memory the ideas of everything he planned to write until it reached perfection, and only then would he write it down. This was his custom; but for that, a great effort of imagination was required, and when he fell into his great infirmities <note>Pascal suffered from chronic pain and neurological issues for much of his adult life</note>, five years before his death, he did not have enough strength to keep everything he meditated upon in his memory in this way. Therefore, to relieve himself, he wrote down what came to him as things presented themselves, so that he could use them later to work—just as he had previously done with what he imprinted in his memory. It is these fragments, written thus piece by piece, that were found after his death, which were published and which the public received with such pleasure <note>These fragments became the famous "Pensées" (Thoughts)</note>.

While Mr. Pascal was working against the atheists, it happened that he was struck by a very great toothache. One evening, the Duke of Roannez <note>Artus Gouffier, a close friend and patron of Pascal</note> left him in very violent pain; he went to bed, and as his pain only increased, he decided, in order to find relief, to apply himself to something that might make him forget his suffering. For this purpose, he thought of the proposition of the Roulette <note>The "Roulette" refers to the cycloid, the curve traced by a point on the rim of a moving wheel</note> formerly proposed by Father Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, a central figure in the 17th-century scientific revolution</note>, which no one had ever been able to solve.

Mr. de Roannez told him there was a much better use to be made of it; that in his plan to combat the atheists, it was necessary to show them that he knew more than all of them regarding geometry and that which is subject to proof; and that thus, if he submitted to matters regarding faith, it was because he knew exactly how far proofs could reach. Upon this, he advised him to deposit 60 <term>pistoles</term> <note>A gold coin of considerable value at the time</note> and to issue a kind of challenge to all the skilled mathematicians he knew, proposing a prize for whoever should find the solution to the problem. Mr. Pascal believed him and deposited the 60 pistoles into the hands of Mr. [blank], named examiners to judge the works that would come from all over Europe, and fixed the term at 18 months. At the end of this time, no one having found the solution according to the judgment of the examiners, Mr. Pascal withdrew his 60 pistoles and used them to have his work printed, of which he only had 120 copies produced.

found the stomach and the liver withered, and the intestines gangrenous, without being able to judge precisely whether this had been the cause of the colic pains or if it had been the effect. It is true that he had formerly possessed the suture called the frontal <note>The frontal or metopic suture, which usually closes in early childhood</note>; but having remained open for a very long time during his infancy, as often happens at that age, and having been unable to close itself, a callus <note>A bony thickening or growth</note> had formed which had entirely covered it, and which was so substantial that one could easily feel it with a finger. As for the coronal suture <note>The joint across the top of the skull from ear to ear</note>, there was no trace of it. The doctors observed that there was a prodigious abundance of brain matter, the substance of which was so solid and condensed that it led them to judge that this was the reason why, the frontal suture being unable to close, nature had provided for it with this callus. But what was noted as most significant, and to which they particularly attributed his death and the final incidents that accompanied it, was that inside the skull, opposite the ventricles of the brain, there were two impressions, like a finger pressed into wax, which were full of clotted and corrupted blood that had begun to gangrene the dura mater <note>The tough outermost membrane surrounding the brain</note>.

<meta>This page introduces a famous anecdotal account of Blaise Pascal's carriage accident at the Neuilly bridge, often cited as a turning point in his religious life.</meta>

## EXCERPT FROM AN ANONYMOUS MANUSCRIPT CONCERNING
## THE LIFE OF PASCAL

Mr. Arnoul de Saint-Victor, the priest of Chamboursy, says that he learned from Mr. Barillon, the Prior—a friend of Madame Perier¹ <note>Pascal's sister, Gilberte Perier</note>—that Mr. Pascal, a few years before his death, having gone according to his custom on a feast day for a drive to the Neuilly bridge² with some of his friends in a carriage drawn by four or six horses, the two lead horses took the bit in their teeth <note>meaning they bolted out of control</note> at a spot on the bridge where there was no guardrail. Having plunged into the water, the traces <note>the leather straps</note> attaching them to the rear carriage frame broke, so that the carriage remained balanced on the edge of the precipice. This event caused Mr. Pascal to resolve to give up his outings and to live in complete solitude³.

<note>1. *See above*, p. 39. Since Henri de Barillon accepted the succession of the Bishop of Luçon in 1672, the account collected by the priest of Chamboursy would date prior to that year.</note>
<note>2. The Neuilly bridge was made of wood and dated from 1639 (Jovy, *Unpublished Pascal*, p. 445).</note>
<note>3. These lines were extracted by Father Guerrier from an anonymous manuscript kept in the library of the Oratorian Fathers of Clermont. They were published by Faugère, *Letters, Minor Works*, 1845, p. 470. However, they had already been used by Barbot for the editing of the *Utrecht Collection*, 1740, p. 158; since that time, they have been part of the dossier regarding Pascal's final conversion. Bossut, in his *Discourse on the Life and Works of Pascal*, had even specified the date: "One day in the month of October 1654." *Works of Pascal*, 1779, vol. I, p. 43. In a study titled *A Legend of the Life of Pascal: The Accident at the Neuilly Bridge*, which can be found reproduced at the end of the third edition of his *Notes on Pascal* (1905), Mr. Giraud has challenged...</note>

1st: The material reality of the accident is regarded as "insufficiently established."

It is difficult to agree with this thesis: the testimony collected here may be unique, and it may be anonymous; nevertheless, it exists, complete with its certificates of origin and authenticity. To have the right to dismiss it, one would need either to rely on testimony that contradicts it or to incriminate the impartiality of the ecclesiastics <note>Members of the clergy, likely referring to the Jansenist priests of Port-Royal</note> through whom the transmission of the account was made. Otherwise, we must accept it, subject to discussing its probable significance in the moral evolution that brings Pascal back to Port-Royal <note>The center of the Jansenist movement in France, where Pascal's sister was a nun and where he found spiritual refuge</note>.

On the 5th day of October, around noon, was born Jacquette Pascal, daughter to the noble Etienne Pascal, King's Counselor and President in the Court of Aids <note>A sovereign court of the Ancien Régime dealing with taxation</note> of Montferrand, and to the lady Antoinette Begon; and the said Jacquette was baptized on the 10th of the said month in the same year. The godfather was the noble Bresmond Paschal <margin>The fourth of the children of Martin Pascal.</margin>, and the godmother was the lady Jacquette Durand, wife to the noble Begon, Counselor elected for the King in the election of Auvergne at Clermont <margin>Who was the godfather of Gilberte Pascal. *See above*, p. 31.</margin>. — Bresmond Paschal, Durand.

### Life of Jacqueline Pascal

<insert>This *Life* appeared in volume II of the *Interesting and Edifying Lives of the Nuns of Port-Royal*, 1751, p. 339-356. Various manuscript copies are also found (National Library, f. fr. 20580 and the Library of Troyes, no. 2203).</insert>

My sister was born at Clermont on the 4th of October in the year 1625. As I was six years older than she, I remember that as soon as she began to speak, she gave great signs of wit. She was, besides that, perfectly beautiful, and possessed a sweet temperament and the most agreeable nature in the world; so much so that she was as loved and cherished as a child can be. My father retired to Paris in 1631, and brought us all there. My sister was then six years old, still very beautiful and entirely charming through the kindness of her mind and her disposition. These qualities made her desired everywhere; so much so that she almost never stayed at home with us.

They began to teach her to read at the age of seven; and as my father had charged me with this care, I found myself quite hindered by it, for she had a...

That same year, 1638, in the month of March, my father <note>Étienne Pascal</note>, having met at the home of the Chancellor <note>Pierre Séguier</note> with many other people who, like him, had an interest in the investments of the City Hall <note>The "Rentes de l'Hôtel de Ville," a form of government bond</note>, certain words were spoken that day, and some actions were even taken, which were a bit violent and seditious. She always satisfied those who expected to hear her say something beautiful; but what is more admirable is that none of this made her proud. She received such praise with such great indifference that everyone loved her all the more for it, and her companions, with whom she spent every day, never felt the slightest jealousy toward her. On the contrary, they contributed with all their hearts to increasing the esteem in which she was held by publicizing the good qualities they recognized in her privately, such as her sweetness, her kindness, and the pleasantness and evenness of her temperament, which was incomparable.

During that time, several opportunities for her to marry presented themselves; but God permitted that there was always some reason that prevented a conclusion. In these encounters, she never showed either attachment or aversion, being very submissive to my father's will, without ever having had any thought for the religious life <note>The original term "religion" here specifically refers to entering a convent or taking holy orders.</note>; on the contrary, she felt a great distance from it and even <insert>a bit of</insert> <note>original: "mesme". She shared this thought with my brother <note>Blaise Pascal</note> who, far from dissuading her, encouraged her in it, for he shared the same sentiments. This approval strengthened her in such a way that from 그hat time on, she never hesitated for a moment in her plan to consecrate herself to God.

My brother, who loved her with a very special tenderness, was overjoyed to see her in this holy resolution, so much so that he thought of nothing else but serving her to ensure the success of this plan; and as neither of them had any acquaintance at Port-Royal <note>Abbreviated as P.R. in the original</note>, he thought of Mr. Guillebert, who was a mutual acquaintance. He went to see him and took my sister there; and Mr. Guillebert, having spoken with her, was so satisfied that he himself took her to Mother Angélique <note>Angélique Arnauld, the famous reformer of Port-Royal</note> who also received her with much satisfaction and grace <note>A variant reading suggests "with much kindness"</note>. After that, my sister went there as often as she could, despite being a great distance away. The Mothers told her that she must approach Mr. Singlin <note>The influential confessor and director of Port-Royal</note> and place herself under his guidance, so that he might judge if the state of a nun was suited to her: she did not fail to do what she was ordered. From the first time that Mr. Singlin saw her, he told my brother that he had never seen in anyone such great signs of a vocation. This testimony greatly comforted my brother and obliged him to redouble his efforts for the success of a plan that they had every reason to believe came from God. All these things took place in the first months of the year 1648, my brother and sister being in Paris and my father in Rouen.

In the month of May of that year, my father having come...

# BIOGRAPHIES

In Paris, Mr. Singlin <note>Antoine Singlin, the influential confessor and spiritual director of Port-Royal</note> thought it appropriate that my sister’s plan be revealed to my father, because by then she was entirely resolved. My brother <note>Blaise Pascal</note> took it upon himself to deliver this news, as he was the only one who could do so. My father <note>Etienne Pascal</note> was greatly surprised by this proposal and was strangely torn; for on one hand, having embraced the principles of Christian purity <note>This refers to the rigorous moral standards associated with the Jansenist movement</note>, he was pleased to see his children sharing these sentiments; but on the other hand, the tender affection he had for my sister bound him so closely to her that he could not bring himself to be separated from her <insert>forever</insert> <note>original: "pour jamais"; another version of the manuscript reads "always"</note>.

This conflict of thoughts forced him to respond first to my brother that he would see and think about it. But finally, after weighing it for some time, he told him plainly that he could not give his consent. He even complained about my brother for having encouraged this plan without knowing if it would be agreeable to him; and this thought embittered him so much against my brother and my sister that he no longer had any confidence in them. Consequently, he commanded a maidservant—who was an old family domestic and who had raised them both—to keep watch over their actions <note>This old servant appears to be Louise Deffaud, who is mentioned in legal documents following Etienne Pascal’s death in 1651.</note>. This order from my father placed my sister under great constraint, so much so that from that time on, she could only go to Port-Royal <note>Abbreviated as P.R. in the original; the center of the Jansenist movement</note> in secret, or see Mr. Singlin through cleverness and ingenuity.

This hardship did not diminish her fervor in the least, and as she had renounced the world in her heart, she could no longer take pleasure in diversions as she [once did]...

...she used to do before; so that although she hid with great care the plan she had to give herself to God, people did not fail to notice it. Seeing that she could no longer hide it, she no longer hesitated to withdraw bit by bit from social circles, and she absolutely broke all her old habits. She found a favorable opportunity for this, because my father moved houses at that time¹; she made no new acquaintances in this new neighborhood, and she shed her old ones by simply not visiting them. Thus, she found herself in complete liberty to live in solitude, and she found this life so agreeable that she gradually grew accustomed to withdrawing even from family conversation, so that she stayed all day alone in her cabinet <note>cabinet: A small private room or study used for prayer, reading, and reflection</note>.

One cannot report what her spiritual exercises were in this strict solitude, and all that can be said is that one noticed from day to day that she was making admirable progress in virtue. However, even though she was very constrained² <note>original: "gênée"; meaning she was under constant surveillance</note>, she still managed to go sometimes to Port-Royal <note>original: "P. R."</note>, to write there often, and to receive letters from them, for she had a remarkable skill for doing so³, and thus she sustained herself.

Her abstinence <note>In this context, abstinence refers to the practice of self-denial, specifically regarding food and physical comforts.</note> also caused us much distress; for although she ate the same food as we did, it was nevertheless in such small quantities that, as she was of a very delicate temperament, she diminished her strength and ruined her stomach. Her vigils <term>vigils|Late-night or overnight periods of wakefulness dedicated to prayer and spiritual reflection</term> were also extraordinary; we did not have a full knowledge of them, but we were well aware of them by the quantity of candles she burned, and by other similar signs.

She had shown an admirable foresight: for considering that the religious habit <term>habit|The distinctive clothing worn by members of a religious order, such as a nun or monk</term>, in the ways it differs from worldly dress, presents certain difficulties that burden the body and hinder the spirit from reaching perfection, she decided to accustom herself as much as she could to the most painful things in order to arm herself against them. To this end, she had very low shoes made for herself, she dressed without a corset <note>original: "corps de jupe"; a stiffened bodice or stays that provided structure to 17th-century women's clothing</note>, she cut her hair, and wore several caps <note>original: "coëffes"; linen head coverings or bonnets worn under or instead of a veil</note> that were even too large and more cumbersome than a veil would have been; in short, she managed so well that, when she entered the convent, she did not have the slightest difficulty with the clothing.

# JACQUELINE PASCAL

-gion <note>Continuing from "reli-" on the previous page to form "religion," a term used here to mean entering a monastic order</note>, as soon as the division of our estate was finalized; however, she intended to spare my brother <note>Blaise Pascal, the famous mathematician and philosopher</note> by making him believe she was going there only for a retreat. She arranged everything for this purpose in my presence; our inheritance settlements were signed on the last day of December, and she chose the 4th of January for her entry.

On the eve of that day, she asked me to say something to my brother about it in the evening, so that he would not be so surprised. I did so with as much caution as I could; but no matter what I told him—that it was only a retreat to experience that way of life for a short while—he was nonetheless deeply affected by it. He therefore retired to his room in great sadness, without seeing my sister, who was then in a small study where she was accustomed to say her prayers. She did not come out until after my brother had left the room, because she feared that the sight of him would break her heart <note>original: "luy donnast au cœur," meaning the emotional sight might weaken her resolve or cause overwhelming grief</note>. I conveyed to her the tender words he had spoken to me, after which we all went to bed. 

But although I consented with all my heart to what she was doing—because I believed it was the greatest good that could happen to her—nevertheless, the magnitude of this resolution so astonished me and so occupied my mind that I did not sleep at all the whole night. Around seven o'clock, seeing that my sister did not rise, I thought she had not slept either, and I was afraid she might be feeling ill; so I went to her bed, where I found her fast asleep. The noise I made having awakened her, she asked me what time it was. I told her, and having asked her how she felt and if she had slept well, she told me she was well and had slept soundly. Thus she rose, dressed, and departed, performing this action as she did all others with a tranquility and a composure <note>The text ends with the catchword "ega-", which likely completes as "égalité d'esprit" or "égalité d'âme," meaning equanimity or steadiness of spirit</note>

# INTRODUCTION

This letter is the only mathematical writing that remains of Étienne Pascal. However, his scientific activity is evidenced elsewhere by numerous testimonies. While living in Paris from 1631 to 1638, he was an intimate member of a small society of mathematicians ^1^ who, gathered around Father Mersenne, formed a kind of informal academy. <note>Father Marin Mersenne was a monk and polymath who acted as a central hub for scientific communication in 17th-century Europe, connecting figures like Descartes, Galileo, and Pascal.</note> There, one would encounter Roberval, Desargues, Mydorge, Hardy, Abbot Chambon, Le Pailleur, and Bouilliaud. These weekly meetings took place most often at Mersenne’s residence at the Monastery of the Minimes, and sometimes at the homes of other individuals ^2^ (“The assembly,” wrote Roberval to Fermat on April 4, 1637, “was held that day at the home of Mr. de Montholon, a counselor.”) After Mersenne’s death in 1648, the academy met every Saturday at the home of Le Pailleur ^3^.

Alongside his colleagues from the Mersenne academy, Étienne Pascal was personally involved in the most important mathematical debates of his time.

In 1634, we see him actively involved in the Morin affair. <note>Jean-Baptiste Morin was a mathematician and astrologer; the "affair" involved a dispute over his method for determining longitude.</note> This curious case is recounted at length in a printed work by Morin, the trace of which seemed lost, and which

we found this work at the Sainte-Geneviève Library (*Rés. 4° v. 65*): *A new and hitherto desired science of terrestrial and celestial longitudes, dedicated to the most eminent Cardinal Richelieu, Duke and Peer of France, by which the longitude and latitude of any place on earth where one is stationed, and of any visible star, can be most accurately discovered, and the principal secrets of astronomy are revealed.
