Morin was soliciting a reward from the Cardinal for his discovery regarding the determination of longitudes. <note>Determining longitude—one's east-west position—was the greatest scientific challenge for 17th-century navigation, essential for trade and naval power.</note> Richelieu then appointed five commissioners whom he charged with examining this discovery: these were the Abbot of Chambon, President Pascal, Mydorge, and Professors Boulenger and Hérigone (*see the cited work, p. 8, for the text of the diploma appointing the commissioners*). The commission met on March 30 and presented several objections to the inventor. However, Morin defended himself and provided a long demonstration before the commissioners (of which the cited book is the full development). After this, he believed he had reduced his adversaries to silence, and he asked Richelieu to attest to his victory by having the commissioners sign the record of the session. Morin triumphed too soon; for, upon leaving the Cardinal's residence, he encountered Pascal and Beaugrand, who declared they were by no means convinced (p. 87). Soon the objections resurfaced even more urgently, and a bitter struggle began. Morin claimed to be the victim of a conspiracy and had his success proclaimed by Renaudot’s *Gazette*: this polemical tactic indignant Étienne Pascal and Mydorge, whose "bile" Morin tried in vain to soothe through the mediation of the "placid man" (*melancholy man*) that was Beaugrand (p. 94). <note>original: "homo melancholicus." In the medical theory of the time, a "melancholy" temperament was associated with a quiet, steady, or pensive nature.</note>

However, Richelieu summoned the five commissioners once again (Pascal, Mydorge, Beaugrand, Boulenger, and Hérigone) and asked them to answer four precise questions:

1. *Whether the science of longitudes has been demonstrated by anyone,* <note>original: "An longitudinum scientia fuerit à quoquam demonstrata"</note>

From 1636 onward, Fermat’s relationship with the Mersenne academy and with Étienne Pascal in particular never ceased to be excellent. We read in a letter from Roberval to Fermat (April 4, 1637, *Works of Fermat, II, p. 102*):

> "Although I received your demonstration of the plane locus <note>original: *lieu plan*; a geometric term for a set of points satisfying a specific condition, resulting in a straight line or circle</note> last Monday, nonetheless my duties, both public and private, did not allow me to consider it until Thursday, when I presented it on your behalf to the assembly of our mathematicians which was meeting, that day, at the home of Mr. de Montholon, a counselor. There, it was received, considered, and admired with such astonishment by those present, and your name was raised to the heavens... However, there was a debate as to who should keep your manuscript to make a copy of it, everyone envying my good fortune in the communication I have with you; but Mr. President Pascal, to whom I had first placed it in hand and who had read it to the Company, issued a ruling in his own favor, based on the maxim: *let him who holds, keep* <note>original Latin: *qui tenet, teneat*; a legal principle suggesting that possession is nine-tenths of the law</note>, and to do justice to the interested parties, he took it upon himself to provide them with copies, ordering that afterward the original should be returned to my hands."

Roberval and Étienne Pascal made themselves his defenders; they sustained, in favor of the geometer of Toulouse <note>Pierre de Fermat</note>, a polemic that has remained famous (See *Works of Descartes*, Ed. Mersenne <note>The OCR begins mid-word due to the page break; the previous page ended with the start of Mersenne's name</note> addresses the former President Pascal: "Sir," he says, "I believe that all scholars will approve of the intention I have to imitate the Ancients, who dedicated their works to those who had a perfect knowledge of them, by presenting you with this *Treatise on the Organ* <note>original: *Traité de l'Orgue*</note>, one of the most admirable pneumatic <term>Pneumatiques: machines or instruments powered by air or wind</term> machines ever invented. For, whether one considers the Practice of Mechanics, or their Principles, and particularly those of Harmony, it would be very difficult to find a man who understands them better than you: and perhaps there is no one so learned who would not consider it a favor to learn what you have meditated upon this subject. This, Sir, is what made me resolve to offer you this book, as much to testify to posterity the esteem I hold for your very profound erudition in all branches of Mathematics, and particularly in this one, and for your very singular virtues, as to address to you the request of all honorable men who love this Art, who desire that you give them its rules, and that you explain to them all its charms and its secrets. I hope that the rare experiments you encounter in this book will invite you to search for their reasons... That is why I dare to promise all those who cherish the Muses <note>A classical reference to those who love the arts and sciences</note> that you will soon put the finishing touch to this part of Philosophy, so that it no longer fears appearing before the most learned in the company of other sciences, and that it may loudly confess that it is more obliged to you than to any other, by reason of the most excellent marriage you have made between Practice and Theory."

Mersenne’s testimony is noteworthy. It should be compared with the letter to Fermat, reproduced below, where Étienne Pascal and Roberval claim a place for experience alongside theoretical speculation <note>original: *spéculation a priori*; reasoning based on theory rather than observation</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the primary text of Mersenne’s dedication (on the previous page) to an editorial commentary or introduction regarding the scientific correspondence between Étienne Pascal, Gilles Personne de Roberval, and Pierre de Fermat concerning the nature of gravity and statics.</meta>

<page-num>175</page-num>

<header>ÉTIENNE PASCAL AND ROBERVAL TO FERMAT</header>

the hypothesis of attraction, the question of gravitation was a current topic in the learned world. Thus, the very year in which Fermat was drafting his *Geostatic Proposition* <note>original: *Propositio Geostatica*</note>, a work on the same subject by Beaugrand appeared which caused some stir in Mersenne’s circle: *Geostatics, or a mathematical dissertation on the varying weight of heavy bodies according to their various distances from the center of the Earth* <note>original: *Geostatice seu de vario pondere gravium secundum varia a Terræ centro intervalla dissertatio mathematica*</note>. Paris, 1636. The work was poor, and it was sharply attacked by Descartes <sup>1</sup>. The latter, moreover, concerned himself on several occasions with the hypotheses of geostatics <term>Geostatics: a 17th-century term for the study of the equilibrium of heavy bodies, specifically considering their weight relative to the Earth's center</term>, as evidenced by his correspondence with Mersenne (See in particular a letter from 1635, *Works of Descartes*, I, p. 324, and a letter from 1638, ibid. II, p. 222).

Étienne Pascal and Roberval lean toward thinking, like Kepler, that heaviness <note>The word "pesanteur" here refers to the force of gravity as understood before Newton</note> is not an internal quality residing in bodies and that it is explained by the laws of attractive motion. This view was developed later by Roberval in the *Aristarchus of Samos on the System of the World* <note>original: *Aristarchi Samii De Mundi Systemate*</note> which appeared in 1644.

But what is especially remarkable in the letter from the two scholars is the clairvoyance with which they identify the contradictions implied by the axioms that Fermat (along with most mechanicians of the time) regarded as obvious. An entire conception of statics <term>Statics: the branch of physics concerned with physical systems in equilibrium (at rest)</term> is called into question, as shown by Mr. Duhem in his fine study on *The Origins of Statics* <note>original: *Les Origines de la Statique*</note> (Volume II, 1906, pp. 169-177 and passim).

Fermat relies on the law of the equilibrium of the lever discovered by Archimedes. But he forgets that this law is only valid when the forces applied to the two ends of the lever are parallel forces: he still makes use of it in the hypothesis where the forces meet at the center of the earth, and even in the hypothesis where they are directly opposed. This paralogism <term>Paralogism: a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning, often committed unintentionally</term>, which leads Fermat into grave errors,

---

1. See the *Works of Descartes* <note>original: *OEuvres de Descartes*</note>, edited by Adam-Tannery, particularly the Addition to volume V, pp. 503-512.

<meta>This page continues the editorial commentary regarding the scientific debate between Pierre de Fermat and the Parisian mathematicians Étienne Pascal and Gilles Personne de Roberval. It specifically addresses the conceptual errors in Fermat’s "Geostatics" regarding the center of gravity and the direction of gravitational forces.</meta>

<page-num>176</page-num>

<header>WORKS</header>

stems from an erroneous opinion regarding the nature of the center of gravity. Most mechanicians <note>The term "mechanicians" refers to early scientists and engineers who studied the laws of physical motion and machines</note> of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance had unconsciously confused the center of gravity with the center of parallel forces. This confusion presents no disadvantages if one regards the forces of gravity as being parallel. However, Fermat’s reasonings specifically assume these forces to be concurrent <term>Concurrent forces: forces that are not parallel but instead meet at a single point—in this case, the center of the Earth</term>. This leads to a series of difficulties that bring the geometer of Toulouse <note>Pierre de Fermat, who served as a lawyer and magistrate in Toulouse</note> to adopt a purely scholastic <term>Scholastic: a traditional method of learning that relies on logic and the definitions of ancient authorities rather than experimental observation</term> definition of the center of gravity: “We shall henceforth define the center of gravity in the following manner: A point placed inside a body such that the body would remain in neutral equilibrium <term>Neutral equilibrium (or indifferent equilibrium): a state where an object, when moved, remains in its new position rather than returning to its start or falling further</term> if this point were joined to the center of the Earth.” (*Works of Fermat*, II, p. 25.)

Roberval and Étienne Pascal object to such principles: they demonstrate that the consequences Fermat drew from them are contrary to the most elementary rules of the composition of forces <term>Composition of forces: the method of finding a single "resultant" force that represents the combined effect of two or more individual forces</term>.

---

The principle that you require for <term>Geostatics</term> <note>Geostatics: a theoretical science proposed by Fermat to study the equilibrium of weights in relation to the Earth's center</note> is that, if two equal weights are joined by a firm and weightless straight line and, being thus arranged, they are able to descend freely, they will never rest until the midpoint of the line—which is the center of gravity as defined by the ancients <note>The "ancients" refers to classical mathematicians like Archimedes who defined the center of gravity for parallel forces</note>—unites with the common center of heavy things <note>A phrase used at the time to refer to the center of the Earth, toward which all objects were thought to "strive" or fall</note>.

This principle, which we considered a long time ago, as was previously sent to you, appears at first very plausible. But, when it comes to a principle, you know what conditions are required for it to be accepted: of which conditions, this primary one is lacking in the principle at issue here, namely that we are ignorant of what the root cause is that makes heavy bodies descend and from where the origin of this heaviness comes. Let CBD be a semicircular arc, and let one half of the weight be placed at D and the other half at C. Then, these two weights C and D, weighing toward A <note>the center of the Earth, which acts as the center of the circular arc</note>, will have no other effect on the lever CBD than to press equally on the ends C and D to bend it. However, if the weight is divided into more than two equal parts and, being spread across equal portions of the lever, two of these parts are located at points C and D, and the others within the space CBD, those located at C and D will not load the support B at all. Thus, it will be far from the case that all these parts, when spread out, would load the support as much as if they were all gathered together at point B.

# APPENDIX I

## JUDGMENT PRONOUNCED BY THE COMMISSIONERS **Ét[ienne]. Pascal**, **Mydorge**, **Beaugrand**, **Boulenger**, **Hérigone** ON THE INVENTION OF MR. **J.-B. Morin**.

We¹, the undersigned Commissioners, state regarding the first article: That generally the theory of finding longitudes through the motion of the moon <note>The "longitude problem" was the great maritime challenge of the era: finding one's east-west position at sea. Morin proposed using the moon's position relative to the stars as a celestial clock.</note> was discovered by several other astronomers: such as Gemma Frisius, Apianus, Werner, Nunes, Metius, and others. In confirmation of this, Gemma Frisius speaks thus of Oronce Fine, in his book *On the Astronomical Staff* <note>original Latin: "libro de Radio Astronomico." The astronomical staff, or cross-staff, was an instrument used to measure the angle between celestial bodies.</note>.

"Oronce Fine writes of a similar method for [determining] the meridians by the application of the moon to the Meridian circle; I wonder why he first attributed the invention to himself, as if almost none of the ancients could find the longitudes of regions by any other means than by eclipses. I, indeed, have already read in several authors the method of observing longitude through the movement of the moon."

Regarding the particular method used by the said Mr. Morin to find the moon's position—which involves the altitude <note>The "altitude" is the height of a celestial body above the horizon, measured in degrees.</note> of one fixed star, the altitude of the moon, and the distance from the moon to the star, all taken at the same moment—this same method is found in Gemma Frisius’s book titled *On the Use of Globes*, chapters 17 and 18. However, it was never judged that Gemma Frisius had successfully "found" longitudes, because of the recurring difficulties which have been overcome neither by Gemma Frisius himself, nor by Mr. Morin, nor by others.

To the 2nd Article we say: That, strictly speaking, the science of longitudes is not demonstrated; however, the triangles

the spherical problems <note>original Latin: "spherica proposita." These refer to the complex calculations of spherical trigonometry used to map positions on the curved surface of the Earth and the sky.</note> proposed by Mr. Morin himself have been excellently resolved and demonstrated. Nevertheless, nothing follows from this solution of triangles, as it lacks certain and true principles; seeing as it is founded upon tables and observations that cannot be sufficiently accurate for this purpose.

Regarding the 3rd point, we state: We are so far from judging his method as fit to bring any utility to Navigation through observations at sea that, on the contrary, we deem its practice on land to be most difficult, if not impossible. This is due both to the sheer number of necessary observations and the lack of required precision in the lunar tables <note>Astronomical tables were books of data predicting the positions of the moon and stars; at this time, they were still notoriously inaccurate.</note>, and because errors in both the observations and the tables are continually compounded throughout the series of calculations.

Regarding the 4th article, we state: That Mr. Morin commits a circular argument <note>original Latin: "circulum logicum." A logical fallacy where the proof relies on the very thing it is trying to prove.</note> by wishing to correct the tables using the methods he proposes, while simultaneously basing those very methods on the truth of the tables. Consequently, it is so far from the case that astronomical tables could be better reformed and made more accurate in a short time by his methods than by all the means used by the ancients <note>A reference to established astronomical traditions from Ptolemy through to contemporary observers like Tycho Brahe.</note>, that, on the contrary, we assert the tables can in no way be restored by these methods.

Done at the Arsenal <note>The Arsenal of Paris was a center for military and scientific administration under King Louis XIII.</note>, April 10, 1634. ...straight lines CI and IF, when extended, meet at points G, H, and E; finally, let GA be joined. The angle AFC at the center is double the angle AGC at the circumference; but angle AIC is equal to angle AFC in the same segment <note>original: "portione." In Euclidean geometry, an angle at the center is twice the angle at the circumference when they subtend the same arc.</note>. Therefore, angle AIC is double angle AGC. But angle AIC is equal to the sum of the two angles AGC and IAG <note>The exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles.</note>; therefore, angles IGA and IAG are equal, and consequently, the straight lines IA and IG are equal. However, since the perpendicular FK falls from the center F onto the line GC, the segments GK and KC are equal, and thus KI is half the difference between lines CI and IG—that is, between lines CI and IA.

Furthermore, the ratio of the perpendicular IB to the difference of the sides CI and IA is given. Therefore, the ratio of BI to IK is given, and when each is multiplied by the line AC, the ratio of the <term>rectangle formed by AC and BI</term> <note>original: "rectangulum sub AC in BI." In early modern geometry, the "rectangle" of two lines refers to the product of their lengths, representing area.</note> to the rectangle formed by AC and IK is given. 

But the rectangle formed by AC and BI is equal to the rectangle formed by AI and CO; for each is half <note>The original Latin "dimidium" (half) is used here, though geometrically these rectangles are double the area of the triangle; the author likely refers to the fact that the area relationship is constant.</note> of triangle AIC: therefore, the ratio of the rectangle formed by AI and CO to the rectangle formed by AC and IK is given. 

Now, the angle AIC is given by the hypothesis, and the angle COI is a right angle by construction: therefore the <term>shape</term> <note>original: "specie." To find the "species" of a triangle means to determine its internal proportions, effectively proving that all such triangles are similar.</note> of triangle COI is given. Consequently, the ratio of CO to CI is given, and thus the ratio of the rectangle formed by AI and CO to the rectangle formed by AI and IC is given. 

But we have proved that the ratio of the rectangle formed by AI and CO to the rectangle formed by AC and IK is given: therefore, the ratio of the rectangle formed by AI and IC to the rectangle formed by AC and IK is given. 

Now, in the <term>isosceles triangle</term> <note>A triangle with at least two equal sides.</note> AFC, the angle AFC is given by the hypothesis; therefore, angle FAC is given, and the equal angle CIF will therefore be given. Moreover, angle FKI is a right angle; therefore the shape of triangle FIK is given. Thus, the ratio of the line KI to IF is given, and consequently, the ratio of the rectangle formed by AC and IK to the rectangle formed by AC and IF is given. 

It has been proved, however, that the ratio of the rectangle AI × IC to the rectangle AC × IK is given. Therefore, the ratio of the rectangle AI × IC to the rectangle formed by AC and IF is given. Now, the rectangle formed by CI and IG is equal to the rectangle formed by CI and IA, because the lines IG and IA are equal, and to the rectangle CI × IG is equal the rectangle...

# PROBLEM PROPOSED BY ÉTIENNE PASCAL

...HIE <note>original: "HIE." This refers to the rectangle formed by the segments HI and IE.</note>: therefore, the ratio of the rectangle $HI \cdot IE$ to the rectangle formed by $AC$ and $IF$ is given. Let the ratio of $ED$ to $AC$ be given: since $AC$ is given, $ED$ will be given, and let it be placed in a straight line with $HE$ as shown in the figure; therefore, the rectangle $HI \cdot IE$ is to the rectangle $AC \cdot IF$ in the given ratio of $ED$ to $AC$. But as $DE$ is to $AC$, so is the rectangle $DE \cdot IF$ to the rectangle $AC \cdot IF$: therefore, just as the rectangle $HI \cdot IE$ is to the rectangle $AC \cdot IF$, so is the rectangle $DE \cdot IF$ to the same rectangle $AC \cdot IF$. Therefore, the rectangle $DE \cdot IF$ is equal to the rectangle $HI \cdot IE$. It has been proven that triangle $AFC$ is given in <term>kind</term> <note>original: "specie." In classical geometry, a figure "given in kind" is one whose shape and angles are known, even if its actual size is not.</note>; but the base $AC$ is given in size; therefore $AF$ is given, and thus twice $EH$ is given. 

To the equal rectangles $DE \cdot IF$ and $HI \cdot IE$, let the rectangle formed by $DE$ and $IH$ be added; the rectangle formed by $DE$ and $FH$ will then become equal to the rectangle $DIH$ <note>The text describes the algebraic-geometric manipulation of areas to isolate unknown segments.</note>. Moreover, the rectangle formed by $DE$ and $FH$ is given, because each of the lines $DE$ and $FH$ is given; therefore, the rectangle $DIH$ is given, and a **deficient square figure** <note>original: "deficiens figura quadrata." This refers to a standard technique in Greek geometry (found in Euclid's *Elements*) for solving a quadratic equation by "applying" an area to a line segment.</note> is applied to the given magnitude $DH$. Therefore, the line $IH$ is given, and consequently the remaining line $IF$ is also given. Since point $F$ is given in position, point $I$ is also given, and the entire triangle $AIC$ is established. It is not difficult to move backwards from the <term>analysis</term> to the <term>synthesis</term> <note>Analysis is the process of assuming the result and working back to known principles; synthesis is the formal proof constructed from those principles.</note>.

But, to remove all doubt, it is very easily proven that the sought-after triangle is similar to the discovered triangle $AIC$ in the second figure (moreover, triangle $AIC$ can have its vertex on either side of point $F$, at an equal distance from point $F$ on both sides; for it will be the same in kind and size, even though the position varies). For if the sought-after triangle is not similar to the one found, while the same base remains, its vertex will fall either between points $F$ and $I$, or between points $I$ and $A$. (It makes no difference which side is chosen; for the same conclusion is reached for triangle $AIC$ regarding the side $FC$ by an equal demonstration). Let the vertex first be between $A$ and $I$, and let the sought-after triangle be placed, if possible, similar to triangle $AMC$. Let $FM$ be joined and the perpendicular $FP$ be dropped. The ratio of the perpendicular $MN$ to $MP$ will be given...

<summary>Étienne Pascal demonstrates the final steps of a geometric construction by showing how unknown line segments can be determined through the "application of areas," concluding that the resulting triangle is unique. He then begins a proof by contradiction to confirm that any other potential triangle must be similar to the one found.</summary>

by hypothesis <note>original: "ex hypothesi."</note>, and therefore equal to the ratio of $IB$ to $IK$ which we have proved equal to the given ratio: which is absurd. For since in triangle $FMP$ the angle at $M$ is equal to the angle at $I$ of triangle $IFK$, the triangles $FIK$ and $FMP$ will be similar; but $FM$ is greater than $FI$; therefore $MP$ is greater than $IK$. However, $MN$ is less than $IB$: therefore the ratio of $MN$ to $MP$ cannot be the same as the ratio of $IB$ to $IK$. If the point $M$ were between $I$ and $F$, it will be proved that the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>The "perpendicular" refers to the altitude of the triangle.</note> increases and the difference of the sides decreases, and this by the same argument, and thus changing the proportion. If the point $M$ were on the segment $FC$, we would use the second triangle $AIC$, and the proof would be the same, so that it would be useless to dwell longer on these cases.

It is established, therefore, that the sought triangle is similar to the discovered triangle $AIC$, and it is clear that the proposal has been satisfied.

It is proposed, if it pleases both Monsieur Pascal and Monsieur Roberval, that this problem be solved:

> *At a given point on the **spiral of Galileo**¹* <note>original: "helice Galilæi." This refers to a specific curve where the radius increases in proportion to the square of the time or angle, studied by Galileo in his work on falling bodies.</note>, *find the tangent.*

Moreover, Monsieur Roberval knows the nature of this kind of spiral.

Having solved this problem ourselves, we await a solution from these most learned men; or, if they prefer, we shall share it with them, and indeed even a general method regarding the <term>contacts</term> <note>original: "contactibus." In the geometry of this period, "contacts" refers to the theory of tangents and how lines touch curves.</note> of curved lines.

But lest we seem to have departed from the present matter of triangles empty-handed, these questions may be proposed:

*Given the base, the vertex angle, and the sum of the altitude and the difference of the sides, find the triangle;*

*Given the base, the vertex angle, and the difference between the altitude and the difference of the sides, find the triangle;*

# PROBLEM PROPOSED BY ÉTIENNE PASCAL

*Given the base, the vertex angle, and the rectangle <note>original: "rectangulo." In this context, it refers to the product of two lengths, conceptually the area of a rectangle formed by them.</note> formed by the difference of the sides and the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>The altitude or height of the triangle drawn from the vertex to the base.</note>, find the triangle;*

*Given the base, the vertex angle, and the sum of the squares of the perpendicular and the difference of the sides, find the triangle;*

And many similar problems, the explanation of which I believe most learned men will find more easily than the proposed problem or theorem regarding the contact <note>original: "de contactu." This refers to finding the tangent line.</note> of the spiral.

But it should be observed in questions regarding triangles that whenever a problem can be solved by <term>plane geometry</term> <note>original: "per plana." Problems solvable using only a straightedge and compass.</note>, one should not resort to <term>solid geometry</term> <note>original: "ad solida." Problems requiring more complex curves like conic sections (ellipses, parabolas, hyperbolas).</note>: which, since most learned men know this, it was perhaps superfluous to add.

# VERSES BY MISS JACQUELINE PASCAL <note>Jacqueline Pascal (1625–1661) was a French child prodigy and the younger sister of Blaise Pascal. She later became a nun at Port-Royal.</note>

## RONDEAU. <note>A rondeau is a traditional French poetic form characterized by a repeating refrain and a specific rhyme scheme.</note>

->*May 1637.*<-

To another, the eye of Melite <note>Melite was a common name for a fictional beloved in 17th-century pastoral poetry and drama.</note>
Would appear to have merit;
But, beside your beauty,
The sweetness of novelty
Can have nothing that excites me.
Love me then, my Chrysolite. <note>original: "Crisolite." A yellowish-green gemstone, used here as a poetic term of endearment for a precious lady.</note>
My extreme love invites you
To keep your cruelty
->For another.<-
For, if my affection is provoked,
You will soon find yourself reduced
To seeking my loyalty.
But preserve your kindness,
And have no fear that I will leave you
->For another.<-

## ANOTHER RONDEAU.

->*May 1637.*<-

For you I gave up my heart;
But you possess such severity <note>original: "rigueur." In the language of 17th-century "gallantry," rigueur referred to a lady's coldness or refusal to acknowledge a suitor's advances.</note>
That if you were not so beautiful
I would, without doubt, be unfaithful.

### SONG TO THE TUNE OF A SARABANDE¹. <note>The Sarabande was a slow, stately dance in triple meter. Though it originated as a lively Spanish dance, by the time of this poem it had become a graceful staple of the French court.</note>

->*December 1637.*<-

Clymene was the queen of my soul.
That ungrateful lady
Despised my vows.
But when I saw the eyes of Dorimene <note>Clymene and Dorimene are "stock" names—fictional personas used in 17th-century "precious" poetry to allow the writer to explore themes of love and fickle hearts without referring to real individuals.</note>
I left Clymene,
I burned for them.

Then my happiness, comparable only to itself,
From a miserable lover
Made me happy,
By showing me the eyes of Dorimene.
Then, leaving Clymene,
I burned for them.

## TO MR. PRESIDENT PASCAL, HER FATHER.

### EPIGRAM. <note>An epigram is a short, witty poem, often written to commemorate a specific event or person.</note>

->*March 1638.*<-

Dear father, do not fear the effort
Of time, nor even of death;
It is in vain that they wage war against you¹.
They may well snatch your presence from our eyes;
But your soul shall live forever in the heavens,
And your renown upon the earth.

Her eye, which has no equal,
Does not wish the sun to suffer
For fear of putting it to shame. <note>This is a classic "precious" conceit, suggesting the lady's beauty is so bright that it would embarrass the sun, so she hides it behind shutters to be merciful.</note>

->ACROSTIC STANZAS. <note>An acrostic is a poem where the first letter of each line spells out a word or name. In the original French, these lines spell out "PHILIBERTE DE MONTELON," the maiden name of Madame de Morangis.</note><-

Trouble no more, I pray, a dejected spirit.

VERSES OF JACQUELINE PASCAL

## STANZAS TO THE QUEEN,

->TO THANK HER MAJESTY FOR THE KIND WELCOME SHE DEIGNED<-
->TO GIVE TO THE PREVIOUS VERSES,<-
->LIKEWISE PRESENTED TO HER MAJESTY.<-

My dear children, my little verses, <note>It was a common literary trope for poets to refer to their poems as their "children."</note>
Can there be found, in this vast universe,
A blessing that one could call comparable to yours?
You are filled with happiness;
The Queen overwhelmed you with honor,
Her Majesty gave you a favorable welcome.

Her hand deigned to receive you,
Her eye full of sweetness looked down to see you,
You were heard in silence by her ears;
And, through an excess of kindness,
Without your having deserved it,
Her mouth called you "little wonders." <note>Historical accounts suggest that Queen Anne was truly charmed by the young Jacqueline Pascal, who was only about thirteen years old at the time, and frequently praised her precocious talent in these very terms.</note>

But despite my glorious fate,
The extreme sorrow of no longer seeing her eyes
Leaves my soul constantly open to grief;
So much so that a moment of pleasure
Only serves to increase my desire
And leaves me with an eternal regret for my loss. <note>The "loss" refers to the poet's departure from the Queen's presence after their meeting.</note>

# POEMS BY JACQUELINE PASCAL

### TO MADAME DE MORANGIS, <note>Marie de Bellièvre, the wife of Antoine d’Aubray, Seigneur de Morangis. The Morangis family were close acquaintances of the Pascals.</note>

#### SONNET.

->*July 1638.*<-

To truly paint Philis, <note>A common pastoral name used in 17th-century "precious" poetry to address a lady of high society.</note> a true miracle of the heavens,
Her divine virtues which have no equal,
The charms of her body, which captivate our eyes,
And those of her mind which charm our ears,

I would say that her eye, ever victorious,
Compels all mortals to dedicate their vigils to her,
That her attractions are such that they captivate the gods,
And make them wonder at their own wonders.

But to properly express her rare qualities,
My painting <note>In this context, "painting" refers to the verbal portrait or the poem itself.</note> does not possess enough great beauties;
Always one of my colors is unpleasing.

Let us then abandon this design full of temerity,
For I feel, to paint a divinity,
My brush is too coarse and my hand too heavy.

->*July 1638.*<-

Claris, <note>Another conventional poetic pseudonym, likely referring again to Madame de Morangis or another lady in her circle.</note> do not be cruel
In equal measure to your beauty;

## STANZAS COMPOSED IMPROMPTU. <note>The French "sur le champ" indicates these were written extemporaneously, a highly valued skill in the literary salons of the 1600s.</note>

### *July 1638.*

One day, deep within a wood,
I was surprised by a voice;
It was the shepherdess Silvie
Who was speaking to her dear lover,
And said to him as her only greeting:
"I love you much more, without doubt, than my life."

Then I heard this handsome lover
Answer her amorously:
"With pleasure my soul is ravished;
I am dying, come to my aid,
And to cure me, say always:
'I love you much more, without doubt, than my life.'"

Live, O happy lovers,
In these perfect joys,
Despite the rage of envy;
And may this mutual discourse
Be commonplace in your loves:
"I love you much more, without doubt, than my life."

### EPIGRAM, <note>An epigram is a short, concise poem, often concluding with a witty or significant thought. Here, Jacqueline uses it to offer a brief, humble dedication of her talents.</note>

#### FOR THANKING GOD FOR THE GIFT OF POETRY.

I am not so strongly seized
By the favors of poetry,
That I do not humbly acknowledge before all,
Great God! that it is not study
That gave me this skill, <note>The original "habitude" implies a natural facility or a state of being rather than just a "habit."</note>

### STANZAS ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

->*August 1638.*<-

Father of this great universe,
If the ardor for making verses
Holds my soul enchanted by powerful springs, <note>The "ressorts" (springs or mechanisms) suggest the internal workings of the mind or soul, a common metaphor in 17th-century thought to describe divine or natural inspiration.</note>
I humbly confess before all
That I hold this ardor from you;
From you, I say, O great God! without having deserved it.

Yes, I hold from your goodness
This beautiful gift so strongly desired
By the ardent desires of so many noble souls; <note>The phrase "belles âmes" (noble or beautiful souls) was a standard term for people of refined character and high social or intellectual standing.</note>
And by a secret judgment,
My young and weak understanding <term>understanding (French: *entendement*): In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to the intellectual power of the soul to conceive ideas and perceive truth.</term>

# LETTER FROM MADEMOISELLE GILBERTE PASCAL
## TO MR. PASCAL, HER FATHER.

->Sir, my father,<-

I rejoice that every time I have the good fortune to write to you, I am compelled to always say the same thing: which is the good state in which, thanks be to God, the whole household finds itself. At present, we have no other desire than the honor of seeing you. While waiting for that, we have no other consolation than the hope of soon having news from you. I entreat you, on behalf of everyone, to send us word as often as you can. In the meantime, I will tell you that since my eye ailment, the first outing I made was to the home of the Lady Constable¹ where Madame de Morangis took me the day before yesterday. She made every imaginable offer of assistance, as is her custom, showing me the sympathy <note>The original French uses "ressentiment," which in the 17th century meant a shared feeling or reaction—here, a sense of grief or compassion—rather than modern "resentment."</note> she felt regarding my sister's accident <note>This likely refers to Jacqueline Pascal, who suffered a severe case of smallpox in 1638 that significantly altered her appearance.</note>. She also told me that the Queen <note>Anne of Austria, wife of King Louis XIII.</note> had asked her for news of it and had shown herself to be touched that this misfortune had befallen her. ### TO MY LORD THE MOST EMINENT CARDINAL DUKE OF RICHELIEU
### AFTER THE COMEDY¹.

### April 3, 1639.

Do not be astonished, incomparable Armand, <note>Armand Jean du Plessis, better known as Cardinal Richelieu, the powerful chief minister to King Louis XIII.</note>
If I have poorly satisfied your eyes and ears;
My spirit, agitated by unparalleled fears,
Forbids my body both voice and movement.
But to make me capable here of pleasing you,
Recall from exile my miserable father.
It is the blessing I expect from a signal kindness;
Save this innocent man from manifest peril.
Thus you will restore to me the entire liberty
Of spirit and body, of voice and gesture.

### LETTER FROM JACQUELINE PASCAL TO HER FATHER.

->Monsieur my father,<-

that took place yesterday at the mansion of Richelieu, where we performed *Tyrannical Love*$^1$ <note>original: "l'Amour tyrannique"</note> before **Mr.** the Cardinal. I am going to tell you point by point everything that happened.

First, **Mr.** de Montdory <note>Guillaume des Gilberts, known as Montdory, was the leading actor of the time and a friend of the Pascal family.</note> entertained **Mr.** the Cardinal from three o'clock until seven o'clock, and spoke to him almost the entire time about you, on his own behalf and not yours; that is to say, he told him that he knew you, and spoke very favorably to him of your virtue, your knowledge, and your other good qualities. He also spoke of this matter of the annuities <note>Étienne Pascal had been in hiding after leading a protest against the reduction of interest on government bonds (rentes).</note>, and told him that things had not happened as people had made him believe, and that you had only been at **Mr.** the Chancellor's house once, and even then it was to calm the disturbance; and, as proof of this, he recounted to him that you had begged **Mr.** Fayet$^2$ to warn **Mr.**..., he also told him that I would speak to him after the play. Finally, he told him so many things that he obliged **Mr.** the Cardinal to say to him: "I promise you to grant her everything she asks of me." **Mr.** de Montdory said the same thing to Madame d'Aiguillon <note>Marie Madeleine de Vignerot, Duchess of Aiguillon, Richelieu's influential niece.</note>, who told him that she felt great pity for the situation and that she would contribute everything she could from her side. That is all that happened before the play. As for the performance, **Mr.** the Cardinal appeared to take great pleasure in it, but especially when I was speaking. He began to laugh, as did everyone else in the room.

As soon as the play was finished, I came down from the stage

# VERSES AND LETTER FROM JACQUELINE PASCAL

...with the intention of speaking to Madame d’Aiguillon; but **Mr.** the Cardinal was leaving, which was the reason I stepped straight toward him, for fear of losing that opportunity by going to pay my respects to Madame d’Aiguillon; besides that, **Mr.** de Montdory <note>Guillaume des Gilberts, the lead actor.</note> was urging me strongly to go speak to **Mr.** the Cardinal. I went there then, and recited to him the verses that I am sending you, which he received with extreme affection and such extraordinary endearments <note>original: "caresses." In the 17th century, this referred to outward signs of favor or paternal affection, such as a kind word or a pat on the head.</note> that it was unimaginable; for, first, as soon as he saw me coming toward him, he cried out: "There is the little Pascal girl"; then he embraced me and kissed me, and while I was reciting my verses, he held me constantly in his arms and kissed me at every moment with great satisfaction; and then, when I had spoken them, he said to me: "Go, I grant you everything you ask; write to your father that he may return in all safety." 

Thereupon, Madame d’Aiguillon <note>Richelieu’s niece and a powerful figure at court.</note> approached, who said to **Mr.** the Cardinal: "Truly, Monsieur, you must do something for that man; I have heard speak of him; he is a very honest man and very learned; it is a pity that he remains useless <note>original: "inutile." Here meaning he is unable to serve the state or use his talents while in hiding.</note>. He has a son <note>Blaise Pascal, who was 15 at the time.</note> who is very knowledgeable in mathematics, and yet is only fifteen years old." 

Thereupon **Mr.** the Cardinal said once more that I should inform you that you might return in all safety. As I saw him in such a good mood, I asked him if he would find it agreeable for you to pay your respects to him; he told me that you would be welcome; and then, among other talk, he said to me: "Tell your father, when he has returned, to come see me." And he repeated that to me three or four times. After that, as Madame d’Aiguillon was leaving, my sister <note>Gilberte Pascal, the eldest sibling.</note> went to greet her, to whom she showed much affection, and asked her where my brother was, saying that she would have very much liked to see him. This was the reason that my sister [presented] him to her...

The Duchess of Aiguillon further advocates for the family by highlighting the mathematical genius of the young Blaise Pascal.</summary>

## REPLY FROM THE YOUNG PASCAL

### TO MR. DE SCUDÉRY <note>Georges de Scudéry (1601–1667) was a prominent novelist and playwright of the era, and a rival to Pierre Corneille.</note>

If I were that Cassandra,
Whose peerless brilliance
Could once reduce to ash
The very heart of the sun,
I would not ask of this god of Parnassus <note>Apollo, the Greek god of poetry and prophecy. In the myth, he granted Cassandra the gift of prophecy in exchange for her love.</note>
The gift of prophecy; and I wish to admit
That if he allowed me to make a wish
I would ask him for the art of praising you well.

## TO MY LORD THE MOST EMINENT CARDINAL-DUKE DE RICHELIEU

### EPIGRAM <note>In the 17th century, an epigram was a short, witty poem often written to praise a patron or comment on a social situation.</note>

### *May 1639.*

I complained of fate, O incomparable Duke!
Which seemed to forbid my eyes from seeing you,
And to make my lot doubly miserable,
Gave me the hope but not the power.
But since the happy day when my ravished soul,
In the joy of seeing you, satisfied its longing,
Tasted more pleasures than one could hope for,
I bless its clemency along with its destiny,
Which had reserved for me within a single day
All the good that I could ever have desired. <note>This poem refers to Jacqueline’s performance before Richelieu, which led to the Cardinal pardoning her father, Étienne Pascal, who had been in hiding due to a dispute over government bonds.</note>

Torments a young beauty,

## DEVOTIONAL SONNET

Great and perfect author <note>In the 17th century, "author" was frequently used as a title for God, signifying Him as the creator and designer of the world.</note> of the earth and the waves,
Creator and support of the least of mortals,
I come with respect, to the foot of your altars,

It is there that with reason all my hope is founded,
And it is there that, awaiting eternal decrees,
I brave the demons and their cruel designs,
And that I hear without fear the rumbling thunder.

Renders my heart downcast, my designs powerless,
And moderates the fire that reanimated my zeal.

Great God! if I end in these cold languors,
Preserve at the very least my sincere ardors,
And grant that my love may never be mortal.

# INTRODUCTION

The *Essay on Conics* <term>Conics: the study of curves—circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas—created by intersecting a cone with a flat plane</term>, a small broadside in the form of a poster, was printed in Paris in 1640. We know of two extant copies: the first is found in the Royal Library of Hanover among the papers left by Leibniz <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), the German philosopher and mathematician who co-invented calculus</note>; the second is inserted into a copy of the mathematical works of Pascal (*Letters of Dettonville and Treatise on the Arithmetical Triangle*) which belonged to Perier <note>Florin Périer, the husband of Pascal's sister, Gilberte</note> and which is kept at the National Library (Res. V, 859). The *Essay* was reprinted for the first time in Bossut’s edition.

It is probable that Pascal’s essay was very little known. We know, in fact, that Huygens <note>Christiaan Huygens (1629–1695), the Dutch scientist who invented the pendulum clock and studied the rings of Saturn</note> was unaware of it in 1656 (*Letter from Huygens to Carcavi, Complete Works of Huygens*, I, p. 428), and we read elsewhere in the *Acts of the Erudite* <note>original: "Acta Eruditorum," the first scientific journal of the German-speaking lands</note> of 1685 (Leipzig, 1685, p. 400), regarding the works of La Hire on conic sections: "Since nothing has been published by Pascal on these matters, and only a few things by Desargues..." <note>original: "Cum nihil de his Pascalii, Desarguesii autem pauca sint edita..."</note> Thus, the *Essay on Conics* never entered the public domain.

->*<-
->* *<-

It was during the winter of 1639-1640 that Pascal composed ¹ the *Essay on Conics*. Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a monk known as the "post-box of Europe" for his massive correspondence with scientists</note> spoke of it for the first time to Descartes in a letter dated November 12, 1639, expressing his admiration for the precocity of the young Pascal ¹. Descartes replied (*Works of Descartes*, Cerf edition, vol. II, p. 627): “I do not find it strange that there are those who demonstrate the properties of Conics more easily than Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 200 BC), the ancient Greek mathematician known as "The Great Geometer" for his work on conics</note>; for it is extreme—”

---

1. See the *Life of Blaise Pascal* by Madame Perier, *above*, p. 57.

# WORKS

...tremely long and muddled, and everything he has demonstrated is in itself quite easy. But one could well propose other things concerning Conics <term>Conics: the study of geometric shapes like ellipses and parabolas formed by slicing a cone</term> that a sixteen-year-old child would have difficulty untangling." — On March 11, 1640, Descartes says he had not yet received Pascal's essay, which Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), the primary correspondent and "hub" for scientists across Europe</note> had promised him (*Works of Descartes*, III, p. 40). On April 1, 1640, he had received it and wrote (ibid., III, p. 47): "I have also received the Essay concerning Conics by the son of Mr. Pascal, and before having read half of it, I judged that he had learned from Monsieur Desargues <note>Girard Desargues (1591–1661), a pioneer of projective geometry and a mentor to the young Pascal</note>; which was confirmed to me, immediately after, by the confession he made himself."

These few lines from Descartes raised a rather unexpected controversy¹, so much so that in the margin of the second edition of the *Letters of Mr. Descartes*, Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), a devoted friend and editor of Descartes' works</note> felt he should comment on them in these terms: "People who believe they know well say that this is false: it may be false; but I do not doubt that Mr. Descartes says the truth, for he was not a man to concoct lies." On the other hand, we read in the *Life of Monsieur Descartes* by Baillet (II, p. 40): "When, following some clarifications, he [Descartes] saw that it was highly unlikely that anything of this work [the *Essay for Conics*] could be attributed to his friend Mr. Desargues, he preferred to believe that Mr. Pascal the Father was the true author, rather than to persuade himself that a child of that age was capable of a work of such force²." (*Cf.* the *Preface* to the *Treatise on the Equilibrium of Liquids*, below, vol. III, p. 273.)

similar because "it would assume, regarding the *Essay*, an admiration on the part of Descartes of which he shows little evidence and which was not in his character to feel." In fact, we have no reason to believe that Descartes was not expressing his true thoughts when he said that the young Pascal had learned from Desargues. That was the exact truth. Pascal did not hide it, and one can see at first glance that the terminology of the *Essay* is partly borrowed from Desargues. Moreover, the influence exerted by Desargues on Pascal was recognized by all his contemporaries. Oldenburg <note>Henry Oldenburg (c. 1619–1677), the first secretary of the Royal Society in London</note>, for example, wrote to Leibniz while pointing out the treatise on conics: "We have heard that this treatise... follows the Desarguesian method, which he perhaps absorbed as a disciple of that man" <note>original: "Inaudivimus hunc tractatum... insistere methodo Des-Argueanæ quam forte ceu viri illius discipulus imbiberat"</note> (Oldenburg to Leibniz, April 6, 1673. Cf. below, Vol. II, p. 218). The same opinion is expressed by both the detractors and the friends of Desargues. Thus, Grégoire Huret¹, in a pamphlet titled: "*Fundamental secret of the treatise on conics of Mr. Desargues entitled: Lessons of Darkness and Rough-draft Project, together with some considerations thereupon*" <note>Desargues often used eccentric titles; Huret is mocking his obscure style</note> speaks of "Mr. Pascal the son, his [Desargues'] disciple in this matter." And Bosse, the favorite student of the geometer from Lyon, declares at the end of his *Treatise on Geometrical Practices* (*Works of Desargues*, II, 58) that Desargues held the esteem of the late Mr. Pascal, Lord of Ethonville, the marvel of the century, "who published about him in 1640 in a printed work titled *Essay on Conics*."

### WORKS

The *Essay* was inspired by the ideas of Desargues. But it was also known that he had found something new. Leibniz stated as much¹; Desargues himself recognized it, saying that he was waiting to provide the key to certain propositions until the moment when "the demonstration of that great proposition, *The Pascal* <note>This refers to Pascal’s Theorem regarding a hexagon inscribed in a conic section, which Pascal himself called the "Mystic Hexagram."</note>, sees the light of day," and adding "that the aforementioned Pascal can say that the four books of Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240–190 BC), a Greek mathematician known as the "Great Geometer" for his definitive work on conic sections.</note> are indeed either a case or a consequence of this great proposition, the explanation of which I have left to the author's discretion." (Cited by Curabelle, one of Desargues' enemies, in his *Examination of the works of Mr. Desargues*, 1644. *Works of Desargues*, II, p. 387).

-> * <-
-> * * <-

Girard Desargues of Lyon (1593–1662) had come to settle in Paris, probably between 1620 and 1630. He distinguished himself through his personal merit and his extensive mathematical knowledge, taking particular care "to ease the labors of craftsmen through the ingenuity of his inventions" (Baillet, *The Life of Descartes*, I, p. 143). He frequented the informal academy of Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a monk and mathematician whose network of correspondents acted as a clearinghouse for scientific ideas across Europe.</note> and Le Pailleur; moreover, he was intimately acquainted with Descartes², and was highly esteemed by Fermat³.

Though bound by friendship with the leading scholars of his time, Desargues nonetheless did not maintain very close scientific relations with them. He boasted of reading nothing, of not...

However, it must be admitted that he pushed things further."

### ESSAY ON CONICS

owing nothing to anyone, drawing everything from his own invention and his own imagination <note>original: "son cru et de son imagination"</note> (*See the Charitable Advice on the various works and loose sheets of Mr. Girard Desargues of Lyon. 1642. Works of Desargues*, II, 263 and throughout). Desargues' beautiful methods, based on projective geometry <note>A field of geometry dealing with the properties of figures that remain unchanged under projection, such as how a circle looks like an ellipse when viewed from an angle.</note> and entirely independent of the works of Descartes and Fermat, belong to him alone; they were generally only half-understood by his contemporaries, who were more preoccupied with analysis <note>In this context, "analysis" refers to the use of algebraic equations to solve geometric problems, a method championed by Descartes.</note> than with pure geometry. Thus, Descartes wrote to Mersenne (*Works of Descartes*, II, p. 499): "Between us, I can hardly imagine what he could have written regarding conics. For although it is easy to explain them more clearly than Apollonius or any other, it is nonetheless, it seems to me, very difficult to say anything about them without Algebra that could not be made much easier through Algebra."

It was only after forty years that the merit and fruitfulness of Desargues' methods were clearly recognized by the geometer La Hire. "In the year 1679, in the month of July," writes La Hire, "I read for the first time and transcribed this booklet by Mr. Desargues to have a more perfect knowledge of it. It had been more than six years since I had printed my first work on conic sections, and I have no doubt that if I had had any communication of this treatise, I would not have discovered the method I used; for I would not have believed it possible to find a simpler way that was also as general" (*Works of Desargues*, I, p. 231).

It is, as we can see, extremely remarkable that, alone among the geometers who met Desargues at the Mersenne Academy, the young Pascal was able to assimilate the ideas of the Lyonnais geometer and undertook to progress along the same path.

It is perhaps not distinct from the *Lessons of Darkness* <note>The "Leçons de ténèbres" or "Lessons of Darkness" refers to a Catholic service held during the last three days of Holy Week, characterized by the gradual extinguishing of candles. Huret (see above), and noted in these terms by Oldenburg to Leibniz:

> "Not so long ago, we saw the *Perspective* of Huret, in which the conics of Mr. Desargues, called 'Lessons of Darkness,' are criticized and rejected; of these, it is said that only fifty copies were printed, such that it is very difficult to obtain even one from so few." <note>original Latin: "Vidimus non ita dudum Perspectivam Heureti in qua perstringuntur rejiciunturque Dni Des Argues conica Leçons de ténèbres nuncupata, quarum non nisi 50 exemplaria impressa dicuntur, adeo ut perdifficile sit vel unum ex tam paucis procurare."</note>

The principal innovation of Desargues, in his research on conics <note>Curves obtained by intersecting a cone with a plane, specifically the circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.</note>, consisted of using perspective as a foundation. It was in this way that he was led to consider the ellipse, the hyperbola, and the parabola as different species of the same family, sharing in common all the properties that projection does not alter. On the other hand, Desargues proposed to bring the study of conic sections back to a unified whole by making it derive entirely from a small number of fundamental propositions:

> "There is," he says, "such a one of the propositions demonstrated here, or such of the consequences which follow from it, which encompasses together several of the propositions on conics by Apollonius <note>A Greek geometer (c. 240–190 BC) known for his definitive work on conic sections.</note>, even from the end of the third book. And, after the lemmas or premises, four of these propositions contain the entire dissection of the cone by the plane" (*Works of Desargues*, II, p. 227).

Pascal, too, takes perspective as his starting point and seeks to encompass all the properties of conic sections in a very small number of propositions (*nearly a single proposition* <note>original Latin: "propositio fere unica"</note>). But the remarkable lemma which he uses for this—

# ESSAY ON CONICS

The end is a new proposition, an invention that belongs to him [Pascal]. This lemma, known today by the name Pascal's theorem, was not, in fact, among the propositions given in the *Rough Draft Project* <note>original: "Brouillon Project"</note> as being those that should "precede all the rest"; it is evidently to this that Desargues refers when he speaks of "this great proposition, the Pascale."

In Desargues' *Rough Draft Project*, the principal questions treated relate to involution—to pencils of lines in involution—to quadrilaterals, whether general or inscribed in a conic, intersected by a transversal—to the theory of poles and polars—and to the focal and diametrical properties of conics. These are undoubtedly the same questions that Pascal intended to resolve with the help of his fundamental lemma. We see, indeed, by the samples given to us in the *Essay*, that Pascal's goal was not so much to treat new problems as to rediscover known properties by "addressing them in a more universal manner than usual." In progressing this way along the path opened by Desargues, Pascal fulfilled the wish of the mathematician from Lyon, who often expressed the hope that others would come to replace him and "clean up" his *Rough Draft*¹.

In Pascal's mind, the *Essay on Conics* <note>original: "Essay pour les coniques"</note> was only intended to be a specimen of an extensive work treating the properties of conic sections. This work, which Pascal was still occupied with in 1654, was likely never completed². Only fragments of it ever existed, of which only a small part has reached us (the *Generation of Conic Sections* <note>original Latin: "Generatio Conisectionum"</note>, see volume II, pages 234 and following).

2. See below, vol. II, p. 217.

# ESSAY ON CONICS

## FIRST DEFINITION.

When several straight lines meet at the same point, or are all parallel to each other, all these lines are said to be of the same <term>order or the same arrangement</term> <note>original: "ordre ou de mesme ordonnance". In modern geometry, this collection of lines is called a "pencil."</note>, and the multitude of these lines is called an order of lines, or an arrangement of lines $^1$.

## SECOND DEFINITION.

By the term <term>conic section</term> <note>original: "section de Cone"</note>, we mean the circumference of the Circle, the Ellipse, the Hyperbola, the Parabola, and the rectilinear Angle: because a Cone cut parallel to its base, or through its vertex, or in the three other directions that produce the Ellipse, the Hyperbola, and the Parabola, produces in the Conic surface either the circumference of a circle, or

<header>ESSAY ON CONICS. By B. P. <note>B. P. stands for Blaise Pascal.</note></header>

# DEFINITION THE FIRST.

<image-desc>Three small circular diagrams numbered 1, 2, and 3, depicting various conic sections: a circle, an ellipse, and an angle/parabola.</image-desc>

When several straight lines meet at the same point, or are all parallel to one another, all these lines are said to be of the same <term>order</term> <note>Pascal uses "order" or "ordinance" to describe what we now call a "pencil" of lines—lines that either intersect at a single point or are parallel (intersecting at infinity).</note> or of the same ordinance, and the multitude of these lines is called an order of lines, or an ordinance of lines.

### DEFINITION II.

By the word <term>section of a Cone</term> <note>Now commonly called a "conic section."</note> we mean the circumference of a Circle, the Ellipse, the Hyperbola, the Parabola, and the Rectilinear Angle, insofar as a Cone cut parallel to its base, or through its vertex, or in the three other directions which generate the Ellipse, the Hyperbola, and the parabola, generates within the Conic surface either the circumference of a Circle, or an Angle, or the Ellipse, or the Hyperbola, or the parabola.

### DEFINITION III.

By the words <term>single straight</term> <note>original: "droicte miſfeul." An archaic term Pascal used to denote a simple straight line.</note>, we mean a straight line.

### LEMMA I.

<image-desc>A large geometric diagram labeled Fig. 1. showing points M and S with intersecting lines and a circle passing through several intersection points, labeled with various letters like K, V, A, µ.</image-desc>

<margin>Figure I.</margin> If, in the plane M, S, Q, two straight lines MK and MV originate from point M, and two straight lines SK and SV originate from point S; and if K is the meeting point of lines MK and SK, and V is the meeting point of lines MV and SV, and A is the meeting point of lines MA and SA, and μ <note>The Greek letter mu.</note> is the meeting point of lines MV and SK, and μ is the meeting point of lines MK and SV; and if through two of the four points A, K, μ, V, which are not in the same straight line as points M and S—such as through points K and V—there passes the circumference of a circle cutting the lines MV, MP, SV, SK at points O, P, Q, N; then it is said that the lines MS, NO, and PQ are of the same order.

<image-desc>A smaller geometric diagram labeled Fig. 2. showing a set of intersecting lines within a triangular configuration, with points labeled D, F, A, E, B, C, N, K, G.</image-desc>

### LEMMA II.

If several planes pass through the same straight line and are cut by another plane, all the lines of the sections of these planes are of the same order as the line through which the said planes pass.

<margin>Fig. 1.</margin> Having established these two Lemmas and some easy consequences of them, we will demonstrate that, the same conditions being set as in the first Lemma, if through points K and V there passes any section of a Cone which cuts the lines MK, MV, SK, SV at points P, O, N, Q, the lines MS, NO, and PQ will be of the same order; this will be a third Lemma.

Following these three Lemmas and some consequences of them, we shall give complete Conic Elements, namely all the properties of <term>diameters</term> <note>Lines passing through the center of a conic.</note> and of <term>latus rectum and transverse axes</term> <note>Technical terms for the primary axes and scaling factors of conic sections.</note>, the properties of <term>tangents</term>, etc., the unfolding of the Cone, the description of conic sections by points, etc.

<margin>Fig. I.</margin> We will also demonstrate that if there are three straight lines DE, DG, DH, which the lines AP, AR cut at points F, G, H, C, γ, β, and if on the line DC the point E is determined, the <term>compound ratio</term> <note>A ratio formed by multiplying other ratios together.</note> of the ratios of the <term>rectangle</term> <note>In 17th-century geometry, the "rectangle" of two lines means the product of their lengths (the area of a rectangle formed by them).</note> of EF and FG to the rectangle of EC and Cγ, and of the line Aγ to the line AC, is the same as the compound ratio of the ratios of the rectangle EF and FH to the rectangle EC and CB, and of the line AB to the line AH. And it is also the same as the compound ratio of the ratios of the rectangle FE, FD to the rectangle CE, CD; if through points E and D there passes a conic section which cuts the lines KN, KO, VN, VO, and cuts the lines AV, AP at points L, M, T, S, it is said that the compound ratio of the ratios of the rectangle PM, Pλ to the line Aλ, to the line AS, to the line SQ, is the same as the compound ratio of the ratios of the rectangle PL to the line LA, and of the line AT to the line TQ.

<margin>Fig. II. I.</margin> We will also demonstrate that if four straight lines AC, AF, EH, EL intersect at points N, P, M, O, and a conic section cuts the said lines at points C, B, E, D, H, G, L, K, the compound ratio of the ratios of the rectangle of MC and MB to the rectangle of the lines PE and PD, and of the rectangle of the lines AD and AF to the rectangle of the lines AB and AC, is the same as the compound ratio of the ratios of the rectangle of lines FK and FP to the rectangle of lines PH and PG, and of the rectangle of lines EH and EG to the rectangle of lines EK and EL.

<margin>Fig. I.</margin> We will also demonstrate this property, of which the first inventor is Mr. Desargues of Lyon, one of the great minds of this time, and among those most versed in Mathematics, especially in Conics, whose writings on this subject—though few in number—have given ample testimony to those who wished to receive understanding of them. I am happy to admit that I owe the little I have found on this subject to his writings, and that I have tried to imitate his method as much as possible, which is to treat the subject generally without [using] the axis. And treating generally of all conic sections, if on the edge of one, having taken the four points K, N, O, V, the lines KN, KO, VN, VO are drawn, such that through any one of these four points only two lines pass, and another line cuts the section at points R and γ, and the lines KN, KO, VN, VO at points s, r, δ, φ, it is said that as the rectangle of lines rR and γr is to the rectangle of lines rs and rφ, so the rectangle of lines δs and δφ is to the rectangle of lines xr and xγ.

<margin>Fig. II.</margin> We will also demonstrate that if in the plane of the hyperbola, or the ellipse, or the circle AGE, whose center is C, one draws the line AB touching the section at point A, and having drawn the diameter CA, one takes the line AB whose square is equal to the "rectangle of the figure" <note>The rectangle of the figure is a term related to the parameter or latus rectum of the conic.</note>, and one draws CB; then whatever line one draws, such as DE, parallel to the line AB, cutting the section at E, and the lines AC, CB at points D and F, [the relationship] will be equal to the square of the line AB; if the section AGE is an ellipse or a circle, the sum of the squares of lines DE and DF will be equal to the square of line AB; and in the hyperbola, the difference of these same squares of lines DE and DF will be equal to the square of line AB.

We will also deduce some problems, for example: from a given point, to draw a line touching a given conic section.
To find two conjugate diameters at a given angle.
To find two diameters at a given angle and in a given ratio.

We have several other Problems and Theorems and several consequences of the preceding ones, but the lack of confidence I have in my little experience and capacity does not permit me to put forward more before it has passed the examination of learned men, who might wish to do us the favor of taking the trouble; after which, if it is judged that the matter deserves to be continued, we shall attempt to push it as far as God gives us the strength to lead it.

->AT PARIS, 1640.<-

...tried to imitate, as much as has been possible for me, his method on this subject, which he treated without using the triangle through the axis <gloss>1. "Let there be an oblique cone with a circular base: the straight line drawn from its vertex to the center of the circle serving as its base is called the *axis of the cone*. The plane drawn through the axis perpendicular to the plane of the base cuts the cone along two edges and determines a diameter in the circle: the triangle having this diameter as its base and the two edges as its sides is called the *triangle through the axis*. Apollonius assumes, to form his conic sections, the cutting plane to be perpendicular to the plane of the triangle through the axis" (Chasles, *Historical overview of the origin and development of methods in Geometry*, 2nd Ed., p. 18). Desargues and Pascal, on the contrary, cut the generating cone by any plane whatsoever.</gloss>. And treating all conic sections <note>The curves formed by intersecting a cone with a plane: the circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.</note> generally, the marvelous property in question is as follows <gloss>2. # ESSAY ON CONICS

...the hyperbola or the ellipse, or the circle AGE, of which
the center is C, one draws the straight line AB, touching the
section at point A, and that having drawn the diameter
CA, one takes the straight line AB whose square
is equal to a quarter of the rectangle of the figure ¹, and that
one draws CB, then, whatever straight line one draws,
such as DE, parallel to the straight line AB, cutting the
section at E, and the straight lines AC, CB, at points D,
F: if the section AGE is an ellipse or a circle, the
sum of the squares of the straight lines DE, DF, will be equal
to the square of the straight line AB; and in the hyperbola, the
difference of the same squares of the straight lines DE, DF,
will be equal to the square of the straight line AB.

We shall also deduce some problems, for
example: From a given point, to draw a straight line touch-
ing a given Conic section. <note>In modern terms, this is the problem of constructing a tangent line to a curve from an external point.</note>

To find two conjugate diameters <note>Two diameters are "conjugate" when the tangent to the curve at the endpoint of one diameter is parallel to the other diameter.</note> at a given
angle.

To find two diameters at a given angle and in a
given ratio.

We have several other Problems and Theo-
rems, and several consequences of the preceding ones;
but the lack of confidence I have in my little experience
and capacity does not allow me to advance further...

---

1. For the square of the segment AB, supposed equal to DE + DF,
to be equal to a quarter of the circumscribed rectangle, the conic
section would have to be a circle. If the conic is an ellipse, AB must be
taken as equal to the axis which is perpendicular to CA. — <term>Desargues</term> <note>Girard Desargues (1591–1661), a French mathematician considered one of the founders of projective geometry.</note> had treated
similar questions in his <term>Draft Project</term> <note>Original title: *Brouillon Project d'une atteinte aux événemens des rencontres du cône avec un plan* (1639).</note> (Works of Desargues,
I, p. 202 and p. 284). It will be noted that the statements of Desargues and
<term>Pascal</term> lead immediately to the equation of conic sections.

# ON THE CONCEPTION OF THE VIRGIN, FOR THE PALINODS OF THE YEAR 1640, WHICH WON THE PRIZE OF THE TOWER¹.

## STANZAS

->*December 1640.*<-

Execrable authors of a false belief, <note>This likely refers to Protestants, who at the time challenged certain Catholic doctrines regarding the Virgin Mary.</note>
Whose hypocritical breast encloses a heart of gall,
Cast your weak eyes upon the Ark of the Covenant,
You will see it is like the Queen of Heaven.

Compare their beauties and their wondrous effects,
And then you will confess with submission
That the Mother of God, this Queen of Angels,
Can only be pure in her conception.

The one holds within her side the happiness of our fathers, <note>The Ark of the Covenant in the Old Testament contained the tablets of the Law, seen as a "happiness" or guide for the Israelites.</note>
And the other in hers, our most cherished hope; <note>The "other" is Mary, carrying Jesus.</note>
The one by her power turns aside their miseries,
And the other by hers keeps us from sinning.

---

1. The subject was mandated by the very statutes of the Confraternity of the Conception of the Virgin; the competition where Jacqueline triumphed had been established since the end of the fifteenth century. The <term>Prix de la Tour</term> <note>The Tower Prize, named after its benefactor's estate or office.</note> had just been founded there by the First President Groulart for the best stanza (See Faugère, *Letters, Opuscules, etc.* Appendix No. VI, p. 484-5). According to an indication I borrow from an interesting lecture by M. Frère on the session of the <term>Palinods</term> <note>The Palinods were famous poetic competitions held in Rouen in honor of the Virgin Mary.</note> of 1640 (p. 9), a manuscript text of Jacqueline’s poetry is found in the Archives of the Academy of Rouen, ms. no. 6, folio 142 verso.

<summary>This page contains a religious poem by Jacqueline Pascal, written for a traditional Rouen competition, using the biblical Ark of the Covenant as a metaphor for the Virgin Mary's purity. It marks a significant moment in her early career as a recognized poet before her eventual withdrawal into religious life at Port-Royal.</summary>

If the one has caused battles to be won many times
Because within its breast a treasure is hidden;
The other does no less, having in her womb <note>original: *entrailles*, literally "entrails" or "innards," used here to refer to the womb as a sacred vessel</note>
That which allows us to conquer and master sin.

The holy Ark, led into a place full of vice,
As soon as it arrives, overthrows the false gods;
It flees that dwelling, and considers it a torment
To inhabit a place so little cherished by the heavens.

If then a simple Ark, far less necessary,
Could not inhabit a profane place,
How would you think that this holy Mother,
If she were an impure temple, could be the temple of God?

# TO SAINT CECILIA

## EPIGRAM <note>An "epigram" in this period was a short, witty, or pointed poem, often concluding with a clever turn of thought.</note>

->*November 1640.*<-

Noble daughter of heaven, when your generous heart,
After having crossed a thousand dangerous steps,
Felt itself consumed by a divine flame,
Your transported spirit found its fire so sweet
That in an instant you wished to burn your husband with it; <note>This refers to the legend of Saint Cecilia, who converted her husband Valerian to Christianity on their wedding night.</note>
You gave him a good share of your soul's ardors;
And yet your zeal always went on increasing.
But let us cease to admire this holy adventure:
The fire that burned you is of such a nature
That the more one lavishes it, the more it is felt.

# THANKS
# FOR THE PRIZE FOR STANZAS, THE FOLLOWING YEAR

->*December 1641.*<-

Prince, <note>Likely referring to the Chancellor Séguier or another high-ranking patron of the literary competition.</note> whose goodness, equaling your merit,
Finds charms in the most paltry object,
Receiving a happiness I did not expect,
Allow my Muse to be moved in return.
I feel her movement; but, in this inspired fervor, <note>The original word *fureur* refers to "poetic fury," a classical concept where the poet is possessed by divine inspiration.</note>
My weakness cannot express my ardor,
Nor how deeply this favor touches me.
And yet I wish it to be known through my mouth
The feelings I have for the gift I have received.
As for you, in this honor of which my verses are unworthy,
You imitate Jesus whose signal kindnesses
Bind the mortals who have never seen him.

### SERENADE

Banish sleep, beautiful and chaste Clarice, <note>Clarice is a conventional name frequently used in 17th-century pastoral and courtly poetry to represent an idealized lady.</note>

->That your charms be blamed<-

And when virtue can subdue it to its will,

Whoever wishes to resist you is immediately the master,
And so little power accompanies your arrows,
That he who is not the victor simply chooses not to be.

### CONTINUATION OF THE STANZAS AGAINST LOVE

->TO MISS DE BEUVRON<sup>1</sup>, UPON SENDING HER THE PRECEDING VERSES<-

It is not that I wish, by these words, to imply
That there is no object capable of capturing us,
Or that all should be equally indifferent to us;
The beautiful eyes of Beuvron serve as our assurance
That some may be encountered who, without being tyrants,
Inspire feelings far removed from indifference.

# VERSES BY JACQUELINE PASCAL

It is true that those eyes are everywhere formidable;
It is true that their strikes, always inevitable,
Have found nothing in hearts that could resist them.
But do not boast, Love <note>original: "Amour." Jacqueline personifies Love here as the Greco-Roman god Cupid, who was often depicted as a tyrant over the human heart.</note>, of this glory;
Her eyes, though beautiful enough to conquer everything,
Owe to her virtue the honor of their victory.

Thus the divine arrows with which they wound souls
Owe nothing, Love, to the torments or the flames
In which you make your weak followers succumb.
With them, reason retains its function,
And it is by its advice that even the least yielding <note>original: "moins complaisans." In the 17th-century "Précieux" social circles, "complaisance" referred to a polite desire to please or accommodate others.</note>
Hold for them a respect that amounts to homage.

Cease, then, to claim dominion over the world:
It is to this beauty, who has no equal,
That the honor of conquering the universe is reserved.
Do not fight the infallible orders of fate,
And consider that in yielding to such varied charms,
One yields to the virtue that renders them invincible.

---

<vocab>Jacqueline Pascal, Love, virtue, beauty, dominion over the world</vocab>

<summary>In these concluding stanzas, Jacqueline Pascal argues that Mademoiselle de Beuvron's beauty is uniquely powerful because it is governed by virtue and reason, unlike the chaotic passion usually inspired by Cupid. She suggests that yielding to such beauty is an act of intellectual respect rather than a loss of self-control.</summary>

->From Rouen, this last Saturday of January, 1643.<-

It is quite certain, if that is the case, that your letters are being lost, for I do not receive even one every three weeks. Having returned to Rouen, I found a letter from M. Périer there, which says that you are ill. He does not say at all if your illness is dangerous, nor if you
