# ON THE APPARENT RECOVERY OF THE KING

## SONNET

### April 1643 <note>Louis XIII, who died on May 14, 1643, "remained six weeks and more, dying every day without being able to finish dying" (Madame de Motteville, *Memoirs*, Charpentier edition, vol. I, p. 95). Since April 20, he had established the regency and the council of regency; on the 23rd he had fallen, says historian M. Chéruel, "into such a state of weakness that it was believed he was about to expire." (*History of France during the minority of Louis XIV*, 1879, vol. I, p. 41). The following detail shows the impact of this "apparent recovery": Mademoiselle de Hautefort, in exile at Blois, had rushed to Paris with her servant La Porte; "so many people had gone there because of the change of reign which was believed to be near that we were there until eleven o'clock at night without finding lodging... the next day... we learned that the King was doing better, that he had had his beard trimmed, and that he was playing the guitar, so much so that we took the road back to Blois." (Cited by Victor Cousin, *Madame de Hautefort*, 2nd edition, p. 54 n. 1).</note>.

At last, vain grandeurs, you are powerless;
And this infinite number of so many courtiers
Could not prevent triumphant death
From carrying the finest of my years to the grave.

These small offshoots <note>The "offshoots" refer to the King's young sons: the Dauphin Louis (the future Louis XIV), born September 5, 1638, and Philippe, Duke of Anjou (who later became Duke of Orléans after the death of his uncle Gaston), born September 27, 1640.</note>, whose nascent virtue
Already carries dread even to the most powerful places,
Served only to mourn this apparent death
And make my sorrows more stinging as I left them.

### TO THE QUEEN ON THE REGENCY <note>Anne of Austria (1601–1666), the widow of Louis XIII, who became Regent for her son, the five-year-old Louis XIV.</note>

#### SONNET

->*May 1643.*<-

Begin, great Queen, a reign of wonders.
Since our happiness depends on you alone,
Sow your peerless virtues throughout the universe;
Make the greatest Kings jealous of your noble deeds.

Continue the cares of your divine vigils,
And let your kindness make known to everyone
That a thousand terrors struck our ears in vain
Concerning a government that you make so sweet. <note>There were widespread fears that a female-led regency would lead to political instability or weakness, especially given the ongoing pressures of the Thirty Years' War.</note>

Learn to respect your illustrious princess,
Whose divine spirit knows how to skillfully join
The sweetness of her sex to the strength of yours. <note>The poet argues that the Queen possesses both traditionally "feminine" grace and "masculine" political strength.</note>

## CONSOLATION ON THE DEATH OF A HUGUENOT WOMAN <note>A "Huguenot" was a French Protestant during the 16th and 17th centuries, a period marked by religious conflict and eventual state-mandated conversion to Catholicism.</note>

### STANZAS ^1

->*May 1645.*<-

Phillis, appease your sorrows;
You have shed enough tears
For the loss of your friend;
Cease this violent grief <note>original: "transport"; in 17th-century French, this referred to an intense, overwhelming state of emotion or passion.</note>
Which, by attacking your life,
Would deliver mine unto death.

Put an end to all these grievances;
Death is deaf to your sighs,
Just as she is blind to your tears.
Had heaven made her otherwise,
She would have respected such charms
Which she destroyed in a single moment.

But what? Nothing escapes here below.
Both ugliness and beauty <term>appas: physical charms or feminine attractiveness</term>
Feel her formidable blows;
The happy, the unfortunate,
The innocent and the guilty
Are destined for the same end.

Within her heart filled with piety.

Was to be faithful to you.
Alas! in her blindness,
Did you give her so much zeal
To lose her eternally?

# WORKS

to Chancellor Séguier <note>Pierre Séguier (1588–1672) was the Chancellor of France and a key patron who granted Pascal the exclusive rights to manufacture his calculator.</note>, all the difficulties he faced to realize his invention: early failures, damages caused by counterfeiters, and the clumsiness of the workers. “There is,” says Tallemant des Réaux <note>Gédéon Tallemant des Réaux (1619–1692) was a French writer known for his *Historiettes*, a collection of short biographies and anecdotes.</note> (*Historiettes*, 188-189), “only one worker in Rouen who knows how to make it (the arithmetic machine); and even then, Pascal must be present.”

The invention of the arithmetic machine solidified the scientific reputation of the young Pascal and sparked general interest. Roberval <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval, a prominent mathematician and friend of Pascal.</note> showed one to Descartes <note>René Descartes, the famous philosopher and mathematician; his meeting with Pascal in 1647 is a celebrated moment in scientific history.</note> for his admiration during the visit the latter paid to Pascal in September 1647 (see vol. II, p. 43 for the letter from Jacqueline Pascal <note>Blaise Pascal's younger sister, who later became a nun at Port-Royal.</note> to Mme Perier), and Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, a friar known as the "center of the scientific world" for his vast correspondence with thinkers like Galileo and Hobbes.</note> reported the discovery to Constantijn Huygens <note>A Dutch diplomat and poet, father of the scientist Christiaan Huygens.</note> (see below <note>original Latin: "vide infra"</note>, vol. II, p. 217). In 1650, Pascal himself offered one of his machines to Queen Christina of Sweden (see below <note>original Latin: "vide infra"</note>, vol. III, pp. 22-34); he also gave one to Carcavi <note>Pierre de Carcavi, a mathematician and royal librarian.</note> (see below <note>original Latin: "vide infra"</note>, vol. III, p. 377). Later, in 1659, Christiaan Huygens <note>The famous Dutch physicist and astronomer who improved the telescope and invented the pendulum clock.</note> wished to obtain a “Pascaline.” (This is how Brunetti refers to Pascal's machine in a letter addressed to Huygens: August 6, 1659, *Works of Huygens*, II, p. 451). On this occasion, he was put in contact with Charles Belair, a gentleman of the Duke of Luynes <gloss>1</gloss> who took it upon himself to send him the machine belonging to one of his friends through the intermediary of the bookseller Petit (See in the *Works of Huygens*, volume II, Belair’s letter of July 4, 1659, and the following letters). At the same time, to keep Huygens waiting, Belair sent him a description of Pascal’s machine, a description which we reproduce below in the appendix.

It is difficult to know how many machines were built based on Pascal's designs. Tallemant des Réaux tells us that some curious individuals had them constructed, and at least ten still exist today, both in the hands of private individuals and in public collections. The Museum of Arts and Crafts <note>The *Musée des Arts et Métiers* in Paris, a major repository for historical scientific instruments.</note> possesses four of these machines in various sizes. Two of these machines display six digits plus the *sous* and the *deniers* <term>sous and deniers: Units of French currency used before the decimal system; twelve deniers made a sou, and twenty sous made a livre (the equivalent of a pound).</term>; they bear escutcheons with Pascal’s coat of arms. The third machine displays six digits only, and the fourth displays four digits plus the *sous* and the *deniers*. The six-digit machine bears (inside the box) the following inscription, which appears to be in Pascal’s own hand: "Let this be the token of the proven instrument: Blaise Pascal of Auvergne, inventor, May 20, 1652" <note>original: "*Esto probati instrumenti symbolum hoc : Blasius Pascal Arvernus inventor*, 20 mai 1652". A sixth is located at the museum of Clermont-Ferrand, as we were informed by a kind communication from Mr. Elie Jaloutre: it bears the escutcheon of Pascal's arms.

One will find a description of Pascal’s machine in the collection titled *Machines and Inventions Approved by the Royal Academy of Sciences*, volume IV, 1735, p. 137. Another description was given by Diderot <note>Denis Diderot (1713–1784), the chief editor of the *Encyclopédie*.</note> in the *Encyclopedia* and reproduced in the edition by Bossut <note>Charles Bossut (1730–1814) was a mathematician who edited an important 18th-century edition of Pascal's works.</note>.

---

Pascal’s arithmetic machine is probably the first adding machine to have ever been built. The only calculating instruments in use before Pascal's invention were Napier’s multipliers (*bones*) <term>Napier’s bones: Invented by John Napier (1550–1617), these were numbered rods used to perform multiplication and division through addition and subtraction of digits.</term>, which relied on a different principle and still required a certain amount of mental effort. # DEDICATORY LETTER TO THE CHANCELLOR

In his *Rhabdology* <note>original: *Rhabdologia* (1617); a treatise by John Napier describing calculating aids using numbered rods</note> (Edinburgh, 1617), the devices described under the name *promptuaria* <note>original Latin: "storehouses" or "handy-books"; refers to a calculating apparatus using multiple rods</note> were perfected during the 17th century by various scholars, notably Gaspard Schott, Grillet, and Petit¹ [(See the list provided by Roth: *Bulletin of the Society for the Encouragement of National Industry*, 1843, p. 415)].

An adding machine, which somewhat resembles Pascal's but appears to have been designed independently, was built by Samuel Morland in 1673 (see the note by Roth, cited above). On the other hand, Grillet (See *The Mathematical Curiosities of Monsieur Grillet*) and Leibniz—both inventors of adding machines—were familiar with Pascal’s machine and drew inspiration from it.

It is also possible that other arithmetic machines were built in the 17th century whose history remains unknown to us. The National Conservatory of Arts and Crafts <note>A major French museum of technological innovation</note> possesses two machines, of unknown authorship, which are similar to Pascal’s machine while remaining distinct from it. Furthermore, among the papers of Roberval <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval, a prominent French mathematician</note> (National Library: New French Acquisitions, 5175), there is an (admittedly obscure) description of an arithmetic machine that is also not the one by Pascal.

# ADVICE
## Necessary for those who have the curiosity to see the Arithmetic Machine, and to use it.

Dear reader, this notice will serve to let you know that I am presenting to the public a small <term>Machine</term> <note>This refers to the Pascaline, the first mechanical calculator, invented by Blaise Pascal in the 1640s.</note> of my invention, by means of which alone you will be able, without any trouble, to perform all the operations of arithmetic, and relieve yourself of the labor that has so often fatigued your mind when you have worked with <term>counters</term> <note>original: "jetton" — small tokens or coins used on a manual counting board, a common calculation method before the widespread use of written algorithms.</note> or with a pen. I may, without presumption, hope that it will not displease you, after **MY LORD THE CHANCELLOR** <note>This refers to Pierre Séguier (1588–1672), the Chancellor of France and a patron who protected Pascal's rights to the invention.</note> has honored it with his esteem, and after those in Paris most well-versed in mathematics have not judged it unworthy of their approval. Nonetheless, so as not to appear negligent in seeking to gain your approval as well, I believed I was obliged to enlighten you on all the difficulties that I judged capable of troubling your senses when you take the trouble to consider it.

->I — 20<-

Now (dear READER), I judge it necessary to warn you that I foresee two things capable of forming some clouds in your mind. I know that there are many people who make a profession of finding fault everywhere, and that among those there may be found some who will tell you that this **Machine** could have been less complex; this is the first vapor that I judge necessary to dissipate. This proposition can only be made to you by certain minds who truly have some knowledge of <term>Mechanics</term> <note>The study of forces and their effect on matter.</note> or <term>Geometry</term> <note>The mathematical study of shapes and proportions.</note>, but who, because they do not know how to join one to the other, and both together with <term>Physics</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Physics" referred to natural philosophy and the study of the material world and its constraints.</note>, flatter or deceive themselves in their imaginary conceptions, and persuade themselves that many things are possible which are not, because they possess only an imperfect **Theory** of things in general, which is not sufficient to make them foresee in particular the inconveniences that arise, either from the nature of the matter, or from the spaces that the parts of a **Machine** must occupy whose movements are different, so that they may be free and not obstruct one another. Therefore, when these imperfect <term>scholars</term> <note>original: "sçavans" — learned men or experts.</note> suggest to you that this **Machine** could have been less complex, I entreat you to give them the response that I would make myself if they made such a proposal to me, and to assure them on my behalf that I will show them, whenever they please, several other **models**, and even an entire and perfect instrument, much less complex, which I have publicly used

Finally (dear reader), now that I consider it to have been put in a state to be seen, and that you even can—if you have the curiosity—see it and use it, I beg you to accept the liberty I take in hoping that the mere thought of finding a third method for performing all arithmetic operations, one totally new and which has nothing in common with the two common methods of the pen <note>Manual calculation performed by writing numbers on paper.</note> and the token <note>original: "jetton." A traditional method of calculating using physical counters on a gridded board or cloth.</note>, will receive from you some esteem. I hope that in approving the design I had to please you by relieving your burden, you will be grateful for the care I took to ensure that all operations—which by the previous methods are laborious, complex, long, and uncertain—become easy, simple, fast, and sure.

**Those curious individuals who wish to see such a Machine should apply, if they please, to Master *Roberval*, Ordinary Professor of Mathematics at the Royal College of France, who will briefly and gratuitously demonstrate the ease of the Operations, will arrange for their sale, and will teach their use.**

**The said Master Roberval resides at the Master Gervais College, Rue du Foing, near the *Mathurins*¹. He can be found every morning until eight o'clock, and on Saturdays the whole afternoon.**

# APPENDIX

## EXPLANATION OF MR. PASCAL’S MACHINE, BY WHICH ARITHMETIC IS PERFORMED <gloss>1</gloss>

->(ADDRESSED BY CH. BELAIR TO CHRISTIAAN HUYGENS, IN 1659)<-

The one I have in my hands is only for whole numbers. It can only extend as far as the tens of thousands: that is to say, the largest number it can show is 99,999.

Externally, this machine appears like a small brass casing bordered at the top and bottom by two small ebony moldings, and supported on four small ebony feet <note>original: "pommes," literally apples, referring to the spherical shape of the wooden feet.</note>.

The sheet marked **First Figure** <gloss>2</gloss> shows the size of the top of this casing and what is visible there.

The letters A, B, C, D, E mark five circles that are slightly raised, on each of which the digits are written; these circles are fixed.

Inside these circles, the letters F, G, H, I, K mark as many wheels, each of which has 10 notches <note>original: "crans." These are the teeth of the internal gears that the user interacts with.</note>. Each notch (when the wheel is left to move freely) always settles opposite one of the digits.

These wheels are turned against the order of the digits (for they cannot move in the other direction) by placing a small stylus <note>original: "petit baston," a small rod used to rotate the wheels, similar to a dial-phone interface.</note> into whichever notch one desires. One never makes them perform a full rotation without lifting the stylus, because one encounters the fixed piece marked L along the way.

Wheel F is for units <note>original: "les nombres." In this context, it refers to the first column of digits.</note>; wheel G is for tens, etc.

<note>2. This First Figure, reduced in the facsimile opposite, is approximately 26 cm by 13 cm.</note>

   But it should be noted that the small part H ☿ ♈︎ ♉︎ is mobile on the axis ♓, that it is pressed by a spring Δ ♃ which always pushes it toward the center, and that this part—sliding by its concave section ♈︎ Λ over the points of the wheel which, in the **tens mechanism**, is similar to wheel *l* in the **units mechanism** <note>original: "machine des nombres" — referring here to the first wheel assembly representing units.</note>—always has its end H ♈︎ resting against one of the teeth of the said wheel. This ensures that when the entire part falls by its own **weight**, this end H ♈︎ pushes this second wheel forward by one notch. There are four parts like this one.
   The first rests on the units mechanism and serves to push the tens mechanism. The second rests on the tens mechanism and pushes the hundreds. The third rests on the hundreds and pushes the thousands. And the fourth rests on the thousands and pushes the ten-thousands. 
   From this it follows that when all these parts are raised and ready to fall (which happens when all the 9s appear in the addition windows), if one adds 1—that is to say, if one moves the units wheel F of the first figure by one notch—all these parts, falling one after another, very quickly transmit this movement from the first wheel all the way to the last. And instead of all the 9s that were showing, zeros appear in their place. <note>This describes the "ripple carry," the most innovative feature of Pascal's machine, where the energy for multiple carries is stored by gravity to prevent the mechanism from jamming.</note>

# INTRODUCTION

In October 1646, a chance visit received by his father in Rouen opened a new horizon to Blaise Pascal’s curiosity. The research he then undertook occupied him until the eve of his final conversion: the Latin memoir of 1654 <note>original: *Vide supra*, t. III, p. 308 (See above, volume 3, page 308)</note> mentions the upcoming printing of a *Treatise on the Vacuum*. Regarding these investigations—which secure for Pascal an important place in the history of barometry <note>The science of measuring atmospheric pressure</note> and an exceptional place in the history of hydrostatics <note>The study of the mechanics of fluids at rest</note>—what exactly were the initial circumstances? How was the first experiment performed, of which the Pascal family were witnesses in Rouen? What relationship did it have with the father’s philosophical opinions, and what reflections did it provoke in the son? To these questions, a letter written in the form of a "formal report" <note>original: "procez-verbal"</note> on November 19, 1646, by the very author of that first Rouen experiment, Pierre Petit, responds with all necessary precision.

Petit, born in Montluçon on December 8, 1594, had been provincial commissioner of Artillery and the King's engineer before becoming Intendant of Fortifications. He played a significant role in the scientific life of the 17th century, as evidenced by his intervention in the controversy sparked by Descartes' *Dioptrics* <note>A groundbreaking work on the laws of refraction and optics</note> (See *Works of Descartes*, edited by *Adam and Tannery*, particularly the letter of March 16, 1638, to Mersenne, vol. II, pp. 86, 90, and 96).

> "He was," says Baillet, "a young man with a great genius for mathematics, who excelled particularly in Astronomy, and who had a specific passion for things where knowledge depends upon experiments." (*Life of Mr. Descartes*, 1691, vol. I, p. 326.)

He was primarily associated with Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a philosopher and scientist who sought to reconcile atomism with Christian thought</note>, for whom he was a collaborator at that time, and who spoke of Petit with warm praise

<summary>This introduction details the origins of Blaise Pascal's scientific interest in atmospheric pressure and the vacuum, highlighting a 1646 visit from the engineer Pierre Petit as the catalyst for his research.</summary>

Petit’s letter is addressed to Chanut, who had just left the treasury of Riom, his birthplace, a few months earlier to take over in Stockholm the position held by La Thuillerie, who had been sent as ambassador to Holland<gloss>1</gloss>. II, pp. 411 and 435).

In October 1647, when the dissertation of the Capuchin Magni arrived—which seemed to claim credit for the invention of the <term>quicksilver experiment</term> <note>the early name for the mercury barometer experiment</note> after Pascal had published a *Summary of his Experiments*—Marc-Antoine Dominicy<gloss>2</gloss> had Petit’s letter printed. The goal of its publication is clearly explained in a notice *To the Reader*: “It will be seen that the glory of the invention belongs to Italy, and in my opinion to that admirable Philosopher and Mathematician Galileo, and not to Torricelli; likewise, the honor of having first observed it in France cannot be disputed with Monsieur Petit. After the news of it had arrived, the most curious had tried it in vain, and after their failures, two or three years had passed without it being spoken of further.... To avoid risking the glory for which he might not be given his due in this dispute—which, having begun in Italy, was renewed by him in France, then

### LETTER FROM PIERRE PETIT TO CHANUT

[recom]mended in the North, and now sent back to Poland, as a very new thing (where it might have been carried by a French Gentleman, who was making the journey there, to whom Monsieur Petit shared it) or because in this innocent war <note>a metaphorical "war of ideas" or scientific dispute</note> which seems to be igniting across all of Europe, people will perhaps only say and repeat in substance what has already been noted by him at the heart of the question—as the aforementioned Capuchin <note>Valeriano Magni (1586–1661), a monk who published a work in 1647 claiming he had discovered the vacuum independently of Torricelli</note> has done, and as has often happened to him in other encounters, due to the ease with which he shares his thoughts. I believe I am fulfilling what is owed to the truth when I now publish, against his intention (but under the approval of the most equitable Protector of sciences and virtue who has ever lived¹) this letter. I can swear that the author prevented me from having it printed more than six months ago because, he told me, one of his most intimate friends <note>Almost certainly referring to Blaise Pascal, who was perfecting his own experiments at the time</note> had greatly improved upon these first observations, and who would have many beautiful things to say, treating the whole matter worthily and thoroughly; he felt that a simple letter written casually, and with no other purpose than to be carried to Sweden and seen by a friend, should not be exposed to the eyes of a public that values nothing unless it is entirely perfect. Furthermore, there were many things in the said letter that were not on this subject, and which concerned only the praises of the Queen of Sweden <note>Queen Christina, a famous patron of science and philosophy</note>, or the merit of her Ambassador, and other social matters <note>original: *galanteries*</note> regarding ballets and books. But all these reasons no longer apply to my situation, now that I see the Lyceum and the academies <note>traditional schools of philosophy and the newer scientific societies</note> stirring themselves for this cause, and that it is being spoken of from one Kingdom to another. In order that the progress and the truth of the history of this experiment may at least be known, I present to everyone’s eyes this authentic piece, of which I took a copy from the one the author sent to Monsieur Pascal, to make him a participant in his thoughts and reasoning just as he had been in the experiment itself.

# INTRODUCTION

The *Account* that we are publishing appears in the manuscript collection of the *National Library, French fund 12,449*, <note>The *Bibliothèque Nationale de France* (National Library) uses "French fund" (*fonds français*) to categorize its vast collection of French-language manuscripts.</note> which contains a copy of the *Pensées*; <note>The *Pensées* (Thoughts) is Blaise Pascal’s most famous work, a collection of fragments on theology and philosophy published posthumously.</note> it is accompanied by the autograph signature of Blaise Pascal; it cannot fail to find a place in a complete edition of his works. Yet it only indirectly concerns Pascal. We can determine neither the part he took in drafting the report—which appears to be written in the hand of Hallé de Monflaines—nor the role he played in the conference itself. We only see that before his arrival, there was already heated debate regarding the relationship between reason and faith. We believe we can also guess, from a few characteristic features, the moments when Pascal is before us. Thus, the insistence on highlighting the irrationality of the transmission of original sin <note>Original sin refers to the Christian doctrine of humanity's state of sin resulting from the fall of Adam and Eve.</note> foreshadows the conference that Pascal was to hold at Port Royal <note>Port Royal was a famous abbey and a center of the Jansenist movement, with which Pascal was deeply involved.</note> some twelve years later; the offer to calculate what resources the matter of the earth could provide for the successive production of human generations heralds the considerations by which, at the end of the *Treatise on the Weight of the Mass of Air*, Pascal evaluates the weight of the Earth's atmosphere.

What we know quite well, on the other hand, are the incidents that took place between the conferences themselves in early February 1647, and the signing of the account that reports their details at the end of April and the middle of May—incidents that led the Archbishop of Rouen <note>Rouen is a major city in Normandy; at this time, Pascal's family lived there while his father served as a tax official.</note> to open a formal proceeding against the interlocutor of Pascal and his friends. The manuscript of the National Library, 20,945 (item 12, folio 130) and the ninth Conrart collection <note>Named after Valentin Conrart, a founding member of the *Académie Française* who kept extensive records of literary and religious life.</note> at the Arsenal (4114, pp. 165-264) contain interesting documents in this regard; they were published for the first [time...]

The editor notes that while Pascal didn't write the whole report, his intellectual influence is visible in arguments about original sin and scientific calculations.</summary>

Jacques Forton, a native of the diocese of Le Mans and a doctor of theology from the University of Bourges, had been a professed monk at the Capuchin <note>The Capuchins are a reform branch of the Franciscan order of friars.</note> monasteries of Paris and Rouen; in religion, he had taken the name of Brother Saint-Ange. He was the author of a work intended to span three volumes: *Conduct of Natural Judgment where all good minds of both sexes may easily draw the purity of their knowledge* (in three parts, 1637, 1641, 1645: *National Library*, 8º R. 10 945-6 and *Mazarine Library* 12 050). In Paris, within the Academy of the Viscountess d'Auchy—a circle frequented by the poet Malherbe and where the philosopher Campanella <note>Tommaso Campanella was an Italian philosopher and theologian known for his defense of Galileo and his work *The City of the Sun*.</note> was a guest during his stay in France—Saint-Ange had held conferences that had achieved some renown, but which also earned him several inconveniences, specifically of the kind that awaited him in Rouen.

> “To complete,” writes Tallemant des Réaux <note>Gédéon Tallemant des Réaux was a 17th-century writer famous for his *Historiettes*, a collection of short biographical sketches and anecdotes about his contemporaries.</note>, who dedicated his 28th article to Madame d’Auchy, “the history of the Academy of the Viscountess d'Auchy, I will say that l'Esclache,¹ who teaches philosophy in French, spoke there often. This inspired a man named Saint-Ange—who claimed, as he said, to prove the Trinity by natural reason, and who tutored young children in philosophy and theology so they could answer in French—to introduce himself to the Viscountess as well.

### ACCOUNT OF TWO CONFERENCES

“Several people, both men and women, went to hear his parrots <note>original: "perroquets"; a mocking term for students who merely repeated their teacher's lessons by rote.</note>; but the Archbishop of Paris, having by chance some business with the Viscountess, happened to be there one day while Saint-Ange and his little disciples were babbling. L’Esclache <note>Louis de Lesclache (c. 1620–1671) was a grammarian and philosopher who taught "philosophy in French" to fashionable society.</note>, being a bit jealous, got into an argument with this man; this hardly pleased the Archbishop, to whom someone pointed out—for I am certain he would have seen nothing on his own—that during the dispute, some errors concerning religion had been put forward, and that furthermore, it was hardly proper. He therefore said to the Viscountess as he was leaving that he advised her to leave theology to the Sorbonne <note>The Sorbonne was the prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris and the supreme authority on Catholic orthodoxy in France.</note>, and to be content with other types of conferences. And when the Viscountess showed him that this surprised her, the Archbishop of Paris, after having strongly urged her to stop these disputes and seeing that he could not bring her to reason, was forced to forbid such assemblies in the future¹.”

Tallemant’s account is undated; we do not know if Jacques Forton’s arrival in Rouen—where he had already been previously—was linked to the prohibition issued by the Archbishop of Paris, Jean François de Gondi. However, it is not without interest to note that this arrival coincided with a measure that the new Prosecutor General of the Parliament <note>The "Parlements" in Ancien Régime France were provincial appellate courts, not legislative bodies.</note>, Louis Courtin, had just taken on December 14th. This measure summoned “those members of the cathedral chapter who were simultaneously parish priests and canons to choose between their prebends <note>A prebend was a portion of the cathedral's revenues granted to a canon as a stipend.</note> and their parishes,” and enjoined all parish priests to maintain their residency. It was in the house of this very Prosecutor that Jacques Forton had taken up residence; it seems probable that he hoped to obtain, through the influence of his friend, one of the parishes that were about to become vacant in the diocese of Rouen. In fact, at the very moment he was being referred to the archiepiscopal council through the initiative of Pascal and his friends, he was presented by Jean—

<header>WORKS</header>

Baptiste Richelieu, commendatory abbot <note>A "commendatory abbot" was a person (sometimes a layman or secular priest) who held the title and drew the revenues of an abbey without necessarily living there or following the monastic rule.</note> of Saint-Ouen of Rouen, for the parish of Crosville.

This is the individual whom Blaise Pascal, assisted by Auzoult <note>Adrien Auzout (1622–1691), a famed astronomer and physicist who collaborated with Pascal on vacuum experiments.</note> and du Mesnil <note>Raoul Hallé, Sieur du Mesnil, a friend of the Pascal family in Rouen.</note>, and supported by his father, pursued for two months with the stubborn rigidity that was the hallmark of his family and his character. We need not investigate, as Pascal's historians have done, to what extent Saint-Ange <note>The pseudonym of Jacques Forton, the priest and philosopher whose unconventional teachings sparked this controversy.</note> justified this long and tenacious hostility. If the rationalism of his theology led him to encounter formulas that remind one of certain views later held by Leibniz <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), a philosopher known for trying to reconcile faith and reason through logic.</note>, the subtle and sometimes whimsical form in which he dressed his original metaphysics was closer to being ridiculous than seductive or dangerous; and one can see in more than one passage of the interview that this nuance did not escape his interlocutors in Rouen. 

But the manner of teaching that he boasted—with some imprudence—to have made fashionable, struck directly at Pascal's religious scruples. When Saint-Ange is abruptly questioned on the burning issue of the antagonism between Jesuits and Jansenists <note>The defining religious conflict of 17th-century France, pitting the Jesuits (focusing on free will and divine grace) against the Jansenists (emphasizing predestination and moral rigor).</note>, they do not forgive him for evading the question by rising to a "superior point of view" where opposites are reconciled, and where error is nothing more than an arbitrary limitation of one's horizon. (It is true, however, that Pascal would later remember this theory, and it would become fundamental to the structure of his *Apology* <note>Referring to Pascal's unfinished masterpiece, the *Pensées*, intended as an *Apology for the Christian Religion*.</note>). And when his questioners insist—as disconcerted by the bold thesis of what would become "the identity of contradictories" as they were anxious to know if they had before them a friend or an enemy—they forgive him even less for the casualness with which he extricates himself by invoking the pagan fable of Orpheus <note>The legendary Greek musician; Saint-Ange likely used the myth as an allegory to avoid taking a hard theological stance.</note>.

Consider now that one of the characteristics of the spiritual renewal attempted by Saint-Cyran <note>Jean Duvergier de Hauranne, Abbot of Saint-Cyran (1581–1643), the primary influence behind the Jansenist movement at Port-Royal.</note>—the one through which he immediately gained the most influence over French Catholicism—was the reform of the national clergy. It was his insistence on recalling the eminent dignity of the priesthood and the agonizing, almost crushing responsibility that the priest assumed toward the faithful. # ACCOUNT OF TWO CONFERENCES

Four years earlier, Father Maignart, of the Oratory <note>The Oratory of Jesus was a society of secular priests known for its focus on education and spiritual rigor.</note>, had abruptly resigned from the parish of Sainte-Croix-Saint-Ouen to obey the scruples that a conversation with Saint-Cyran <note>Jean du Vergier de Hauranne, Abbot of Saint-Cyran, a major influence on the Jansenist movement and a proponent of strict moral conscience.</note> had awakened in his conscience. One can understand, then, why Pascal—once the nomination of Jacques Forton to a parish in Normandy was proposed—refused any compromise and pushed his efforts with the Archbishop of Rouen to the absolute limit.

We know of this action through the official records of the legal proceedings, and also through the curious correspondence between the Archbishop and Camus, the Bishop of Belley. François de Harlay had occupied the see of Rouen for some thirty years (he was to resign it five years later in favor of his nephew, François Harlay de Champvallon, the future Archbishop of Paris and future persecutor of Port-Royal); he was ill and had retired to Gaillon. Camus, the disciple of Saint Francis de Sales and one of the most prolific writers of the century<gloss>1</gloss>, served as his coadjutor <note>An assistant bishop appointed to aid or succeed a diocesan bishop.</note>. Clearly, to Camus, the Saint-Ange affair was of no great importance; he sought only to close the incident in the simplest and quickest manner. But every time Camus believed he could announce an agreement that would clear Jacques Forton, Pascal, Auzoult, and Dumesnil would rush to Gaillon—both to justify their good faith and to renew their accusations. The Archbishop, whether for doctrinal reasons or for fear of increasing the divide between political and religious factions, forced Camus to reopen the investigation until the requirements of the most rigorous formalists were satisfied.

Here now are the various phases of the procedure, along with their dates.

I. — First of all, following the various rumors circulating in the city regarding the lectures of Jacques Forton and the stir they caused within the world of Parliament and the clergy, Camus questioned Jacques Forton and sent him to explain himself in person before the Archbishop’s council. Camus, who presided over this council, seems to have immediately accepted Jacques Forton’s explanations; Forton was merely invited to repeat them before the Archbishop at Gaillon, and on March 13, 1647, "the vicar general Gaude officially received the presentation of Saint-Ange to the parish he was seeking¹."

But Pascal intervened with his friends; as early as March 15, the Archbishop of Rouen informed Camus of both the meaning and the result of this intervention: "This is not a matter to be dismissed lightly <note>The original French 'estourdir' suggests brushing a matter aside or treating it as a trifle.</note>: things have gone too far. It could very well involve the Prosecutor General <term>Procureur général</term> <note>The highest-ranking legal officer in the regional Parliament.</note> who protects the man under accusation and those of our Priests who are said to favor them under the impression that the canons and the monks are meddling; for in these times the Council of Conscience <note>A powerful committee advising the King of France on the distribution of ecclesiastical benefices and religious matters.</note> and the Bastille <note>The infamous state prison in Paris, used here to suggest the threat of royal arrest.</note> reach very far; that is why, as much for them as for us, and more for God and his Church and the people scandalized by the renunciation of the habit <note>original: 'defroquement'. Jacques Forton was a former Capuchin monk who had left his order, a fact used against his character.</note>, the accusation, and the nomination of the Lord of Saint-Ange, let us hold the balance high and even. He has departed, with Mr. Bachelet who assists him on behalf of the Prosecutor General, quite satisfied with me. But Messrs. Pascal the younger <note>Blaise Pascal, as distinguished from his father, Étienne.</note>, de Montflaines, and Auzoult, who followed him, maintain that it is a manifest deception <note>original: 'imposition'.</note> that it was claimed he refused to sign the articles, and that you and the Prosecutor General, who believed him, have been deceived. I have made them resolve to see him to inform him, in the presence of the said Lord of Saint-Ange, of the entire fact, and notably of that point so that he may bring order to it through his prudence, and to consider the means of satisfying the Church scandalized by this rumor; otherwise, they are to make their declaration before you, in my council, for which a formal record shall be delivered to them as well as to the said Lord of Saint-Ange, whom I had..."

II. — The second act of the procedure consists, therefore, in demanding an official declaration from Saint-Ange <note>Saint-Ange was the name used by Jacques Forton, a priest whose theological views were being challenged by Blaise Pascal and his associates in Rouen.</note>. The latter complies with a rather bad grace, referring back to the third part of the *Conduct of Natural Judgment*. These are his own words:

->RESPONSES TO THE PROPOSITIONS THAT SOME HAVE ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT-ANGE, UNDER THIS TITLE: PROPOSITIONS ADVANCED IN TWO PRIVATE CONFERENCES.<-

> "Although these propositions are not admissible, as I have neither preached, dogmatized, nor taught in the city of Rouen; and even though these words—*advanced in two private conferences*—constitute more than half of my justification, since private conversations, especially between people who have never met before, serve more as reciprocal tests of each person’s ability than as a profession of faith, and since one is not obliged to give a public account of what transpires in private; it is nevertheless glorious and advantageous for a Priest and a Doctor <term>Doctor</term> <note>In this context, a "Doctor" refers to a scholar who has attained the highest academic degree in theology, authorized to teach the faith.</note> to make known his orthodox doctrine, especially when some wish to strike a blow against it, as is seen now. This is why I felt obliged to respond; and following the example of Jesus Christ, who, when questioned about His disciples and His doctrine, referred His interrogators to His disciples and to what He had taught publicly: *I have spoken openly* <note>original Latin: "Ego palam locutus sum". A reference to the Gospel of John 18:20.</note>, I am convinced that I can provide no better response to the propositions where I am made to speak than by pointing out that I published the opposite in my book, which bears the title: *Theological Meditations*, printed with appro—

<summary>Jacques Forton (Saint-Ange) responds to accusations of heresy by arguing that his private conversations do not constitute formal teaching and by asserting his orthodoxy through his published works.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological proceedings against Jacques Forton (known as Saint-Ange). On the previous page, Forton began his defense by arguing that his private conversations should not be treated as formal professions of faith, preferring to be judged by his published writings.</meta>

<page-num>356</page-num>
<header>WORKS</header>

...approval of doctors and royal privilege <note>A "privilege" was a legal monopoly and authorization granted by the King to publish a book, ensuring it had been vetted for orthodoxy.</note>, in the year 1645, which ought to be more faithful witnesses of my thoughts and my doctrine than the ears and the minds of those who have provided them in writing..."

There follow the *Suspect Propositions* and the "*Contradictory Responses to the first four propositions in the very words of my book, pages 2 and 3 of the preface, etc.*"

All of this concludes with these words: 
> "Yet it is a joy for me to be able to respond by the same doctrine that I have always taught, professed, and submitted to the Church and to the correction of the doctors who, being capable of penetrating and conceiving the mysteries of religion and faith, would have the kindness to instruct me; and I protest once more by these presents that I submit all my thoughts and my discourses to the censure of the apostolic and Roman Church, in faith of which I have signed them with my hand.
> 
->*Signed*: J. **Forton**,<-
->*Unworthy priest, called* **de Saint-Ange**,<-
->*with a flourish.* <note>A "paraphe" or flourish is a decorative stroke made with the pen after a signature to prevent forgery.</note><-

Camus <note>Jean-Pierre Camus was the Bishop of Belley and a friend of the Archbishop of Rouen; he acted as a mediator in this dispute.</note> wrote to his Archbishop (dated March 20 or 21, 1647): 
> "My Lord, after much advice and trouble, here finally is the declaration we have had Monsieur de Saint-Ange make in your council, according to your orders, of which we send you the copy for your judgment. I have had all words struck out that might cause offense, and have allowed only simple and modest terms to remove all occasion for those who seek it to continue such a tiresome altercation, from which, in my opinion, no edification can come—the Apostle <note>Referring to Saint Paul.</note> teaching us that those who bite and devour one another consume and destroy each other, besides the great offenses against God that multiply in these disputes, *not in strife and envying...* <note>original: "non in contentione et æmulatione..." — A quote from Romans 13:13 in the Latin Vulgate.</note>"
